Mechanistically, the ssDNA backbone demonstrated favorable biocompatibility, without exacerbating autoimmune phenotypes or inducing Toll-like receptor-mediated signaling pathways. In conclusion, this study establishes a robust proof-of-concept for pathology-targeted PET/CT imaging of immune complex deposition. By directly visualizing the disease-driving renal autoantibody deposition at the preclinical stage, prior to overt organ damage, this strategy shifts LN diagnosis to non-invasive, mechanism-based molecular visualization.

articles.title: Physics-informed and data-efficient machine learning for storm surge forecasting during typhoons
articles.abstract: This study addresses the challenge of accurately forecasting storm surges during tropical cyclones, which is crucial in reducing coastal damages. We develop a physics-informed and data-efficient model, a storm surge neural network (SSNN), that embeds shallow water equations into a machine learning (ML) framework with a specifically designed piecewise loss function to effectively incorporate physical constraints. The SSNN is iteratively trained to make rolling forecast and can produce more accurate forecasts than a standard data-driven model even with a smaller size of training data. The improvement in the performance by the SSNN model is evident, particularly in coastal areas with varying strong winds. This is especially true for forecasts beyond 16 hours, where the data-driven model struggles to provide accurate predictions. Combining physics with ML could offer a promising way to improve storm surge forecasting and support coastal hazard preparedness.

articles.title: Raising mountains for a habitable Earth
articles.abstract: The formation of mountain belts (orogens) elevates rocks above sea level, making them available for chemical weathering and altering the composition of the atmosphere and oceans, which in turn control habitability. Peak-metamorphic pressures recorded by crustal rocks buried in orogens increased between 2.7 to 2.2 and 0.8 to 0.7 billion years ago, indicating that rocks could be buried deeper and that orogens could grow substantially thicker after each of these periods. The two periods of orogenic growth were broadly synchronous with major increases in terrigenous element and nutrient fluxes and changes in biological sulfur metabolism and surface oxygenation. These changes could be explained by enhanced weathering of higher mountains. The findings support the hypothesis that there are first-order mechanistic links between secular geodynamic change and changes in Earth system state and habitability, which shaped the conditions for the evolution of complex life during the past 3 billion years.

articles.title: Single-nucleus multiomic profiling uncovers epigenetic dysregulation driving hippocampal vulnerability in Alzheimer’s disease
articles.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) exhibits region- and cell-type–specific vulnerability, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. We performed integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of human hippocampus to resolve gene regulatory architecture in AD. By linking chromatin accessibility to transcription, we identified more than 1000 disease-associated cis-regulatory interactions, highlighting coordinated epigenomic-transcriptomic remodeling. Excitatory cornu ammonis (EX.CA) neurons exhibited disproportionate regulatory disruption, characterized by increased chromatin accessibility coupled to activation of apoptosis-related gene programs, whereas dentate gyrus (EX.DG) neurons remained comparatively resistant. In glial cells, regulatory network inference revealed activation of transcription factor modules centered on SPI1/KLF4 in microglia and STAT3 in astrocytes, defining epigenetic programs that are highly associated with inflammatory and metabolic state transitions. Comparative evaluation with the prefrontal cortex uncovered conserved inflammatory activation alongside region-specific immune regulatory divergence, indicating spatially distinct microglial responses. Furthermore, cross-species integration demonstrated that a substantial fraction of AD-associated regulatory elements are human-specific, with AD-risk variants enriched in microglial cis-regulatory elements at loci including BIN1 and APOE . Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking chromatin remodeling to cell-type–specific dysfunction and reveal human-specific regulatory architecture as a crucial factor to AD vulnerability and translational limitation.

articles.title: Structural and biochemical insight into allosteric regulation of the human 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase
articles.abstract: Multiple clinically relevant inborn errors of metabolism occur in lysine degradation, yet the regulation of this biochemical pathway remains poorly understood. The initial rate-limiting step of lysine catabolism is catalyzed by the bifunctional enzyme 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS). Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the full-length 400-kilodalton tetrameric AASS enzyme complex with substrates and products bound to both the lysine-2-oxoglutarate (LOR) and saccharopine dehydrogenase (SDH) catalytic domains. We also identified allosteric compounds that modulate the activity of AASS by reacting with cysteine-414 and shifting the pH optimum for biochemical activity. The mutagenesis of this allosteric Cys 414 has marked effects on the enzyme’s conformation and activity despite being more than 12 angstrom from the active site. We find that small changes near the hinge of an enzyme can have large effects on its catalytic properties. Last, targeting allosteric cysteines may be a general strategy for modulating enzyme activity by altering the dynamics of the enzyme.

articles.title: Swarm-inspired magnetic metal-organic framework-based microbots for on-demand moisture manipulation
articles.abstract: Hygroscopic metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising candidates for atmospheric water harvesting (AWH) and humidity control. Nevertheless, their practical application is often hindered by the poor manipulability of inherent powder forms and mass transfer limitations caused by the shaping. Drawing inspiration from the “hot defensive ball” aggregation morphology of honeybee swarms, a versatile magnetic shaping strategy hereby was reported to assemble MOF-based microbots, which enhances the formability of MOF powders. The obtained magnetic hygroscopic MOF (mMOF-303) exhibits enhanced water adsorption kinetics and enables efficient regeneration via multimodal heating strategies, including photothermal, electrothermal, and magnetothermal heating. Besides, the magnetic MOF-based microbots can change their aggregation patterns and perform directional motion according to application scenarios, enabling rapid water vapor sorption-desorption rates and precision confined space humidity control. This work provides a universal strategy to impart versatile formability to static MOF powders, paving the way for MOF engineering and advanced moisture management.

articles.title: Symmetry as a common origin of hierarchical emergence and abstraction
articles.abstract: Many systems of interest exhibit nested emergent layers with their own rules and regularities, and our knowledge about them seems naturally organized around these levels. How do such hierarchical structures arise, and why should observers track these hierarchies so closely? This paper proposes symmetry as an answer to both questions. By combining principles from information theory, group theory, and statistical mechanics, it is shown that dynamical processes that are equivariant with respect to a symmetry group give rise to multiple emergent macroscopic levels arranged according to the algebraic structure of the symmetry. The same symmetries shape the Bayesian beliefs of an observer with only partial access to the system, yielding a matching hierarchy of “abstract” beliefs that can be updated autonomously at different levels of resolution. These ideas are illustrated in Hopfield networks, where familiar macroscopic quantities emerge from known symmetries, and in Boolean models of gene regulation, where symmetries are instead found from the dynamics. The computational advantages provided by symmetry are showcased in Ehrenfest diffusion and epidemic modeling, where abstract beliefs enable Bayesian inference over exponentially large state spaces. These results identify symmetry as a sufficient mechanism for hierarchical emergence and—at the same time—for the capacity of abstract beliefs to mirror the systems they track, making feasible inferential problems that would otherwise be intractable.

articles.title: Tellurium-assisted rapid synthesis of violet phosphorus via solid-phase thermal transformation
articles.abstract: Violet phosphorus (VP), the thermodynamically most stable allotrope among crystalline red phosphorus phases, remains challenging to synthesize due to its sluggish growth kinetics. Here we report a tellurium (Te)-assisted rapid solid-phase thermal transformation approach that yields pure, homogeneous VP powder within 7.8 hours (including 3 hours of holding at 500°C), and develop a pressure-gradient transport (PGT) method that indirectly measures the vapor pressure in the Te-assisted system. We further proposed a complete evolutionary model for crystalline red phosphorus growth starting from amorphous red phosphorus and proceeding through transition-state molecular clusters to the final VP or fibrous phosphorus products. This model reveals that Te lowers the high kinetic barrier of VP formation by reshaping the transition-state energy landscape, rendering VP both the kinetic and thermodynamic product. This work resolves the long-standing kinetic bottleneck in VP growth and offers mechanistic insight into the polymorphic synthesis of elemental phosphorus crystals.

articles.title: The Azores plume origin of the New England Seamounts chain
articles.abstract: Age-progressive seamount chains are fundamental archives in revealing the past plate motion and mantle convection. However, for a representative example such as the New England Seamounts chain on the North American Plate, both its plume source and its evolutionary trajectory remain debatable. This long-lasting uncertainty is mainly caused by the absence of quantitative high-resolution constraints on plume dynamics and its interactions with multiple plates. Here, we aim to answer this question using data-assimilation–based numerical simulations. We propose that the New England chain and the Corner Seamounts on the North American Plate, the Great Meteor Seamounts on the African Plate, and the Azores archipelago on the Eurasian Plate were created by a single plume—the Azores plume. This plume experienced two stages of motion through time. Subduction-induced sublithospheric mantle flow exerts a dominant control on the spatiotemporal distribution of volcanoes along the track and the geometry of this track, surpassing the influence of plume-plate interaction. The latter primarily affects the continuity of this trans-plate hotspot system. These findings offer a reinterpretation of hotspot-track formation and new constraints on how mantle flow reorganizes across multiple plates.

articles.title: The persistent multidomain health effects of the early-life exposome
articles.abstract: The environments experienced early in life can shape health across multiple body systems, yet most research on exposome health effects has focused on isolated exposure windows and health outcomes, limiting understanding of their combined and enduring effects. Leveraging the Human Early Life Exposome (HELIX) European cohort—the largest exposome dataset from the general pediatric population—we studied 586 mother-child pairs with nearly 200 prenatal and childhood exposures, including air pollutants, chemicals, lifestyle (diet, physical activity, and toxic habits), and neighborhood outdoors factors. Associations between these exposures and 11 outcomes across mental health, cardiometabolic, respiratory, and allergic domains, assessed in both childhood (6 to 11 years) and adolescence (12 to 18 years) were sought using an outcome-wide exposure-wide analysis. We identified a set of “master regulator” exposures, such as maternal smoking, indoor air pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and dietary and urban factors, that influenced multiple health domains, with effects persisting into adolescence. By providing an atlas of exposome-health associations across developmental stages—available as an open-access interactive resource—this work pinpoints critical early-life risks and offers a platform to guide prevention and policy.

articles.title: Time-evolved hetero-alkali interphases enable long-life sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries
articles.abstract: Sulfide-based anode-free solid-state batteries (AFSSBs) offer high energy density and improved safety, but their practical implementation is hindered by parasitic reactions between freshly plated lithium (Li) and sulfide solid electrolytes. These reactions continuously consume the limited cathode-derived Li inventory, increase interfacial impedance, and promote nonuniform Li plating and stripping. Here, sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) is incorporated into Li 5.4 PS 4.4 Cl 1.6 (LPSC) to kinetically program interphase evolution. Heat treatment initially generates a NaF/LiF-rich interphase on the LPSC surface. This fluoride-rich region chemically stabilizes the interface and suppresses direct LPSC reduction. During the early cycles, the outermost region progressively evolves into a LiF/Li 3 N-rich layer, while the NaF-containing phase becomes buried beneath the Li-rich surface region, producing a time-evolved compositional gradient. Although NaF provides effective chemical passivation, its poor Li + conductivity can impede interfacial ion transport. The subsequent formation of Li 3 N-rich domains, which exhibit substantially higher Li + conductivity than NaF, provides more favorable transport pathways, homogenizes interfacial Li + flux, and promotes uniform Li plating and stripping. This time-evolved gradient interphase therefore combines early-stage chemical stabilization and Li conservation with improved long-term ion transport kinetics, suppressing impedance growth, localized inactive Li accumulation, and filamentary shorting. Consequently, the AFSSB using the NaFSI-modified LPSC interlayer retains 77.6% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 0.2 C, whereas the cell with bare LPSC retains only 32.1% after 100 cycles. These findings establish temporally programmed gradient interphases as a general strategy for conserving active Li and stabilizing sulfide-based AFSSBs.

articles.title: Upper plate structure controls nearshore subduction mechanics in Cascadia
articles.abstract: Along-strike upper plate heterogeneity is widely observed at subduction margins, but its direct influence on slab geometry and interseismic deformation remains debated. Here, we investigate the effect of continental crustal segmentation on nearshore subduction mechanics at the Cascadia margin. Using a high-resolution, shore-crossing 3D seismic tomography model from central to southern Oregon, we image sharp along-strike contrasts in seismic velocity associated with distinct accreted terranes. We show that the subducting slab is systematically deeper beneath the coherent, higher-velocity Siletz terrane and shallower beneath lower-velocity faulted Siletz and Franciscan terranes. Numerical simulations constrained by the tomographic velocities demonstrate that rheological contrasts, represented by viscoelastic end-member models, generate the magnitude and pattern of coastal uplift, while upper-plate density contrasts reproduce the observed variation in slab depth. These findings demonstrate that inherited upper-plate structure, despite being ignored in geodetic locking models, can exert a first-order influence on nearshore subduction mechanics by controlling the partitioning of interseismic deformation and contributing to along-strike variations in slab geometry.

articles.title: When and how particles are removed by drops
articles.abstract: Particulate contaminants decrease the power output of solar panels and the transparency of windows and are detrimental to microelectronics, where even a single particle can induce a short circuit. Despite substantial research on particle adhesion and self-cleaning, it remains unclear when and how a drop can remove a particle from a surface, thus efficiently cleaning the surface. Here, by combining lattice Boltzmann simulations and confocal microscopy experiments, we show that at least six different scenarios arise from the complex interplay between capillary and friction forces when a drop collides with a particle on a surface. Notably, the capillary force plays a dual role in particle removal: While its tangential component always drives removal, its normal component can also hinder it. We introduce a dimensionless capillary capture parameter that successfully predicts particle removal across a wide range of particle and surface properties. Our results reveal that the design of easy-to-clean surfaces should focus not only on maximizing hydrophobicity but also on minimizing the particle-surface friction.

articles.title: ZSCAN4 links a transient reset of repetitive DNA to genome integrity and cellular plasticity
articles.abstract: ZSCAN4 is transiently expressed in a small subset of embryonic stem cells and early embryos and has traditionally been linked to telomere elongation and genome stability. However, accumulating evidence indicates that ZSCAN4 does not function as a classical stemness factor. ZSCAN4 acts as a temporally restricted regulator of genome plasticity. Recent mechanistic studies indicate that ZSCAN4 preferentially operates at repetitive DNA regions. In particular, at telomeres, it supports maintenance and elongation, whereas, at microsatellite-rich and two-cell (2C)–associated loci, it has been proposed to enable a brief, locally restricted window of chromatin relaxation. This process involves noncanonical mechanisms, such as proteostasis-dependent removal of repressive chromatin complexes, coordinated engagement of genome surveillance pathways, and rapid restoration of chromatin constraint. ZSCAN4 activity is regulated by multilayered regulatory mechanisms acting at the transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and posttranslational levels, ensuring a sharp burst followed by active shutdown. We propose a unifying model in which ZSCAN4 functions as a transient genome reset factor that facilitates cellular plasticity during zygotic genome activation, 2C-like transitions, and cellular reprogramming, while preserving long-term genome integrity. This framework redefines the role of ZSCAN4 beyond stemness maintenance and highlights repetitive DNA as a central regulatory platform during developmental and reprogramming-associated genome transitions.

articles.title: IFN-γ–driven MHC class II on gut epithelium induces cytolytic TH1 cell differentiation and stem cell loss in graft-versus-host disease
articles.abstract: The molecular cues by which CD4 T cells are invoked to mediate lethal gut graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) at the epithelial interface after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation are unclear. Here, we demonstrate that MHC class II (MHCII) but not MHC class I expression by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) within the first 3 days of transplantation promotes lethal GVHD in mice. This was dependent on direct IFN-γ–dependent induction of MHCII on IECs, which expanded perforin/granzyme B–expressing cytolytic donor T H 1 cell while restraining T H 17 cell differentiation locally within the ileum. In contrast, intestinal stem cells (ISCs) were preferentially and progressively depleted by cytolytic T H 1 cells as a result of IFN-γ–induced MHCII expression. Together, IEC-intrinsic IFN-γ signaling is critical for the MHCII-dependent early local generation of cytolytic T H 1 cells that thereafter mediate MHCII-dependent ISC deletion. These data demonstrate a critical IFN-γ–MHCII feed-forward axis in the initiation of cytolytic T H 1 cell–dependent gut disease.

articles.title: TOX and PD-1 are required for the maintenance of CD4 T cell precursors during chronic infection
articles.abstract: In contrast with the well-established mechanisms that maintain exhausted CD8 T cells, our knowledge about the differentiation and in particular the molecular control of CD4 T cells in chronic infections is limited. Using the lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection model, we identified that CXCR5 + TCF-1 + CD4 T cells, found mainly in secondary lymphoid organs, serve as precursors for the CD4 population. These cells transition into terminally differentiated cells and combine T follicular helper (T FH ) cell features (IL-21 expression) with T helper 1 (T H 1) cell characteristics (CXCR6 expression and IFN-γ and TNF secretion). In the CXCR5 + TCF-1 + population, CD62L + cells exhibit the highest re-expansion potential in adoptive transfer settings. All subsets express TOX and PD-1, which ensure the maintenance of the CD4 T cell population. Absence of either factor reduces the number of CD62L + precursors and impairs their further differentiation. Overall, we define a hierarchical framework for CD4 T cell maintenance in chronic infection and reveal common mechanisms that sustain both exhausted CD4 and CD8 T cell responses.

articles.title: Effects of plastic exposure on human health
articles.abstract: Plastic pollution is a critical environmental and public health challenge, with growing evidence linking human exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics, and associated chemicals to adverse health outcomes. This review summarises current knowledge on the health effects of plastic exposure, addressing both established findings and critical knowledge gaps. We examine human exposure to plastics and associated health risks based on available clinical and epidemiological evidence. Additionally, we explore chemicals associated with plastic, including their potential as carcinogens and disruptors of endocrine and immune function. Recognising the urgent need for preventive measures, we examine emerging strategies for reducing plastic burdens, including global regulatory efforts like the United Nations Plastics Treaty and proposed public health guidelines. By integrating current evidence, this review aims to provide a foundation for advancing research and informing strategies to mitigate health risks associated with plastic.

articles.title: Gaza: US doctor condemns “shocking murder” of fellow surgeon in Israeli attack on hospital
articles.abstract: Six people, including a surgeon featured in a documentary on American doctors in Gaza, have been killed in an Israeli attack on a hospital.Rizk Abu Shaaira, a Palestinian surgeon, was killed when the surgical department at Nasser Hospital was hit by an Israeli airstrike in the early hours of Thursday 12 November.Abu Shaaira’s colleague and friend, US doctor Feroze Sidhwa, called it a “shocking murder.”media-1vid1Video 1Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital, Gaza, November 2026bmj-2026-101452-vid1Five other people, patients and their companions, were also killed, while at least 27 patients and surgeons were injured.1Three missiles reportedly hit Nasser Hospital just after midnight. Two caused extensive damage to intensive care wards and the surgical department, while one failed to explode and remained inside the building.2Israel’s military, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF), claimed responsibility for the hospital attack, posting on X: “The Commander of Hamas’ Khan Yunis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, and additional terrorists hiding...

articles.title: “I’m not like other medics:” deconstructing the medical student stereotype
articles.abstract: Medical school often comes with a heavy set of unspoken expectations. From how you spend your free time to what you’re “supposed” to be good at, the pressure to fit a specific mould can be exhausting. But what happens when you don’t—or won’t—conform?In an episode of the Sharp Scratch podcast (https://open.spotify.com/episode/4PYI9EmWsmmOliekGYsORl), Zaynah Khan talked with panellist George Webster and expert guest Sabina Dosani (doctor, author, and editor) to explore the bittersweet reality of being different in medicine. They dive into:The myth of the “ideal medic:” why the stereotypes we chase might not exist.Belonging without conformity: how to find your space in the profession while staying true to yourself.Professional identity: the idea that being a doctor isn’t a role you inherit, but something you create through your own unique actions and adaptations.Whether you’re a “traditional” student or someone who feels as if they’re constantly resisting the status quo, conversations in the...

articles.title: [Comment] Cangrelor for myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock
articles.abstract: Acute myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) fosters a unique combination of opposing, competing thrombotic and haemorrhagic risk. Strategies to mitigate these crucial events represent an actionable target to reduce the high mortality that still burdens AMI-CS patients.1,2 With primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) being the cornerstone prognostic treatment of AMI-CS,3 the identification of an optimal dual anti-platelet therapy (DAPT) in this setting is a clinical priority, but remains largely uncharted.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Emerging Shamonda virus: a new threat to pregnancy?
articles.abstract: The emergence of Shamonda virus in Europe raises new questions about the potential consequences of orthobunyavirus infections during pregnancy. In June, 2026, Shamonda virus was identified in cattle in central Europe, including France, Germany, and Switzerland.1 Transmission is thought to occur through bites from Culicoides midges. Detection of viral RNA in aborted bovine fetuses suggests transplacental transmission.2

articles.title: [Correspondence] Lula's new term—safeguarding science, health, and the Amazon
articles.abstract: Although Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's victory in Brazil's presidential election promises executive commitment to science, public health, and environmental protection, the political reality signals a serious governability crisis. The unprecedented conservative surge in the 2026 legislative elections created a deeply hostile Congress, leaving a divided nation in which evidence-based governance, public health systems, and ecological preservation face imminent institutional gridlock. This political split, reflected in the 51·79% to 48·21% election result,1 is heightened by memories of past anti-democratic actions following the 2022 election, including civilian encampments outside military installations, demands for military intervention, and the January 2023 storming of Brasília's democratic institutions.

articles.title: Following nature’s design: strengthening endogenous metabolite glues in purine synthesis
articles.abstract: Molecular glue mechanisms have never been described in human endogenous pathways; historically, they are limited to plants and therapeutics. A study by Witus et al. combines metabolic and mechanistic studies to unveil an endogenous purine ‘metabolite glue’. This regulatory mechanism is exploited by purine analog chemotherapeutics, revealing a therapeutically tractable interaction.

articles.title: Understanding plant UPR from structural and comparative perspectives
articles.abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is central to protein, lipid, Ca2+, and redox homeostasis. ER stress occurs when oxidative protein-folding capacity is exceeded or lipid composition becomes abnormal. To restore ER and cellular homeostasis, the cell initiates the unfolded protein response (UPR)—a transcriptional response that amplifies the ER’s capacity for protein folding, degradation, and lipid biosynthesis. Our understanding of plant UPR activation mechanisms remains limited compared with yeast and mammalian systems. Here, we compare the structural composition of the plant UPR sensors, inositol-requiring enzyme 1 and basic-region leucine zipper 28, with their yeast and animal homologs; predict their potential activation and regulatory mechanisms; and discuss which small-molecule inhibitors developed for mammalian UPR research may be applicable to plant UPR studies.

articles.title: Photocatalytic anti-Markovnikov hydroalkylation
articles.abstract: Anti-Markovnikov alkene hydroalkylation offers a direct route to linear C(sp3)–C(sp3) coupling products. However, nucleophilic alkyl radicals are polarity-mismatched with electron-rich alkenes, impeding addition. Here, a removable carboxyl group enhances radical electrophilicity to facilitate alkene addition, with malonic acids (MAs) serving as readily available radical precursors. Subsequent decarboxylation delivers the desired products through a strategy termed traceless radical polarity reversal (TRPR).

articles.title: A Variational Principle for the Emergence of Neural Geometry Underlying Bayesian-Like Behavior
articles.abstract: Neural population geometry constrains how task variables are represented and read out into behavior. We propose a variational principle in which learning balances task accuracy and representational smoothness under stimulus-dependent weighting. This balance links stimulus statistics to the shape of a latent neural coordinate. For magnitude estimation, the principle predicts distortions near the edges of bounded ensembles, global affine contraction for Gaussian ensembles, and warping toward high-probability regions for bimodal ensembles. We test the bounded-uniform case in recurrent neural networks trained to reproduce time intervals. Their learned geometries occupy three regimes as the boundary distortions change from too narrow to resolve, to measurable, to extending across the stimulus range. A shape parameter selected from an empirical neural coordinate predicts the nonlinear component of mean behavior through an affine readout, with only behavioral gain and offset fitted afterward. In this bounded-uniform setting, the variational coordinate and Bayesian least-squares mean response have closely matching shapes after affine normalization. These results suggest a variational account of how stimulus statistics shape neural geometry and yield Bayesian-like behavior.

articles.title: A brief breathing challenge reveals a cardiac correlate of generalized anxiety beyond resting physiology and interoceptive measures
articles.abstract: Physiological markers measured at rest, such as heart rate variability, have proved relatively weak predictors of mental health symptoms. One potential reason is that resting measures are influenced by uncontrolled state factors, such as spontaneous breathing, whereas a standardized challenge holds these constant and may reveal regulatory differences not evident at rest. Here we asked whether respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) during slow paced breathing, a challenge that strongly increases RSA, carries information about symptoms beyond resting RSA and interoceptive measures. In 207 young adults (mean age 23.6 years, SD = 3.1), electrocardiogram (ECG) was recorded at rest and during slow (6 breaths/min) and fast (20 breaths/min) paced breathing. Lower RSA during slow breathing, relative to that predicted by resting RSA, was associated with more severe generalized anxiety symptoms ({beta} = -0.21, BF = 13), also when depressive symptoms were controlled, whereas resting RSA was not. The association was concentrated among participants with at least moderate anxiety symptoms, whose resting RSA was typical but whose rest-adjusted slow-breathing RSA was 0.62 SD lower, and who in exploratory analyses also showed weaker phase coupling between heart period and respiration. Interoceptive accuracy, measured with heartbeat counting or heart rate discrimination, was unrelated to symptoms, self-report and slow-breathing RSA, and interoceptive questionnaires tracked distress shared across anxiety and depressive symptoms rather than generalized anxiety symptoms. At the group level, slow-breathing RSA thus carries information about generalized anxiety symptoms beyond resting RSA and self-reported interoception. Brief paced-breathing challenges may therefore increase the sensitivity of autonomic markers in anxiety research and merit testing in clinical samples.

articles.title: A conserved tyrosine in the S1/S2 loop shapes SARS-CoV-2 spike processing and host protease usage.
articles.abstract: Both spike processing efficiency and host protease usage play critical roles in SARS-CoV-2 infection, pathogenesis, and transmission. The SARS-CoV-2 spike contains two motifs, a furin cleavage site (FCS) and an extended S1/S2 loop, which improve both cleavage efficiency and host protease usage. Disruption of these motifs significantly attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection and pathogenesis. Importantly, modifications and changes within the S1/S2 loop can also shape infection and disease outcomes following infection. In this study, we examined mass spectrometry data generated from purified virions from wild-type (WT) or mutant SARS-CoV-2 infection. We identified phosphorylation occurring at highly conserved residue Y674 and used reverse genetics to generate a mutant that ablates phosphorylation capacity in the S1/ S2 loop (Y674F). Our results show that the Y674F mutant replicated equivalently to wild-type SARS-CoV-2 in Vero cells but had attenuated replication in a human respiratory cell line. Golden Syrian hamsters infected with the Y674F mutant had equivalent weight loss, lung viral titer, and similar immune pathology to WT SARS-CoV-2. However, the mutant had reduced viral load in the nasal wash and reduced antigen staining in the large airways in the lung. Notably, loss of Y674 ablated spike processing to the S1/S2 cleavage product on virions. In addition, Y674F mutant had a diminished capacity to utilize host protease TMPRSS2 for entry. Together, these data indicates that post-translational modification of Y674 impacts SARS-CoV-2 infection of the airway by disrupting both spike processing and host protease function. These results add to data demonstrating the importance of spike S1/S2 loop modifications to SARS-CoV-2 infection, pathogenesis, and transmission. ### Competing Interest Statement VDM has filed a patent on the reverse genetic system for SARS-CoV-2. All other authors declare no conflicts of interest. Other authors declare no competing interests. articles.title: A molecular glue degrader-antibody conjugate for HER2-targeted cyclin K degradation
articles.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase 12 (CDK12) is an attractive therapeutic target due to its critical role in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage response and is frequently co-amplified with ERBB2 (HER2) in breast cancer. CDK12 forms an active complex with its obligate partner cyclin K (CCNK), and pharmacological degradation of CCNK has emerged as a promising strategy for disrupting CDK12-dependent transcriptional programs. However, the broad expression and essential functions of the CDK12/CCNK complex may limit the therapeutic window of highly potent molecular glue degraders. Here, we investigate whether antibody-mediated delivery can impart cellular selectivity to a molecular glue degrader through targeting the HER2 receptor. Molecular glues lack the modular architecture of PROTACs, thus linker placement can be the central design problem. We designed SAS1001, a CCNK molecular glue degrader with a solvent-exposed piperazine primed for linker attachment. SAS1001 induced potent and ubiquitin-proteasome system-dependent degradation of CCNK and inhibited proliferation in a range of breast cancer cells. Conjugation to trastuzumab (Tz) generated the HER2-targeted degrader-antibody conjugate Tz-SS2009, which internalized preferentially in HER2-positive cells and produced enhanced CCNK degradation and antiproliferative effects, relative both to HER2-negative cells and to an isotype-matched non-targeting conjugate. Whole proteome analysis further demonstrated CCNK depletion and revealed downstream changes consistent with established roles of the CDK12/CCNK complex in transcriptional regulation. These findings demonstrate that antibody-mediated delivery can redistribute the cellular activity of a potent molecular glue degrader towards antigen-positive cells. In the CR8/DS18 purine series, substitution at a solvent-exposed position preserved CCNK degradation when the degrader was delivered on a full-length IgG. More broadly, this work extends antibody-directed degradation beyond the CRBN-based glues that have dominated the field and illustrates how structural characterization of a glue scaffold can identify a linker attachment point that does not compromise activity.

articles.title: A polarized genome is required for fitness of the obligate intracellular, tick-borne pathogen Rickettsia parkeri
articles.abstract: Alphaproteobacteria of the order Rickettsiales include biomedically important, yet understudied arthropod-borne human pathogens. These pathogens lack obvious morphological asymmetry, but encode homologs of key mediators of polar processes in the model Alphaproteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus. These include the polar organizing protein PopZ, the chromosome segregation proteins ParA and ParB, and the spatial regulator of cell division MipZ. Motivated by this observation, we used the tick-borne human pathogen Rickettsia parkeri to ask if the chromosome is polarized and coordinated with cell division in this group. Consistent with that hypothesis, we found that transposon insertion mutants in parA, parB, mipZ, or popZ resulted in cell division defects. Fluorescence imaging revealed cell cycle-dependent unipolar-to-bipolar localization dynamics of ParB and MipZ, and pole-to-midcell dynamics of the division protein ZapA. This patterning parallels the model of chromosome segregation and cell division site selection established in Caulobacter. Unlike its unipolar-to-bipolar dynamics in Caulobacter, however, PopZ remained at a single cell pole throughout the cell cycle in R. parkeri. PopZ maintained its direct interaction with ParA and ParB. Interestingly, disruption of parA or parB, but not popZ or mipZ, caused a small plaque phenotype, suggesting a defect in growth or spread in a monolayer of host cells in the absence of proper chromosome segregation. We propose that genome polarization in R. parkeri and other rickettsiae is critical both for fundamental cellular processes and for interactions with host cells that promote fitness in their infectious niche.

articles.title: A reversible YbbR-domain hinge switch senses extracellular pH to control bacterial cyclic-di-AMP signaling
articles.abstract: Acidification is a principal antimicrobial host defence: during infection, bacteria have to survive the stomach, the vaginal tract or the phagolysosome of immune cells, where the pH falls below 5. To persist, bacteria must sense and adapt to extracellular pH. In Gram-positive bacteria, the membrane protein CdaR, a regulator of the c-di-AMP-synthesizing enzyme CdaA, has been proposed as a pH sensor, but the molecular basis of this sensing remains unknown. Here we show, using the model organism Bacillus subtilis, that CdaR is essential for growth below pH 5. SEC-MALS, mass photometry and circular dichroism demonstrate that its extracellular YbbR domains neither oligomerize nor unfold at low pH. Instead, tryptophan and ANS fluorescence reveal a reversible conformational change that requires at least two tandem YbbR domains and occurs between pH 4.5 and 5.5. Crystallography, molecular dynamics and solution NMR localize this transition to a conserved hinge between YbbR domains 1 and 2, where a network of charged residues rearranges to rigidify it and restrict inter-domain motion. Mutagenesis identifies a highly conserved aspartate whose substitution abolishes the conformational switch in vitro and accelerates adaptation to low pH in vivo. These findings define a structural mechanism by which CdaR senses extracellular acidification through its YbbR domains and couples this signal to intracellular c-di-AMP signaling. As the hinge and its aspartate are the most conserved features of the YbbR family, found in pathogens including Staphylococcus aureus and Listeria monocytogenes, we propose this as a general mechanism of acid adaptation in Gram-positive bacteria.

articles.title: A statistical framework for identifying candidate genetic interactions from adaptive laboratory evolution data
articles.abstract: Background Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) is widely used to improve microbial fitness under defined selective pressures. Mutations accumulated during ALE may interact epistatically, with the effect of one mutation depending on another. Understanding these interactions can help explain adaptive phenotypes and inform combinatorial strain engineering, but experimentally testing all mutation combinations is impractical. We developed a computational framework that uses gene-pair co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity patterns to identify candidates for experimental investigation of epistasis. Results We applied the framework to a curated compendium of 141 Escherichia coli ALE experiments from ALEdb, using the Fisher exact test and DISCOVER as complementary statistical screens. Testing and multiple-testing correction were performed separately within each experiment, method, and direction (co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity). At a 5% false discovery rate threshold, the Fisher exact test identified 74 significant gene pairs, comprising 36 co-occurrences and 38 mutual exclusivities. DISCOVER identified 5 significant pairs, all for mutual exclusivity and also significant under the Fisher exact test. These shared pairs suggested alternative adaptive routes involving temperature tolerance, glycerol utilization, and associations between RNA polymerase subunit genes. The two methods produced similar expected overlaps for Fisher-significant pairs, but the broader null distributions of DISCOVER yielded larger raw p-values. Of the 69 pairs significant only under the Fisher exact test, 60 arose in experiments with multiple strain labels or involved a gene with only one distinct mutation recorded across all affected endpoints (final samples from lineages evolved in parallel), highlighting the need to examine genetic backgrounds and mutation origins when interpreting the results. Power analysis indicated that the Fisher exact test required 70 independent endpoints for co-occurrence and 215 for mutual exclusivity to achieve 80% power under pre-specified scenarios. We implemented the framework as a reusable Nextflow pipeline that automates statistical screening of ALEdb and user-supplied mutation datasets. Conclusions By combining gene-pair screening with mutation-level interpretation, this reproducible framework narrows the search space for experimental investigation of epistasis and can contribute to combinatorial strain design. The power analysis provides sample-size benchmarks for planning future ALE experiments with adequate power to screen for candidate genetic interactions.

articles.title: A unique sixth-order reversible assembly of hexameric mimetic nucleic acid
articles.abstract: Complementary dipeptides bearing the non-canonical nucleobases melamine and cyanuric acid (alpha DPNA) assemble into a cylindrical hexameric structure containing a stacked heterocyclic core with its beta-sheet peptide backbones on the surface. Circular dichroism spectroscopy and singular-value decomposition show that the evolution of CD spectra after mixing equimolar strands is an apparent two-state process, accounted for by only the spectra of free strands and the assembled hexamer, with no detectable intermediates. Equilibrium measurements reveal a highly cooperative, enthalpically driven assembly with a molecularity of 6.2 +/- 0.2 and an association constant of (2.3 +/- 0.2)X10^22 " " M^(-5). Over total strand concentrations of 20 to 100 micromolar, the assembly progress curves are described by an apparent reversible sixth-order macroscopic rate law. This deceptively simple behavior cannot represent an elementary six-strand collision. The apparent forward rate constant has a negative activation energy, showing that the observed rate law masks additional steps in the assembly reaction. A minimal model in which strand pre-isomerization precedes hexamer formation restores a physically reasonable positive activation energy while retaining the observed two-state CD behavior. Constrained simulations further show that a sequential pathway with low-population, spectroscopically silent, intermediates can give rise to the same deceptively simple sixth-order progress curve. These results provide an unusual example of highly cooperative hexamer formation and show how a simple high-order macroscopic rate law can conceal a more complex microscopic assembly mechanism. The thermodynamics and kinetics provide insights into how and why the hexamer assembles, offering some design principles for supramolecular assemblies in water.

articles.title: Additive genes underlie Mendelian inheritance and contribute to heterosis
articles.abstract: Mendel proposed the laws of segregation and independent combination in his study. However, he focused on "dominant" characters but left "intermediate" ones. Using genotypic and phenotypic data for four representative genes, we reveal connections between the "intermediate" and "dominant" characters. We demonstrate that the fundamental inheritance patterns of these genes are additive effects on both component and compound traits. Additive effects involving more than two genes generate non-additive effects in hybrids. For compound traits such as grain yield, their inheritance depends on differential patterns of component traits in parents; only parents with optimal balances of reciprocal differences in component traits produce overdominant effects, which is important for hybrid breeding. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. 2026 National Innovation Center for Salt-Tolerant and Alkali-Tolerant Rice Project, ZDYF2026GCZX001

articles.title: Aging exacerbates muscle loss induced by semaglutide treatment in female mice
articles.abstract: Background Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), including semaglutide, have transformed the pharmacological treatment of obesity. While highly efficacious in promoting weight loss, these drugs also induce substantial reductions in lean mass, raising concerns for skeletal muscle loss, particularly in older individuals vulnerable to sarcopenia. Nevertheless, there are currently no published human studies that investigated the effects of GLP-1RAs on skeletal muscle mass using gold standard methods. Meanwhile, studies in young mice demonstrate that skeletal muscle loss induced by GLP-1RAs might not be a major concern. The purpose of the current study was to investigate the effects of semaglutide on skeletal muscle mass and strength in aged mice. Methods Eighteen-month-old male and female C57BL/6J mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks to induce obesity. At 21 months of age, mice received daily subcutaneous injections of vehicle or semaglutide (3 or 30 nmol/kg) for 3 weeks. Body composition was assessed weekly by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. After 3 wks, mice were terminated to assess masses of individual organs including skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle force-generating capacity was assessed by ex vivo electrical stimulation-induced contraction. Myofiber cross-sectional area and fiber-type composition were also assessed. Results Semaglutide induced dose-dependent weight loss in both sexes, with reductions of 11.3% and 20.2% in males and 21.1% and 26.1% in females receiving 3 or 30 nmol/kg dose, respectively. There was a substantial sex-difference in the loss of lean mass, with relatively minor reductions in males (2.3% and 6.6%) and greater loss in females (8.6% and 8.3%). Skeletal muscle mass was largely preserved in males but females exhibited greater muscle mass loss, including 14.2% reduction in quadriceps mass at 30 nmol/kg of semaglutide treatment. In contrast, skeletal muscle force-generating capacity was not compromised in semaglutide-treated females, while males exhibited 19.2% reduction in force generating capacity of the extensor digitorum longus (EDL) muscles at the 30 nmol/kg dose. Conclusion Unlike young mice, semaglutide treatment may induce meaningful loss in skeletal muscle mass in aged female mice and muscle strength in aged male mice. These findings highlight the importance of considering age as a potential factor that may negatively influence muscle mass and function in humans treated with GLP-1RAs. Clinical studies examining the influence of pharmacological weight loss on skeletal muscle mass and strength should consider both age and sex as a potentially important determinant of these outcomes.

articles.title: AlphaScreen profiling of extracellular vesicle-associated platelet, immune, and vascular markers reveals disease-specific signatures in ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and long COVID
articles.abstract: Introduction: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), fibromyalgia (FM), and long COVID (LC-19) are chronic diseases with overlapping clinical features and poorly understood pathophysiology. Increasing evidence suggests the involvement of immune dysregulation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered vascular physiology. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are key mediators of intercellular communication and are envisioned as sensors of homeostasis and disease. The aim of this study was to determine whether EV marker profiling could provide a basis for the differential diagnosis of ME/CFS, FM and LC-19 and/or patient stratification. Methods: EV-enriched plasma from ME/CFS, FM, cases co-diagnosed with ME/CFS and FM, LC-19 patients, and matched healthy controls (n = 10 per study group) were analyzed. EV concentration and size distribution were assessed by nanoparticle tracking analysis, followed by targeted profiling of EV-associated surface markers via AlphaScreen, including tetraspanins CD9 and CD63, platelet- (CD41/CD61), myeloid- (CD13), immune- (CD74 and CX3CR1), and renin-angiotensin system- associated ACE1 (also known as CD143), and ACE2 surface markers. Results: The studied disease groups presented distinct EV signatures. LC-19 samples exhibited the most pronounced and coordinated alterations, characterized by increased levels of CD9/CD74, CD9/CX3CR1, and CD9/ACE1-positive EVs, along with reduced overall particle concentrations. Notably, platelet-derived CD9/CD41/CD61-positive EVs were significantly elevated in both LC-19 and ME/CFS, as compared to healthy controls, indicating enhanced platelet activation. Immune-associated markers revealed differential pathway activation in LC-19, with CD74-positive EVs reflecting antigen presentation and inflammatory signaling, and CX3CR1-positive EVs indicating altered leukocyte trafficking and vascular interaction. Increased ACE1-positive EVs in LC-19 further suggested a shift toward pro-inflammatory renin-angiotensin signaling. Conclusion: Collectively, these findings support a disease-specific dysregulation of platelet, immune, and vascular pathways. The integrated EV signatures distinguish LC-19 from the related chronic conditions ME/CFS and FM, highlighting the potential of EV-based profiling for differential diagnosis. Our results provide a systems-level perspective on the differential pathophysiology of these disorders and identify EV-associated markers as candidate biomarkers with clinical value.

articles.title: Amyloidosis and tauopathy progressively disrupt near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits
articles.abstract: Mechanistically distinct neurodegenerative diseases result in similar cognitive deficits, and pathology is often concentrated in a set of circuits known to be selectively vulnerable. Selective vulnerability is an intrinsic property of a circuit: in APP/PS1 mice, where plaques are global, functional disruptions are confined to circuits within the default mode network. What characterizes the dynamics of vulnerable circuits from those of spared circuits is unknown. We asked whether the distinguishing property is the proximity of population dynamics to criticality, a homeostatic set-point of network activity that determines computational capacity. We recorded single units simultaneously in three selectively vulnerable regions (retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and CA1 hippocampus) and in primary visual cortex of freely behaving young and old APP/PS1 and wild-type mice. Firing rate and spike-time variability differed by genotype inconsistently across regions and ages. In contrast, three measures from criticality theory each revealed deficits that emerged only with age and only in the vulnerable regions. No measure detected a progressive change in V1. Avalanche scaling is not fixed in neural activity, but varies along a scaling line as the network state changes. As a result, the lines generated by each genotype revealed a constitutive effect of the transgene in young animals, which inverted with age in amyloid-bearing animals, but only in vulnerable circuits. If the destabilization of near-critical dynamics directly reflects a circuit's functional capacity, the same signature should identify a mechanistically distinct degenerative disease. In a model of tauopathy (P301S/E4), CA1 dynamics were displaced from the control scaling line with the same age-dependent reversal observed in APP/PS1. Our results suggest a network-level principle of neurodegenerative diseases: molecularly unrelated pathologies converge on the loss of near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits.

articles.title: An interplay of multilayered regulatory mechanisms underlies the RNA solubility phase transition during vertebrate oocyte-to-embryo transition
articles.abstract: Dynamic RNA-protein interactions influence RNA transport, storage, stability, and activity and are fundamental to a broad range of biological processes. During the oocyte-to-embryo transition (OET), fully differentiated gametes fuse and regain totipotency. Throughout the OET, the transcription remains silent. Spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression relies on the dynamic interactions between maternal transcripts and various protein complexes. Despite its fundamental importance, RNA-protein interaction dynamics at the global level during the OET remain poorly understood. Here, we leverage fractionation RNA-seq to profile RNA insolubility, a proxy for the interaction between RNAs and protein complexes, during zebrafish OET. We identify transcripts that transition between the soluble (relatively protein-free) and insoluble (heavily protein-associated) states and demonstrate that these phase transitions are driven by ribosome-dependent and ribosome-independent mechanisms. We demonstrate that the capacity of maternal RNAs to engage with protein complexes changes dynamically during the OET through remodeling of cis-regulatory features. We developed a machine-learning framework and uncovered multiple cis- and trans-regulatory features that may contribute to RNA insolubility. To validate these predictions, we examined poly(A) tail length and m6A dynamics. We found that poly(A) tail length is associated with both ribosome-dependent and ribosome-independent RNA phase transitions. In parallel, fractionation m6A-pulldown RNA-seq revealed highly dynamic changes in the m6A landscape during the OET. A correlation between m6A modifications and RNA insolubility is gradually established during the OET. Together, our findings uncover a multilayered regulatory mechanism governing RNA phase transitions during the OET, providing fundamental insights into post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression during development. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. National Institutes of Health, https://ror.org/01cwqze88, T32ES007326, T32HD108075, R35GM131810, R01ES036194

articles.title: An oxidative mutational signature in normal tissues of a monoallelic MUTYH carrier
articles.abstract: Biallelic loss of MUTYH causes MUTYH-associated polyposis (OMIM: 608456), characterized by the oxidative base-excision-repair mutational signature SBS18, but whether the roughly 1 in 100 individuals who carry a single pathogenic MUTYH allele acquire a mutational phenotype in normal tissue is unknown. Analysis of multi-tissue sequencing of 25 donors from the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network identified three heterozygous carriers of MUTYH p.Gly396Asp. One carrier showed SBS18 across multiple normal tissues, ranking first of 25 donors with three independent methods and remaining significant after adjustment for tissue, without a somatic, epigenetic or transcriptional second hit at the MUTYH locus. A single hypomorphic MUTYH allele can therefore leave a measurable oxidative mutational mark in healthy tissues, supporting tissue-level mutational readouts as an approach to cancer risk stratification within this common carrier state.

articles.title: Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) restrains the maintenance and acquisition of the anti-inflammatory identity of monocyte-derived macrophages.
articles.abstract: The Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is an essential environmental sensor bridging metabolic cues with immune regulation, yet its precise role in defining human monocyte-derived macrophage identity remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that AhR functions as a critical transcriptional rheostat that selectively restrains the anti-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic identity of M-CSF-dependent monocyte-derived macrophages (M-Mac). Integrated ChIP-Seq and transcriptomic profiling revealed that AhR activity is enriched in M-Mac in a MAFB-dependent manner, directly occupying regulatory regions of core M-Mac identity genes, including CD163, LGMN, and IL10. Unexpectedly, siRNA-mediated knockdown and CRISPR/Cas9 ablation demonstrated that AhR primarily functions as a repressor; its deficiency accelerated and exacerbated the acquisition of a "resident-like" (LYVE1+/FOLR2+) and pro-fibrotic phenotype. Functionally, AhR restricted the M-Mac anti-inflammatory response to TLR7 ligation, and limited an overly tolerogenic profile during M-Mac-driven T-cell responses. Pharmacological modulation using the endogenous ligand FICZ and the antagonist SR1 confirmed that AhR activity limits the magnitude of the MAFB-driven program and the autocrine IL-10 signaling axis. Collectively, these findings establish AhR as a fundamental checkpoint that prevents macrophages from acquiring an excessive anti-inflammatory state, thereby ensuring balanced responses essential for tissue homeostasis and immune surveillance.

articles.title: Binary Patterning as a Probe of Protein Language Model Representations
articles.abstract: Do protein language models (pLMs) encode the physical rules that govern protein folding? The four-helix bundle provides a classic test case because binary patterning, the ordered placement of polar and nonpolar residues along an amphipathic α-helix, is sufficient to generate folded proteins with high probability. Here, we ask whether ESM2 captures the sequence grammar underlying this design strategy. Libraries of synthetic sequences constrained only by binary patterning were predicted by ESMFold to form four-helix bundles. Predicted helicity, compactness, and topological diversity changed with sequence length in the same direction as experimentally characterized libraries, although the model did not distinguish successful from unsuccessful individual designs. Principal component analysis of ESM2 embeddings revealed representations of hydrophobic patterning, helix-loop boundaries, and heptad register. Extending the analysis to all 128 heptad binary patterns produced a jellyfish-shaped manifold in which hydrophobic composition formed the dominant axis, while paired components encoded pattern phase. Manifold geometry depended on amino-acid chemistry, repeat number, and linker sequence, and collapsed when amino acids were assigned to arbitrary categories. ESM2 therefore combines general repeat recognition with protein-specific physicochemical information. More broadly, synthetic sequence libraries provide experimentally grounded probes of protein language model representations and their relationship to protein biophysics.

articles.title: Biochemical reassessment of the activation of PANK1 by SGLT2 inhibitors
articles.abstract: Although SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) show cardiovascular benefits in addition to glycemic control, their molecular target for cardiovascular effect remains unclear. A recent study reported that two SGLT2i, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, directly activate pantothenate kinase 1 (PANK1), which mediate their cardioprotective effect. PANK1 phosphorylates pantothenate with ATP to yield 4'-phosphopantothenate and ADP, representing the rate-limiting enzyme of coenzyme A (CoA) biosynthesis. We therefore reassessed this claim using purified recombinant human PANK1. The malachite green assay detected free inorganic phosphate (Pi) but neither ADP nor 4'-phosphopantothenate and its signals do not reflect PANK1 activity. In the ADP-Glo assay, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin did not stimulate PANK1 under either basal conditions or acetyl-CoA feedback inhibition, while the activator PZ-2891 enhanced the activity of PANK1. These results show that SGLT2i do not directly activate PANK1, challenging the proposed PANK1-dependent cardioprotection mechanism.

articles.title: COVID-19 and Active Tuberculosis Exhibit Distinct Maturation-Associated Neutrophil Transcriptional Programs
articles.abstract: Neutrophils can promote pathogen control or drive tissue-damaging inflammation, but the mechanisms that determine these divergent outcomes remain poorly defined. COVID-19 and active tuberculosis (TB) offer a purposeful comparison since both are pulmonary infections with substantial neutrophil involvement, yet differ in pathogen class, inflammatory duration, and the balance between neutrophil-associated host defense and pathology. We therefore tested whether their divergent neutrophil programs align with distinct maturation-associated transcriptional states. We integrated six publicly available whole-blood bulk RNA-sequencing datasets, comprising three COVID-19 and three active TB cohorts. A curated panel of 770 genes covered activation, degranulation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, chemotaxis, cell surface receptors, and maturation. Study-associated variation was reduced using ComBat-Seq, and differential expression relative to disease-appropriate controls was assessed with DESeq2. Most genes changed in the same direction in both diseases, but 348 (45.2%) differed significantly in response magnitude, with 159 genes showing a stronger response in COVID-19 and 189 in TB. COVID-19 samples showed reduced expression of the maturation markers CD10 (MME) and CD16 (FCGR3A), alongside elevated expression of granule-cargo and NET-associated genes, including MPO and ELANE, consistent with a greater contribution from immature, emergency granulopoiesis-derived neutrophil populations. In contrast, TB samples showed higher maturation-associated, receptor, oxidative, and recruitment responses, consistent with a relatively mature receptor-competent neutrophil transcriptional signature. Independent COVID-19 Ward and pulmonary TB cohorts showed directional agreement for maturation and NET-associated signatures (100% and 90% concordance, respectively), while chemotaxis and select receptor and degranulation genes showed weaker reproducibility indicating that maturation represents the most consistently reproduced axis of distinction between the two diseases. Together, these findings identify maturation-associated transcription as the most consistently reproduced axis distinguishing COVID-19 from TB. These signatures provide candidate biomarkers for future studies linking neutrophil states to clinical outcomes and informing host-directed therapeutic strategies that preserve antimicrobial function while limiting immunopathology.

articles.title: Characterizing Multimodal Mutational Processes in Cancer Using MOTET
articles.abstract: Mutational signatures are characteristic patterns of somatic alterations in cancer genomes. A single aberrant mechanism can simultaneously generate coordinated patterns of alterations across multiple mutation modalities, including single-base substitutions (SBSs), doublet-base substitutions (DBSs), and small insertions and deletions (IDs). However, these signatures are typically inferred separately and linked post hoc, obscuring their shared underlying mechanisms. To resolve this, we formally define a Mutational Process (MP) as a unified latent activity that induces coupled mutational signatures across these modalities. We developed MOTET, a Bayesian framework that jointly infers multimodal MPs. Applied to 2,583 whole genomes from the PCAWG cohort, MOTET recovers known MPs more accurately than standard post hoc correlation methods. MOTET also identifies a process linking an SBS37-related signature with a TG>CA-dominated DBS component and resolves canonical SBS12-like activity into two separate MPs with distinct tissue distributions. These results establish a paradigm for formally defining catalogs of MPs and demonstrate that integrating across modalities enhances the ability to discover new mutational patterns.

articles.title: Chimera: Cross-Species Single-Cell Generative Modeling of Expression Deployment Relative to Protein Conservation
articles.abstract: A protein's sequence says what a gene could do in another species; the cells of that species say what it does there. Comparative genomics measures the first. Chimera measures the second, a gene's deployment, on the same genes and reports the difference. It aligns single-cell atlases across species in one generative model and returns, for every one-to-one ortholog, the evidence in the counts for a shared expression pattern, and {Delta}[a], the position of that evidence above or below what the protein's identity predicts. This difference is not sequence constraint under another name: across eight tissues, protein identity tracks dN/dS, whereas {Delta}[a] tracks neither. A gene therefore has two coordinates, not one, and the second can contradict the first: spermatocyte genes such as ZPBP2 keep their stage pattern on less conserved proteins, in eight held-out species, whereas conserved hepatocyte enzymes such as ALAS1 share their pattern but not their level. More broadly, genes of specialized cells sit above what their proteins predict in 23 of 24 cohorts, and approved drug targets do so more often than matched genes. Even among nearly identical proteins, where sequence can no longer tell genes apart, the count evidence still does. Nor does this rest on the model alone: independent data support the count evidence in liver and testis and, in a pre-specified test, {Delta}[a] in liver. With both coordinates, one can ask whether another species uses a gene as humans do, the premise of every animal model of a disease gene or drug target.

articles.title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
articles.abstract: Background. Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. Evans Leaders Fund and the Ontario Research Fund Small Infrastructure Fund, 46612

articles.title: Combining non-linear and spectral cardiac variability metrics differentiates rat alcohol drinking with and without challenge
articles.abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remains a substantial global challenge, with notable individual and sex differences. Heart rate variability (HRV) offers a potential link into the autonomic system underlying alcohol drinking. While simpler, time-domain HRV metrics have been explored, non-linear indicators could provide unique insights into more complex states like compulsive drinking, intake that persists despite negative consequences. We examined heart rate traces from male and female rats during intake of alcohol-only and alcohol+10mg/L quinine, a putative compulsive drinking model. In particular, we re-analyzed previously published findings, but newly focused on several non-linear HRV metrics: the Poincare ratio (possibly reflecting sympathovagal balance) and MultiScale entropy (MSE, perhaps reflecting unpredictability in broader and narrower time windows), along with the previously unexamined spectral HRV metrics (the parasympathetic indictor high-frequency HRV, HF-HRV%). HRV was assessed for the first ~1100 heart beats (~2.5 minutes), to assess HRV correlates of greater alcohol front-loading while having approximately similar amount of data per session. Lower Poincare ratio and higher HF-HRV% were overall related to higher alcohol consumption. In contrast, compulsive drinking, but not alcohol-only, was associated with lower broader-window HRV entropy, which was more pronounced in males. Drinking- and sex-related patterns were further identified using Principle Component Analysis, Ordinary Least Squares, and Linear Mixed Models. Limitations included perhaps being underpowered to detect significant relationships, especially in females. Thus, our preliminary findings suggest that combining HRV metrics could represent useful biomarkers for consumption levels during front-loading, which distinguished general intake from compulsion.

articles.title: Contact-phagy remodels ER-mitochondria contact sites
articles.abstract: Membrane contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and other organelles coordinate cellular organization, metabolism and stress responses, yet how these interfaces are selectively remodeled and removed remains poorly understood. Here we identify a selective autophagy pathway that targets defined ER-mitochondria contact-site (ERMCS) subdomains for turnover, a process we term Contact-phagy. The ER-resident chaperone SIGMAR1 forms a functional complex with the ER-phagy receptor CCPG1, and SIGMAR1-CCPG1 nanoclusters define ERMCS-associated sites of autophagy initiation. Contact-phagy is selectively engaged by metabolic and mitochondrial stress and promotes turnover of defined contact-site components without broadly affecting general ER-phagy, mitophagy or bulk autophagy. At these sites, SIGMAR1-CCPG1 function is coupled to mitochondrial fission: MFF promotes DRP1 recruitment to ERMCS, whereas loss of CCPG1 or SIGMAR1 causes abnormal persistence and clustering of DRP1 and MFF, accompanied by altered mitochondrial remodeling. Loss of CCPG1 further disrupts ER-mitochondria organization and mitochondrial function in pancreatic tissue, while pancreatic cancer cells depend on CCPG1 and SIGMAR1 for organelle integrity and bioenergetic capacity. Together, our findings establish Contact-phagy as a selective pathway for the turnover of defined organelle contact site subdomains and suggest a broader principle by which interorganelle interfaces are maintained.

articles.title: Daily light exposure differences between extreme chronotypes persist after alignment to habitual sleep timing
articles.abstract: Purpose: Morning and evening chronotypes may receive light at different clock times, thereby providing differently timed signals to the circadian pacemaker. Prior studies have suggested phase-specific exposure patterns that could counter further advances in early types and delays in late types. We examined whether photoperiod modifies these exposure patterns in a way that could reasonably counteract timing extremes. Methods: We analysed near-eye melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) in 140 participants from an international cohort across seven countries (778 participant-days; 35,949 half-hour observations). We compared four quartiles of midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSF sc ) in clock time and relative to MSF sc using cyclic generalized additive mixed models, accounting for day type, site, photoperiod and individual patterns. In exploratory analyses, we tested moderation of these differences by daylength and used phase-response-curve (PRC) weighting as a conceptual comparison of exposure timing. Results: The modelled extreme evening-type/morning-type exposure ratios averaged 0.16 (95% CI 0.06–0.40) 9.6–11.3 hours before MSF sc (pre-MSF sc ) and 14.0 (5.6–34.8) 0.9–4.4 hours after MSF sc (post-MSF sc ). The models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R 2 (0.795 for clock time; 0.794 for MSF sc -relative time). Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days, with the pre-MSF sc contrast descriptively attenuated on free days. The post-MSF sc ratio increased by a factor of 2.59 (95% CI 1.06–6.34) between civil photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with no significant moderation of the pre-MSF sc contrast. Exploratory weighting by the published PRC gave higher advance-weighted point estimates in extreme evening than extreme morning types; the group difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Extreme chronotypes differ in daily exposure both in clock time and relative to MSF sc . The established questionnaire-based MSF sc measure showed significant post-MSF sc daylength moderation. The exposure patterns and conceptual PRC comparison suggest a possible pathway linking daylight availability to entrainment in extreme chronotypes.

articles.title: Darwinian and Wallacean evolution both explain sexual dichromatism in avian iridescence.
articles.abstract: One of the longest-standing arguments in evolutionary biology is that between Darwin and Wallace on the evolution of sexual dichromatism, and which sex changed colour over time. While Darwin argued that males became more colourful over time, Wallace argued that females became less colourful, and numerous studies have lent support to each hypothesis over time. Iridescent colouration provides a particularly interesting system for studying sexual dichromatism because its conspicuousness is often associated with sexual selection and it has evolved multiple times. Here, using a dataset on iridescent colouration of 25,432 patches from 3,151 bird species, we provide one of the most comprehensive tests to date of the evolutionary origins of sexual dichromatism. We show that both hypotheses explain the evolution of iridescent sexual dichromatism in birds, but that Darwin's hypothesis is more strongly supported with males contributing stronger to evolutionary changes in dichromatism. Furthermore, our analyses support Darwin's prediction that sexual selection is associated to the evolution of dichromatism, but also Wallace's prediction that safer nests facilitate more colourful females (and males), and mostly in patches exposed during incubation. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. articles.title: DeepRNAi: Predicting on- and off-target siRNA activity and establishing a benchmark
articles.abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) silence target genes through RISC-mediated hybridization and cleavage, but can silence unintended transcripts and cause toxicity or complicate regulatory approval. In drug development, empirical assessment by qPCR and RNA-seq is slow, forces early candidate prioritization, and is limited by available species- and genome-appropriate cell models. While extensive empirical screening remains standard practice, there is a significant opportunity for modern AI methods to change this paradigm. We introduce DeepRNAi, a deep learning model that accurately predicts on- and off-target knockdown from siRNA and mRNA sequence. Trained on 16 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 2,031 siRNAs designed to interrogate known siRNA failure modes, and incorporating transcript context from biological foundation models, DeepRNAi is the first in silico method that approaches experimental accuracy. It generalizes across cell models, transcripts, genomes and species, and in a small study distinguishes approved therapeutics from hepatotoxic candidates. The value of DeepRNAi for prioritizing better candidates up front improving likelihood of success later in development is evidenced by a genome-wide survey of 24.4 million siRNAs targeting 7,946 genes, which indicates that 90.1% of the 100 most potent siRNAs have at least some off-target concerns. To support the community, we are publishing a training and benchmark dataset containing 1.84 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 240 siRNAs.

articles.title: Deoxycholic Acid (DCA) a Secondary Bile Acid, Mitigates Ovariectomy-Induced Bone Loss and promotes Bone Healing: A Novel Candidate for Orthopaedic Applications
articles.abstract: Introduction Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMO) is a metabolic disorder, characterized by accelerated bone loss, gut microbiota (GM) dysbiosis and altered microbial metabolites. Deoxycholic acid (DCA) is a secondary bile acid with an FDA-approved drug status for submental fat treatment in adults; however its effect on bone health remains underexplored. Materials and Methods This study investigated the effects of DCA on bone health using both preclinical animal model of PMO and clinical samples from PMO women. DCA (20 mg/kg) was administered to ovariectomised (OVX) mice for 45 days, and its effects on bone microarchitecture and serum cytokines were analysed.
