articles.title: Mechanosensitive YAP–RUNX1 signaling drives TH1 cell dysfunction and tumor immunosuppression
articles.abstract: Tissue stiffening is a predominant malignant physical alteration in cancer progression, yet its effect on specific immune subsets within the tumor microenvironment is not well defined. Here we show that elevated tissue stiffness subverts tumor-infiltrating type 1 helper T (TH1) cells to drive immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, stiffness triggers integrin-mediated mechanotransduction to activate YAP, which translocates to the nucleus and cooperates with RUNX1 to transcriptionally upregulate a set of dysfunction-associated genes. These reprogrammed TH1 cells acquire a distinct dysfunction-associated secretory phenotype, which in turn drives M2-like polarization of macrophages and amplifies local immunosuppression. Notably, inhibiting YAP expression or disrupting YAP–RUNX1 interaction reverses the dysfunctional state of TH1 cells and restores antitumor immunity. These findings delineate a mechano–immunological mechanism by which tumor stiffness subverts TH1 cell functions, indicating a possible therapeutic avenue to alleviate immunosuppression and potentiate immunotherapy efficacy in stiff tumors. Solid tumor stiffness can limit the ability of immune cells to enter and kill tumor cells. Here the authors show that this stiffness activates YAP signaling in type 1 helper T cells, making them dysfunctional and thereby leading to a more immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.

articles.title: Spin order steers a light–matter condensate
articles.abstract: Light–matter condensates get a magnetic control knob. In the layered magnet CrSBr, reorienting the spins with a modest field shifts the condensate’s colour by more than 10 meV.

articles.title: An ulcerative colitis taxonomy defined by individual patient-reported response trajectories
articles.abstract: A barrier to precision medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) is the inability to predict and mechanistically explain treatment responses. Using patient-reported outcomes (PROs) from a phase 3b comparative trial of 768 participants, we identified four distinct patient response-trajectory groups for vedolizumab (anti-integrin) and adalimumab (antitumor necrosis factor). Validation in a second phase 3 trial of 576 participants linked PRO-defined vedolizumab trajectories to long-term disease complications. Bulk, single cell, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics identified vascular inflammation as associated with vedolizumab nonresponse through interactions between SPP1+ macrophages and endothelial cells. In two separate real-world cohorts of 4,981 and 3,854 patients with UC, concomitant use of renin–angiotensin system inhibitors (modulators of vascular inflammation) was associated with reduced long-term complications for vedolizumab but not anticytokine therapies. These findings define a response-trajectory-based taxonomy that requires prospective validation for clinical utility and applications for selecting vedolizumab combination therapy in UC. An analysis of patient-reported trajectories of response to vedolizumab in ulcerative colitis defines disease endotypes and identifies vascular inflammation as a potential resistance mechanism.

articles.title: Deep learning-based gait analysis predicts multisystem health phenotypes
articles.abstract: We developed a gait foundation model from three-dimensional skeletal motion data of 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults, recorded using a depth camera during five motor tasks. Embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 phenotypic targets and provided predictive gains across all 18 body systems in men and 17 out of 18 in women, while also improving prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use.

articles.title: Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial
articles.abstract: Incretin mimetics as obesity therapy induce substantial weight and fat loss but also decrease lean soft tissue mass, possibly impairing skeletal muscle function. Here, in this two-arm randomized controlled trial of adding resistance exercise (REx) to tirzepatide (T), 120 adults with overweight or obesity were treated with tirzepatide and randomized to thrice-weekly resistance exercise training or usual activities for 40 weeks. Tirzepatide was safe, and most participants tolerated up-titration to 15 mg weekly. Adherence to resistance exercise was 91%. Weight loss achieved was similar (T = -22.61 kg, T+REx = -22.28 kg, P = 0.694). For primary outcomes, loss of total fat mass was similar (T = -17.19 kg, T+REx = -17.98 kg, P = 0.700; between-group difference = -0.77 kg, 95% confidence interval (CI): -2.14 kg to 0.60 kg), but resistance exercise reduced loss of total lean soft tissue mass (T = -4.67 kg, T+REx = -3.57 kg, P < 0.001; between-group difference = 1.09 kg, 95% CI: 0.43-1.75 kg). For related endpoints, resistance exercise reduced loss of appendicular lean soft tissue mass (T = -3.55 kg, T+REx = -2.92 kg, P < 0.001). Upper and lower body muscle strength decreased with tirzepatide (bench press -4.09 kg, lat pulldown -4.42 kg, knee extension -4.42 kg) but increased with T+REx (+4.68 kg, +8.58 kg, +5.88 kg, respectively, all P < 0.001 versus tirzepatide). In conclusion, resistance exercise training attenuated loss of total lean soft tissue mass, representing an effective adjunct to tirzepatide anti-obesity therapy. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12623001236684 .

Bound states in the continuum through quantum interference in ultracold atomic collisions
articles.abstract: Quantum-mechanical interaction potentials support localized bound states below the dissociation threshold or delocalized scattering states above it. Although bound states are energetically isolated, scattering states couple a quantum system to environmental modes, making dissipation and loss intrinsic to open systems. Bound states in the continuum are an exception, as destructive interference keeps them localized within the scattering continuum. Theory predicts that such states can arise through interference between two Feshbach resonances coupled to a common continuum. Here we form such an interference-stabilized state in ultracold collisions of 6 Li atoms by coherently coupling two tunable Feshbach resonances using Floquet engineering. At a critical parameter point, elastic and inelastic coupling to the continuum vanish, producing a molecular state above the dissociation threshold. Consequently, resonant scattering features disappear and the colliding atoms become effectively transparent to one another. Full coupled-channel calculations and a minimal non-Hermitian model quantitatively reproduce our observations and identify the state as a Friedrich–Wintgen bound state in the continuum. These results show how quantum interference can control openness in quantum matter and enable the engineering of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.

Conditional biologics in cancer immunotherapy: mechanisms, applications and clinical progress
articles.abstract: Conditional biologics (CBs) — protein therapeutics engineered to selectively activate within the tumour microenvironment — have the potential to increase the potency and limit the off-target adverse effects of cancer immunotherapies. This Review describes the design principles and activation mechanisms of CBs, assesses those being investigated in the clinic, and addresses ongoing challenges and future directions for the field.

articles.title: Histone lysine demethylases in the third decade: biology and therapeutic prospects
articles.abstract: Histone lysine demethylases regulate gene expression and chromatin structure and help to integrate epigenetics with metabolic and immune responses. This Review discusses the diverse contributions of these demethylases to disease pathogenesis, particularly cancer, and the efforts underway to target them with small molecules.

articles.title: The mammalian archaeome: diversity, function and emerging roles in health and disease
articles.abstract: In this Review, Moissl-Eichinger and colleagues explore the distribution, diversity and function of the mammalian archaeome, with a focus on humans and ruminants. They explore the ecological and physiological roles of Methanobrevibacter spp. as key gastrointestinal colonizers, the archaeal interactions with bacterial communities and the host, and the impact of health and disease on the human archaeome.

articles.title: The microbiome’s voyage beyond Earth
articles.abstract: This Genome Watch discusses how spaceflights affect microbiome composition and dynamics, highlighting how integrating metabolic and host data with microbiome monitoring could support astronaut health during long-term deep-space missions.

articles.title: Mitsunobu reactions using iminophosphorane reagents
articles.abstract: An in situ-generated iminophosphorane enables C–O, C–N, C–S and C–C bond formation from primary and secondary alcohols. The process overcomes the pronucleophile pKa limitation associated with traditional Mitsunobu reactions while simplifying purification and avoiding the requirement for explosive azodicarboxylate reagents.

articles.title: ANGPTL4 Inhibition in Adults with Elevated Triglyceride Levels
articles.abstract: BackgroundAngiopoietin-like protein 4 (ANGPTL4) inhibits lipoprotein lipase and regulates triglyceride-rich lipoprotein metabolism. MAR001 is a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL4 that is being evaluated for lowering triglyceride levels.MethodsWe conducted a two-part, phase 2b, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. In part A, the focus of this report, we enrolled adults who had a nonfasting triglyceride level of at least 175 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 35 mg per deciliter at initial screening, followed by a fasting triglyceride level of at least 150 mg per deciliter and a remnant cholesterol level of at least 30 mg per deciliter on confirmatory screening. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1 ratio to receive MAR001 at a dose of 300, 450, or 900 mg or matching placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. The primary end point was the percent change from baseline in the fasting triglyceride level at week 12, reported as the difference between each MAR001 dose group and the placebo group (placebo-adjusted change).ResultsA total of 236 participants were enrolled in the trial, with 177 assigned to receive MAR001 and 59 to receive placebo; a total of 235 participants received at least one dose of MAR001 or placebo and were included in the primary efficacy analyses. The mean age of the participants was 60.4 years, and 39% were women. The median triglyceride level at baseline was 249.5 mg per deciliter (interquartile range, 210.0 to 313.0). At week 12, in an intention-to-treat analysis, the placebo-adjusted least-squares mean percent changes in the fasting triglyceride level were -39.1 percentage points, -40.5 percentage points, and -45.3 percentage points for the 300-mg, 450-mg, and 900-mg doses, respectively (PConclusionsInhibition of ANGPTL4 with MAR001 significantly reduced fasting triglyceride levels at 12 weeks. (Funded by Marea Therapeutics; TYDAL-TIMI 78 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT07028749.).

articles.title: A promoter variant enables watermelon to escape waterlogging
Chlorophagy targets chloroplasts irreversibly damaged by photoinhibition
articles.abstract: Proposed model of intracellular responses of Arabidopsis leaf mesophyll cells to photoinhibition, as suggested in this study. Summary Chlorophagy removes photodamaged chloroplasts in plants, while individual chloroplasts are also protected by mechanisms that limit damage to the photosynthetic apparatus caused by excess light energy, known as photoinhibition. How chlorophagy is functionally coupled with chloroplast‐level protective mechanisms during acclimation to photoinhibition remains unclear. We investigated acclimatory responses to photoinhibition at the intracellular level in Arabidopsis thaliana through an integrative analysis combining Chl fluorescence measurements, microscopy imaging, and genetic analyses using mutants defective in nonphotochemical quenching (NPQ) or the chloroplast avoidance response. The functionality of individual chloroplasts was further assessed by Chl fluorescence lifetime imaging and probe‐based visualization of singlet oxygen and starch. Severe photoinhibition of photosystem II precedes the appearance of abnormally swollen chloroplasts, which are subsequently recognized by the autophagy machinery for degradation. The swollen chloroplasts represent irreversibly damaged chloroplasts that accumulate reactive oxygen species and lose photosynthetic function. The formation of these nonfunctional chloroplasts was enhanced in mutants defective in NPQ or the chloroplast avoidance response, and hyperaccumulation of nonfunctional chloroplasts led to necrotic cell death. Together, our findings illustrate how multilayered responses coordinate acclimation to photoinhibition: Chloroplast protective mechanisms minimize the formation of nonfunctional chloroplasts while chlorophagy removes them when they arise.

articles.title: Strigolactones modulate iron uptake in plants
articles.abstract: Model for strigolactone regulation of basal iron uptake in Arabidopsis and maize. Summary Strigolactone (SL) hormones influence a wide range of developmental and physiological processes but have not previously been linked to plant iron homeostasis. Here, we identify the gene underlying the iron‐deficient maize mutant interveinal yellow (ivy) as ZmCCD8, a key enzyme in SL biosynthesis. Maize ivy/ccd8 mutants exhibit reduced expression of iron‐regulated genes, including IRO2 and genes involved in iron chelator and transporter biosynthesis. Application of the synthetic SL rac‐GR24 restores gene expression and alleviates chlorosis. Under iron‐deficient conditions, ccd8 mutants show normal upregulation of iron uptake genes, indicating that SLs are not required for the deficiency response but are essential for maintaining basal iron gene expression under sufficient iron. Similar chlorosis in Arabidopsis and rice SL mutants under moderate iron suggests a conserved role for SLs in iron regulation, with potential agricultural applications. We propose that strigolactone signaling acts as an upstream regulatory input to the established FIT/IRO2‐centered iron‐deficiency network, with SMXL/D53 proteins functioning as negative regulators and iron deficiency providing the principal activating cue.

articles.title: The cyanobacterium Anabaena uses pleomorphism as an acclimation strategy to high‐light stress
articles.abstract: The cyanobacterium Anabaena exhibits remarkable morphological plasticity in response to changes in light intensity. These reversible changes are associated with the repositioning of thylakoids within the cytoplasm. Here, we show that cell morphology is determined by the balance between the activities of two peptidoglycan assembly systems, the elongasome and class A penicillin‐binding proteins, which respond oppositely to light intensity. By modulating light absorption and photosynthetic performance, changes in cell morphology enable large globular cells to mitigate the deleterious effects of high‐light stress, revealing morphological plasticity as a previously unrecognized mechanism of acclimation to high light. Summary Phytoplankton species display characteristic morphologies that are generally assumed to confer adaptive advantages, yet the functional significance of cell shape remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether pleomorphism contributes to acclimation to changing light environments. Using the cyanobacterium Anabaena sp. PCC 7120 as a model system, we combined molecular genetics, microscopy, physiological measurements and biophysical analyses to determine how morphology is regulated and how it affects photosynthetic performance under different light intensities. We show that Anabaena undergoes a reversible light‐dependent morphological transition from rod‐shaped cells under low light to large globular cells under high‐light stress. This transition is controlled by the relative activities of the elongasome and class A penicillin‐binding proteins and is accompanied by thylakoid reorganization. The globular morphology reduces light absorption and enables cells to maintain photosynthetic activity under photoinhibitory conditions. Our findings establish a mechanistic link between cell‐wall remodeling, cellular optics and photosynthetic performance, revealing pleomorphism as a dynamic acclimation strategy to high‐light stress. More broadly, this work provides experimental support for the packaging effect and highlights morphology as an active determinant of phytoplankton acclimation capacity.

articles.title: Atomistic Simulation of Subcritical Crack Growth in Glass in Vacuum
articles.abstract: We report atomistic simulations of subcritical crack growth rates in silica glass that quantitatively align with experimental data. This result was achieved by a careful selection of simulation cell geometry and boundary conditions, a novel crack tip tracking algorithm, a robust interatomic potential that balances accuracy with computational efficiency, and high-performance parallel computing algorithms and resources. The simulations reveal a succession of burst-arrest events that produce subcritical crack growth across a broad range of rates, extending up to kilometers per second.

articles.title: Dark-Matter-Induced Nuclear Deexcitation at the Short-Baseline Near Detector with Ab Initio Nuclear Theory
articles.abstract: We explore the sensitivity of the short-baseline near detector (SBND) experiment to light dark matter using MeV-scale electromagnetic activity. Inelastic scattering of dark matter with argon nuclei can excite nuclear states that subsequently deexcite via the emission of MeV-scale photons, producing localized low-energy ``blip'' signatures in a liquid argon time projection chamber. We perform state-of-the-art ab initio nuclear calculations, including all relevant argon excited states with energies up to 18 MeV, to provide reliable predictions for these signals. After accounting for relevant backgrounds, we find that SBND can probe previously unexplored regions of parameter space for light dark matter.

articles.title: Deconfined Quantum Critical Point in a Dissipative Spin-1/2 Chain
articles.abstract: Open quantum spin systems offer a previously unexplored route to realizing deconfined quantum criticality. We consider a spin-$1/2$ $J\text{\ensuremath{-}}{Q}_{3}$ chain composed of an antiferromagnetic (AFM) Heisenberg exchange and a competing multispin interaction favoring a valence-bond solid (VBS) state, with each spin component coupled to an independent bosonic bath. Combining non-Abelian bosonization and renormalization-group (RG) analysis with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, we map out the phase diagram and characterize the associated phase transitions. We show that strong dissipation stabilizes an AFM phase for sub-Ohmic, Ohmic, and super-Ohmic baths. Continuous AFM-VBS transitions at finite dissipation are found upon increasing the multispin interaction in both the sub-Ohmic and Ohmic regimes, with their critical properties obtained through perturbative RG analysis and QMC simulations. In the Ohmic case, the critical point features spinon deconfinement and emergent O(4) symmetry. In the sub-Ohmic regime, the transition is controlled by a continuous family of nontrivial fixed points parameterized by the bath spectral exponent $s$ and may also exhibit spinon deconfinement provided that spinons remain deconfined in the dissipative VBS phase. Furthermore, in the super-Ohmic regime, we propose a transition from the AFM to the quasi-long-range ordered (QLRO) phase in addition to the QLRO-VBS transition.

articles.title: First-Principles Effective Mass in the Three-Dimensional Uniform Electron Gas
articles.abstract: The quasiparticle effective mass m* of the three-dimensional uniform electron gas is a fundamental Fermi-liquid parameter whose value and density dependence have remained controversial for decades. Using renormalized perturbation theory with explicit counterterms, we determine m* in the metallic reg…

articles.title: Hydrodynamics of the Viscous Electron Fluid in Cadmium
articles.abstract: Measurements on micrometer-scale cadmium samples provide definitive evidence of an unusual charge-transport regime in a 3D metal.

articles.title: Intracycle Interference in Strong-Field Photoemission from a Tungsten Needle Tip
articles.abstract: Electrons photoemitted by strong laser fields can rescatter, generating attosecond high harmonics. Spectral peaks arise from inter- and intracycle interference of coherent electron wave packets. While intercycle interference is well known, intracycle interference of plateau electrons has not been ob…

articles.title: Superparamagnetism in an Interacting Nanomagnet Array: A Tale of Three Temperatures
articles.abstract: Superparamagnetic collections of thermally fluctuating nanomagnet moments undergo a dynamic freezing known as a blocking transition upon cooling. The collective behavior becomes more complex when neighboring nanomagnets interact, and is further complicated when the constituent material of the nanomagnets has a temperature-dependent magnetization. Such a system can exhibit loss of ergodicity or the development of long-range order, and is experimentally accessible in artificial spin ice arrays, which provide an excellent framework for investigating ergodicity loss and equilibration on laboratory timescales. Using a macrospin model and a nonstandard Monte Carlo method, we describe the range of phase space that is thermally accessible, framing the problem within the context of the three relevant temperatures: the Curie temperature, the blocking temperature, and the collective ordering temperature of the nanomagnetic system. Our approach is generalizable and can be extended to a wide range of similar magnetic systems that are available for rigorous experimental tests.

articles.title: Terahertz Switching of Two-dimensional Antiferromagnetic Order
articles.abstract: Identifying the transition pathway for ultrafast switching between distinct antiferromagnetic orders, while holding promise to realize unprecedentedly small and fast spin devices, remains largely unexplored. Herein, we show that rectifying structure with light can serve as a powerful tool to achieve nonthermal antiferromagnetic order switching in a monolayer antiferromagnet ${\mathrm{MnPSe}}_{3}$. By resolving the spin-phonon coupling strength, we identify a highly selective coupling of the magnetic order with a Raman-active ${\mathrm{E}}_{g}$ phonon. After resonantly pumping two degenerate infrared-active ${\mathrm{E}}_{u}$ modes, we obtain a new metastable out-of-equilibrium state holding shifted structure along the ${\mathrm{E}}_{g}$ mode. Such lattice distortion offers a sustained nonthermal driving field to trigger a phase switch from a N\'eel-type to a zigzag-type antiferromagnetic order within the coherent phonon lifetime. By varying the pumping polarization and intensity, we provide a parameter regime for realistic light-driven magnetic phase transitions. Such an ultrafast antiferromagnetism switch can be identified by pump-probe measurements of the order-parameter-like behavior in the second harmonic generation signal or absorption spectrum.

articles.title: Universal Criticality of Entropy Production in Chemical Reaction Networks
articles.abstract: In homogeneous reversible chemical reactions, a prototypical nonequilibrium phenomenon, entropy-production fluctuations represent a sharper probe of nonequilibrium criticality than entropy-production response to variations in the chemical species concentrations.

articles.title: Noninvertible Bosonic Chiral Symmetry on the Lattice
articles.abstract: Construction of a continuous chiral symmetry in a 3D quantum rotor model demonstrates that gauging charge symmetry yields noninvertible, duality-like lattice operations.

articles.title: Spectral Small-Incremental Entangling: Breaking Quasipolynomial Complexity Barriers in Long-Range Interacting Systems
articles.abstract: Researchers establish universal limits on quantum entanglement-spectrum evolution, enabling efficient classical simulations of long-range interacting systems.

articles.title: Rare-earth recycling efforts multiply
articles.abstract: As global demand for powerful magnets swells and tensions with China fester, Western countries are renewing efforts to achieve independent supply chains.

articles.title: [Articles] Cardiovascular outcomes with survodutide in adults with obesity at increased cardiovascular risk (SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: In participants with obesity with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease or at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, survodutide was not associated with increased risk for the primary composite endpoint of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event compared with placebo. This cardiovascular safety trial provides clinicians with reassuring data that treatment with survodutide, a novel glucagon receptor–GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk.

articles.title: [Articles] Efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2–3 fibrosis: a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled study
articles.abstract: Treatment with efinopegdutide resulted in a significantly greater proportion of participants with MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis compared with placebo. The 7 mg dose showed the most favourable benefit–risk profile, improving fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis in approximately half of participants after 1 year of treatment. These findings support the potential utility of efinopegdutide as a once-weekly GLP-1–glucagon receptor co-agonist in MASH.

articles.title: [Comment] Efinopegdutide: a step towards precision in MASH therapy?
articles.abstract: The global impact of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) across diverse populations is significant. MASH cirrhosis has become a leading indication for liver transplantation and a primary driver of hepatocellular carcinoma. Advanced MASH fibrosis is associated with increased all-cause mortality and a nearly two-times increased risk of extrahepatic malignancies.1

articles.title: Lipid II flipping in monoderms: structural insights from Staphylococcus aureus
articles.abstract: Peptidoglycan synthesis in diderm and monoderm bacteria depends on lipid II flipping between membrane leaflets, but how this process occurs remains unclear. Li et al. report cryogenic electron microscopy structures of a lipid II flippase from the monoderm Staphylococcus aureus and provide a direct comparison with similar flippases from diderm bacteria.

articles.title: The best-laid plans are not worth it
articles.abstract: Planning is essential for achieving long-term goals but is fraught with challenges in an uncertain world. In a timely study, Lei et al. show that uncertainty diminished people’s willingness to plan and that people reduced planning effort by treating uncertain choices as deterministic and planning less carefully.

articles.title: Ab Initio Molecular Dynamics-Guided Machine-Learning Potentials for Mapping Nitric Oxide Interactions with Oxygen-Covered Graphite
articles.abstract: Exploratory ab initio molecular dynamics is used to construct machine-learning interatomic potentials for NO interactions with highly oriented pyrolytic graphite at 33\% bridge-site oxygen coverage. Representative configurations sampled across surface temperatures and incidence energies provide reference energies and forces for training and validation. The selected potential enables relaxation of 300 adsorption configurations and construction of spatial and angular interaction maps. These maps reveal increasingly restricted attractive regions during vertical approach and reduced short-range repulsion upon molecular reorientation. The resulting adsorption geometries and interaction landscapes guide further first-principles sampling toward refining potentials for NO oxidation dynamics.

articles.title: Analytic $GW$-Bethe--Salpeter Gradients with Quasiparticle Response in the Resolution of the Identity
articles.abstract: Analytic nuclear gradients for excited states from the Bethe$-$Salpeter equation (BSE) in the static screening approximation are presented within this work. The response of the screened interaction to nuclear displacements is treated within the resolution-of-the-identity (RI) approximation, in close analogy to RI random phase approximation gradients, and is folded into the Lagrangian formalism of time-dependent density functional theory gradients. Quasiparticle gradients enter via the full analytic derivative of the corrections for RI contour-deformation $G_0W_0$ and ev$GW$, also taking into account that incomplete quasiparticle spectra are typically supplied. Comparisons to earlier approaches using a geometry-independent fixed quasiparticle correction are made. For the latter, the orbital-rotation terms are derived exactly, too. The implemented gradient scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$, and the three-index integrals are processed in batches with a memory demand of $\mathcal{O}(N_\mathrm{aux}^2 + N_\mathrm{occ}^2 N_\mathrm{aux})$. Excited-state geometries of a set of small molecules are compared to EOM-CCSD references and to TD-DFT. It is shown that the full quasiparticle gradient removes most of the systematic underestimation of the bond lengths in singlet excited states. A comparison along the C$-$C stretch of acetylene shows that the neglected derivative of the quasiparticle corrections is modest, but becomes erratic for $G_0W_0$ near poles of the self-energy, which ev$GW$ avoids.

articles.title: Autonomous Optimization of Numerical Algorithms by an AI Agent: Application to Atomistic Simulation
articles.abstract: Coding agents built on large language models, run in automated improvement loops, can discover more efficient algorithms. We present AIOA, a framework that brings this approach to the numerical algorithms of atomistic simulation: an agent improves an algorithm against a pre-specified metric in a loop guarded by verifiers it cannot alter. Applied to ASE, a widely used atomistic simulation library, AIOA targets two facets of an algorithm: its implementation, rewritten to run faster with unchanged results, and the method itself, redesigned to converge with fewer force evaluations. Agents made six kernels 22-24 times faster on average in Python with NumPy and SciPy. On unseen problems, optimizers from the best configuration needed 3.1-3.4 times fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS for structure relaxation and 4.6-17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for reaction paths. The agents' optimizers also contain two algorithmic components we did not find in the literature.

articles.title: Catalysis-induced phase separation of enzymes via diffusivity contrast
articles.abstract: Catalysis can drive phase separation by coupling local chemical composition to molecular transport, even in the absence of attractive interactions. Here, we demonstrate such catalysis-induced phase separation in a microscopic particle-based model of enzymes catalyzing the interconversion of substrate and product molecules with different diffusivities. We derive an analytical instability criterion in the dilute limit, showing that a homogeneous mixture becomes unstable when the nonequilibrium chemical drive and the diffusivity contrast are sufficiently large, and the substrate and product concentration exceeds a threshold set by the enzyme volume. Brownian-dynamics simulations confirm the predicted instability and reveal macroscopic coexistence of enzyme-rich and enzyme-poor phases, including in regimes where equilibrium depletion interactions cannot account for demixing. Finally, we show that, upon eliminating the fast chemical degrees of freedom, the reactive ternary mixture maps onto an effective binary mixture nonreciprocal interactions. Our results establish an explicit microscopic mechanism for catalysis-induced phase separation and connect chemically driven phase separation to the physics of motility-regulated and nonreciprocal matter.

articles.title: Damped polarizability and first hyperpolarizability of large systems with hybrid functionals: self-consistent and Lanczos solvers
articles.abstract: We present a damped coupled-perturbed Kohn-Sham method to compute the dynamical polarizability and first hyperpolarizability of finite systems, implemented in the CRYSTAL code for semi-local, global and range-separated hybrid functionals. The approach is based on the adiabatic time-dependent density functional theory for the complex-valued (hyper)polarizabilities, describing optical phenomena such as absorption, and the nonlinear second-harmonic generation, rectification and Pockels effect. These are obtained either at individual frequencies with a self-consistent solver based on Pulay extrapolation, or at an arbitrary grid of frequency and damping factors with a Lanczos solver, from which the first-order amplitudes required in the hyperpolarizability can be reconstructed. With hybrid functionals, the self-consistent solver tends to become impractical at some point beyond the absorption onset, where there are many excitations for which the external frequency lies between their energy and those of their contributing single-particle transitions, and its convergence eventually stalls for large systems. In contrast, the convergence of the Lanczos method is essentially independent of size, hence the cost of the dynamical response calculation scales with system size as the hybrid ground-state calculation. The implementation is validated in a small molecule and, as an application, we study the first and second-order optical response of a series of hexagonal boron nitride flakes of up to 324 atoms. The use of range-separated hybrid functionals allows to capture the strongly-bound first excitation of the monolayer, and evidences the failure of the self-consistent method to converge excitations with strong electron-hole attraction.

articles.title: Extending the reach of real-space real-time TDDFT: new developments in the Octopus code
articles.abstract: Octopus is an open-source package implementing time-dependent density functional theory in a real-space, real-time formulation. Here we report on the developments since our previous contribution to the Special Topic Issue on Electronic Structure Software [J. Chem. Phys. 152, 124119 (2020)]. New exchange-correlation functionals extend the range of systems that can be treated, while advances in relativistic and all-electron methods open the door to core-electron spectroscopy. New capabilities for lattice dynamics - stress-tensor calculation, geometry optimization, support for machine-learned force fields, and phonon calculations - enable a fully ab initio description of light-induced lattice dynamics in real time. We also present developments that move beyond the dipole approximation, capturing light-matter interaction more faithfully. Improved methods for exciton dynamics complement a set of algorithmic advances - new propagation schemes, imaginary-time evolution, and a refactored grid handling more than a billion points - that together substantially improve performance and scalability. Combined with technical improvements such as AMD GPU support and a modernized build system, these developments consolidate Octopus as a versatile, high-performance platform for exploring electronic excitations, light-matter interaction, and nonequilibrium dynamics in molecules, nanostructures, and extended systems.

articles.title: Integer electron-count cuts in variational second-order reduced-density-matrix theory. II. A convergent hierarchy of rigorous relaxations for real-space pair-density representability
articles.abstract: Variational second-order reduced-density-matrix calculations can dissociate molecules into fractionally charged fragments; Part I largely removed this failure with integer electron-count conditions on fixed partitions. Building on the realizability theory of point processes, we place these conditions in a convergent hierarchy of rigorous relaxations, defined by finite occupation linear programs (LPs) on spatial partitions, for real-space pair densities at fixed one-particle density. Every level contains all representable pair densities, the levels tighten under nested refinement, and their intersection characterizes pair densities admitting a symmetric $N$-particle probability-measure extension. In a fixed orbital basis the levels give monotonically increasing lower bounds to the full configuration-interaction energy, which they need not reach, even for the Coulomb repulsion. The spin-summed real-space cuts of Part I are its two-cell members. The LP optimum is also a measure: at fixed one-particle density it equals the $L^1$ distance of the coarse-grained candidate from representability and increases under refinement to that of the candidate, with a vanishing coarse-graining error; its primal law constructs a representable approximation, and its dual a violated valid inequality, used as a cut in molecular calculations. The count conditions are not implied by the usual positivity conditions: moment data that satisfy all three-particle positivity conditions, including $T_1$ and $T_2$, give through Gaussian orbitals a smooth pair density that violates an integer count. For atoms at fractional electron number, ensemble relaxations with the integer-count condition lie closer to the exact piecewise-linear energy than the zero-variance fixed-$N$ form.

articles.title: On the Method of Projection onto Localized States for Describing Reactions and Clustering
articles.abstract: The method of projection onto localized states intended for describing reactions and clustering is examined. In particular, the method offers a simple extension of the no-core shell model to continuum- and clusterized bound states. A critical analysis of a previous realization of the method is provided. A way to minimize the number of basis functions required for convergence is given. An easy way to obtain exactly unitary and symmetric $S$ matrix from calculations is pointed out. The method is tested in one- and two-channel $np$ scattering problems with the Daejeon $NN$ interaction. It is shown that excellent convergence can be reached even when only oscillator states with low number of excitation quanta are retained.

articles.title: SATE: Transferable Spin-Adapted Neural Wavefunctions
articles.abstract: Accurate prediction of molecular reactivity requires both accurate and computationally efficient description of electron correlation and spin across various molecular geometries and electronic states. We introduce SATE, a spin-adapted transferable neural wavefunction architecture with effective core potentials. SATE combines a transferable neural wavefunction, the spin-adapted antisymmetrization method, and effective core potentials into a single foundation model architecture pretrained on compositions containing selected elements from hydrogen to bromine. After pretraining and adaptation, our model is able to predict 3d transition-metal spin-state gaps, bond dissociation energies, and reaction energies by addressing two key issues. First, including the core potentials into the model allows us to reduce the number of explicitly treated electrons. Second, using spin-adapted antisymmetrization enforces the prescribed total spin by construction. By testing our model with 3d transition metal chemistry, we evaluate our model's description of strong electron correlation and competing electronic states in such compounds. We find that pretraining improves most tested component energies at matched adaptation budgets, while improvements in spin-state gaps, dissociation energies, and reaction energies remain system dependent. Ultimately, our work lays the foundation for more accurate and transferable modeling of molecular systems by combining the computational efficiency of effective core potentials with explicit control over total spin.

articles.title: Variational free complement method with Gaussian expanded complement functions: extensions of general atomic framework including helium and lithium ground states with geminal induced expansion length
articles.abstract: We expand the previous framework of hierarchical-decontraction Gaussian expanded complement functions approach (arXiv: 2603.16262v2) of the free complement (FC) method to $N$-electron atomic systems including general permutations. We consider the possibility that the Gaussian expansion length depends on the presence of the geminal $g$ function. To be more specific, fewer expansion length shall be used when the two-electron $g$ function is combined with the initial wavefunction. The present approach is applied to the ground states of the helium and lithium atoms. The complement function generations via 2s$\rightarrow$1s channel in the lithium ground state are discussed. Symmetries for the associated $N$-electron integrals are analyzed.

articles.title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
articles.abstract: Sensory neurons are traditionally viewed as feature detectors that respond with an increase in firing rate to preferred stimuli while remaining unresponsive to others. Here, we identify a dual-feature encoding strategy in macaque visual cortex, wherein many neurons in areas V1 and V4 are selectively tuned to two distinct visual features—one that enhances and one that suppresses activity—around an elevated baseline firing rate. By combining neuronal recordings with functional digital twin models—deep learning-based predictive models of biological neurons—we were able to systematically identify each neuron’s preferred and non-preferred features. These feature pairs served as anchors for a continuous, low-dimensional axis in natural image similarity space, along which neuronal activity varied approximately linearly. Within a single visual area, visual features that strongly or weakly activated individual neurons also had a high probability of modulating the activity of other neurons, suggesting a shared feature selectivity across the population that structures stimulus encoding. We show that this encoding strategy is conserved across species, present in both primary and lateral visual areas of mouse cortex. Dual-feature selectivity is consistent with recent anatomical evidence for feature-specific inhibitory connectivity, complementing the feature-detector principle through circuit mechanisms in which selective excitation and inhibition may together enhance the representational capacity of the neuronal population.

articles.title: Virus-specific impacts on honey bee flight performance are mediated by the octopamine pathway
articles.abstract: High annual honey bee colony losses are associated with environmental and biological stressors, including virus infections. In insects, the octopamine (OA) pathway orchestrates the ‘fight-or-flight’ response, regulating energy mobilization, temperature, and flight. We determined that sacbrood virus (SBV) infections induce expression of an OA receptor and enhance honey flight performance, whereas deformed wing virus (DWV) infections reduce flight performance, but how viruses interface with this pathway remained unknown. To elucidate the relationships between the OA response, virus infection, and flight, honey bees were infected with SBV or DWV and exposed to OA, epinastine (EP) – an OA receptor antagonist, or both OA and EP; flight and gene expression were assessed. Pharmacologic manipulation revealed that OA supplementation rescued flight deficits in DWV-infected bees, but diminished performance in SBV-infected bees, while blocking OA receptors altered these effects. Transcriptome analyses indicated that SBV infections, and DWV infection with OA treatment, activated honey bee metabolic pathways, and that SBV-infected bees had greater expression of genes involved in OA synthesis, unless treated with OA. These results provide mechanistic insight for virus-specific impacts on honey bee flight, which may have consequences for foraging efficiency, colony health, and virus transmission.

articles.title: Abstract 11758: Optineurin-Mediated Selective Autophagy Regulates Connexin 43 Expression and Attenuates Electrical Remodeling in Atrial Fibrillation
articles.abstract: Background: Connexin 43 (Cx43) gap junctions are abnormally accumulated and lateralized in Atrial fibrillation (AF), however, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. The purpose of this study is to explore the role of optineurin (OPTN), a selective autophagy receptor, in maintaining Cx43 homeostasis and protecting against AF. Methods: Firstly, three publicly available AF-related datasets were analyzed to evaluate the potential relationship of OPTN with AF. Then, to examine whether OPTN-mediated selective autophagy is involved in regulating the fate of Cx43 in AF, Co-IP and immunofluorescence staining were used to determine Cx43/LC3B/OPTN colocalization; 3-MA (autophagy inhibitor) and MG132 (proteasome inhibitor) were used to check the Cx43 degradation pathway in AC-16/H9C2 cells, which underwent programmed electrical stimulation (1 Hz, 10 V, 4 ms, 24 h). Finally, rats with AAV-mediated OPTN overexpression and autophagy regulators were used to detect the effect of OPTN-mediated autophagy on the expression and distribution of Cx43 in AF. Results: OPTN was downregulated in AF (datasets and patient tissues), accompanied by a decrease in LC3B-II/I and an increase in p62. Co-IP confirmed OPTN-Cx43 binding. In OPTN-overexpressing H9C2 cells, MG132 treatment failed to change Cx43 expression level, whereas inhibition of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway by 3-MA led to marked accumulation of Cx43. OPTN overexpression promoted the colocalization of Cx43 with LC3, whereas opposite results were observed in cardiomyocytes transfected with OPTN-specific siRNA. In AF rats, autophagy activation or OPTN overexpression reduced heart weight/body weight ratio, AF duration, left atrial enlargement, structural disorganization, fibrosis, Cx43 lateralization, apoptosis, and oxidative stress. Concurrently, these treatments improved conduction time, conduction velocity, conduction heterogeneity, and AF susceptibility. Conclusions: OPTN-mediated selective autophagy has an important effect on reducing pathological accumulation and abnormal distribution of Cx43 in AF, which provides new mechanistic insights and potential therapeutic targets for AF. articles.title: Abstract 13429: Association of Fibrosis-4 Scores as a Time Varying Covariate with Cardiovascular Disease Outcomes: A Retrospective Cohort Study in A National Cohort of Primary Care Patients
articles.abstract: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, a manifestation of the metabolic syndrome affects around 38% of Americans. It is associated with a higher risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD) events-i.e., acute myocardial infarction (AMI), congestive heart failure (CHF), and ischemic stroke. Fibrosis-4 Index (FIB-4) is calculated using aminotransferases [aspartate (AST) and alanine (ALT)], and platelets [FIB-4 =(Age x AST)/(Platelets x √ALT). It assesses advanced fibrosis risk in patients with chronic liver disease. FIB-4 has been shown to have an association with CVD events but is not utilized as a predictor of CVD outcomes in clinical practice. We wanted to understand the additional predictive information of FIB-4 beyond traditional CVD risk indicators and how this association varies over time, while controlling for cardiometabolic therapies like statins, insulin, metformin, glucagon like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1a). Methods: This is a retrospective cohort study of electronic health record data from a national cohort of Veterans, extracted from the VA Corporate Data Warehouse. Veterans with calculable FIB-4 scores from January 2011 to December 2025 were identified, and excluded if CVD event occurred before 2011. FIB-4 scores were categorized as low (FIB-4 <1.3), indeterminate (1.3 ≤ FIB-4 <2.67), or high-risk (FIB-4 ≥ 2.67) for advanced fibrosis. We used multivariable complementary log-log (cloglog) regression models to evaluate the association between FIB-4 scores and other potential confounders and covariates with time to composite CVD event outcome (AMI, CHF, and stroke). Results: A total of 2,431,410 unique patients were identified. Approximately 45% of patients were 64 years of age or older, male (93.5%), and White (73.9%). Among this cohort, 43% had diabetes mellitus, 24% had chronic kidney disease (CKD), and 24.2% had severe liver disease (SLD). During a mean follow-up of 10.23 years, patients with FIB-4 scores at high- (HR=1.26; 95% CI [1.25 - 1.27]) or indeterminate-risk (HR=1.26; 95% CI [1.09 - 1.1.09 - 1.10]) for advanced fibrosis were more likely to experience a CVD event compared to those with low-risk FIB-4 scores. Other factors associated with an elevated hazard for CVD events included CKD (HR=1.58; 95%CI [1.57 - 1.59]), SLD (HR=1.31; 95%CI [1.30 - 1.33]), prescription for insulin (HR=1.94; 95% CI [1.93 - 1.96]) and statin (HR=2.02; 95% CI [2.01 - 2.03]). Alternatively, a prescription for GLP-1a and metformin had an associated 19% (HR=0.81; 95% CI [1.93 - 1.96]) and 12% (HR=0.88; 95%CI [0.87 - 0.89]) reduction of CVD event hazard, respectively. Conclusions: In a large cohort of Veterans from primary care, FIB-4 scores at high- and indeterminate-risk for advanced fibrosis were associated with an increased risk of incident CVD over time. The utility of adding FIB-4 components to future CVD risk prognostication requires further exploration.

articles.title: Abstract 15594: Integrated Analysis of Cite-Sequencing and Plasma Proteomics Reveals Immune Signatures of Doxorubicin Cardiotoxicity
articles.abstract: Introduction: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin (Dox) are highly effective chemotherapeutic agents that treat a variety of malignancies, but their use is limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxic effects. While specific immune cell types have been implicated in the pathogenesis of cardiotoxicity, a comprehensive understanding of the immune landscape of Dox cardiomyopathy is lacking. Methods: Wild-type mice were treated with either saline or low-dose Dox (3 mg/kg x 8 intraperitoneally), a regimen that replicates delayed cardiomyopathy seen in patients. CD45+ cardiac immune cells were isolated using magnetic-activated cell sorting. CITE-seq was used to map the cardiac immune composition within the tissue. The top 500 differentially expressed genes between saline-treated and Dox-treated hearts were further investigated using mouse and human plasma proteomics. Flow cytometry and ELISA were further used to validate findings in mice with Dox cardiomyopathy. Results: Nineteen distinct immune cell clusters were identified in mouse hearts treated with saline or Dox. Dox increased both the number and proportion of cardiac neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, NK cells, dendritic cells, and T-cells. Several of these populations were validated by flow cytometry, and remained increased at a chronic time point. Differential gene analysis across immune cell types revealed an increase in both pro-inflammatory genes and pro-repair mediators in Dox-treated hearts. We compared these top genes to the plasma proteome of mice treated with Dox and found 48 to be similarly changed after correction for false discovery rate, suggesting overlap between the cardiac and systemic immune response. We then looked for matching proteins in the plasma proteome from lymphoma patients treated with anthracyclines and found 3 proteins to be associated with early cardiac toxicity: IGFBP-3 (R=-0.4, p=0.01), IGFBP-7 (R=-0.35, p=0.03), and IEX1 (R=-0.37, p=0.02). Validation by ELISA showed correlation of IGFBP-3 (R=-0.38, p=0.002) and IGFBP-7 (R=-0.31, p=0.01) with Dox cardiotoxicity, both of which were expressed by highly inflammatory and pro-fibrotic leukocytes. Conclusion: This study provides novel insight into the immune response to Dox treatment. Mediators of local cardiac and systemic inflammation, such as IGFBP3/7, have the potential to serve as mechanistic biomarkers of early cardiotoxicity in patients treated with Dox.

articles.title: Abstract 17319: Distribution and Phenotypic Concordance of the Proposed Lancet Commission Definition of Obesity: A National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey Analysis
articles.abstract: Background: BMI is an imperfect surrogate for adiposity and cardiometabolic risk. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology Commission proposed an expanded obesity definition that adds waist circumference (WC), waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) to BMI, and further distinguished preclinical obesity from clinical obesity based on the presence of organ dysfunction or functional limitation. The population distribution of individual anthropometric components, and how they differ across preclinical and clinical obesity phenotypes, remains unknown. Aim: To characterize the distribution of Lancet components and assess how each combination differs in identifying preclinical versus clinical obesity phenotypes in U.S. adults, using DXA-derived adiposity as a reference. Methods: We analyzed adults aged 20-59 years in NHANES 2017-2018 undergoing whole-body DXA. The reference standard for excess adiposity was DXA (Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry) total body fat ≥25% (men)/≥35% (women). Secondary outcomes were DXA-estimated visceral obesity (≥130 cm 2 men; ≥100 cm 2 women) and clinical obesity (Lancet obesity plus a metabolic or end-organ manifestation); participants meeting Lancet anthropometric criteria without these manifestations were classified as preclinical obesity. Participants were cross-classified into mutually exclusive combinations of the Lancet components; for each subset we estimated the survey-weighted proportion with each true outcome (the positive predictive value [PPV]) and the subset’s share of total disease burden. Results: Among 1,900 adults (≈98.7 million weighted), 69% (95% CI 67-71) had true DXA-verified excess adiposity, versus 36% (35-38) classified as obese by BMI alone. PPV for DXA-defined adiposity varied widely across combinations (Table 1). BMI≥40 kg/m 2 and BMI plus all anthropometrics carried the highest PPVs, with 100% and 96% for excess adiposity and 88% and 62% for visceral obesity, respectively. BMI+WC+WHtR (no hip metric) performed comparably (95% excess adiposity; 66% clinical obesity). In contrast, isolated WHR positivity captured only 16% with excess adiposity and 7.4% with visceral obesity. BMI plus all anthropometrics also accounted for the largest absolute share of visceral (53%) and clinical (41%) obesity (Table 2). Conclusion: The Lancet’s multi-metric components vary substantially in their distribution across preclinical and clinical obesity phenotypes. While the combination of BMI with all central and hip anthropometrics captures the highest proportion of absolute visceral and clinical obesity in the U.S. population, we found that the hip-derived WHR performs poorly alone. Simpler waist-centric combinations (BMI+WC+WHtR) achieve comparable PPVs here. Thus, implementation of the Lancet framework may have the potential to be streamlined.

articles.title: Abstract P1076: Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Re-Cannulation: Patient Characteristics, Clinical Outcomes, and Predictors of Success at a High-Volume Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Center
articles.abstract: Background: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiac arrest and severe shock. Although cannulation strategies are standardized, decannulation decisions remain variable. When hemodynamic collapse occurs after decannulation, emergent re-cannulation may be the only life-saving option. Outcomes after a second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization are poorly defined, particularly among extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) patients, a group often presumed to have especially poor prognosis. Hypothesis: A second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization is associated with meaningful survival to discharge. Aim: To evaluate survival and predictors of outcome after repeat VA-ECMO cannulation during the same hospitalization. Methods: This is a retrospective single-center study of patients who underwent two VA-ECMO runs during a single hospitalization between 2016-2024. Among 1,000 patients treated with VA-ECMO, 40 required emergent re-initiation after initial decannulation. Clinical characteristics, indications for re-cannulation, survival to hospital discharge and predictors of outcome at the time of re-cannulation were analyzed. Results: Survival to hospital discharge after repeat VA-ECMO was 32.5% (Table 1). The most common indications for re-cannulation were refractory cardiogenic shock (52%) and cardiac arrest requiring ECPR (40%) (Table 2). Patients re-cannulated for ECPR had survival comparable to, and numerically higher than, those re-cannulated for other indications, including refractory cardiogenic shock (44% versus 24%; p=0.29). Survivors were younger and less likely to have a history of coronary artery bypass grafting (Table 1). At the time of re-cannulation, survivors had lower serum lactate, international normalized ratio levels and higher platelet counts (Table 2). On multivariable analysis, older age and higher serum lactate were independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: Repeat VA-ECMO cannulation was associated with meaningful survival after post-decannulation hemodynamic collapse. The observation that patients re-cannulated for ECPR had outcomes similar to, and numerically better than other major re-cannulation groups, challenges the assumption that repeat ECPR is uniformly futile and suggests that carefully selected patients may still derive substantial benefit. Younger age and less severe metabolic derangement at the time of re-cannulation were associated with improved outcomes.

articles.title: Abstract P1077: Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Cardiac ICUs: Benefit of Linking AHA GWTG ® -R AND PC 4 Registries
articles.abstract: Background: Significant heterogeneity exists in pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) populations that suffer in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). While individual registries provide sizable cohorts, they lack diagnostic and procedural granularity. We propose a novel linkage of national cardiac arrest and pediatric cardiac critical care quality registries to evaluate IHCA in children with heart disease, characterize cardiac disease profiles, and identify unique outcome-related risk factors. Methods: We linked the American Heart Association’s Get With the Guidelines-Resuscitation (GWTG-R) and the Pediatric Cardiac Critical Care Consortium (PC 4 ) registries. We included medical (MC) and surgical (SC) cardiac patients < 18 years of age admitted to CICUs between 8/1/2014-2/13/2023 with an index IHCA event. Cross-referencing identified 22 centers participating in both registries (Fig. 1). Primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge (SHD). Secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), return of circulation via extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ROC), and survival with a favorable neurologic outcome (FNO) from GWTG-R, defined by pediatric cerebral performance category (PCPC) scores. A composite survival with FNO variable was created by adding neurologic complications collected in PC 4 to GWTG-R’s definition. Generalized linear mixed-effects models accounting for hospital clustering examined associations between illness categories, and within MC subgroups, with outcomes. Adjustment covariates included single ventricle (SV) and congenital heart disease (CHD) status derived from PC 4 . Results: A total of 1,012 children were evaluated (418 MC; 594 SC); 42% were infants, 27% were SV, 85% had CHD, and 51% of SC patients had STAT 4-5 operations (Table 1). IHCA cumulative incidence was 0.91% for STAT 1-3 and 4.6% for STAT 4-5. Median CPR duration was similar between groups (MC 9 [IQR 3-35] vs SC 13 [IQR 3-38] mins, p=0.10). Overall, SHD was 55%, FNO in survivors was 62%, and composite FNO in survivors was 53%. In multivariable models, MC patients had lower odds of SHD (OR 0.45 [0.32-0.62]), ROSC (OR 0.43 [0.27-0.69]) and ROC (OR 0.38 [0.24-0.58]) compared to SC groups (Table 2). Among MC cohorts, having CHD was associated with lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.35 [0.14-0.88]) and ROC (OR 0.44 [0.20-0.96]), but similar SHD versus those with structurally normal hearts. No differences in FNO or composite FNO were seen between MC and SC cohorts. Conclusion: In this linkage analysis, adjusted for covariates including SV and CHD status, MC patients had higher hospital mortality compared with SC patients. Although MC cohorts with CHD had lower rates of ROSC and ROC, SHD was similar to MC patients without CHD. This study framework enables new procedure- and complexity-specific insights not feasible in either registry alone to more accurately predict outcomes.

articles.title: Abstract P1078: Association of Transport Difficulty with Prehospital Time and Clinical Outcomes in Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Study in Japan
articles.abstract: Background: In Japan, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel must obtain prior approval from the hospital before transporting a patient, which can cause refusal of admission or delays in treatment. Pediatric patients may be particularly affected because hospitals and specialists capable of managing pediatric emergencies are limited. Although transport difficulty has been associated with adverse outcomes in adults, its impact in pediatric OHCA remains unclear. Hypothesis: Transport difficulty is associated with prolonged prehospital time and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric OHCA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective nationwide, population-based study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency transport records from 2021 to 2023. Pediatric patients (<20 years) with OHCA were included. Transport difficulty was defined as ≥4 hospital acceptance requests before transport. Total prehospital time (emergency call to hospital arrival) was categorized into call-to-scene arrival time, scene time (scene arrival to departure), and transport time (scene departure to hospital arrival). The primary outcome was 1-month survival. Secondary outcomes were a favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) and prehospital ROSC. Primary analyses compared patients with transport difficulty (≥4 requests) and those without (≤3 requests). Exploratory analyses evaluated outcomes according to the number of hospital acceptance requests. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial rhythm, cause of arrest, population density, and regional pediatric healthcare resources, including pediatric intensive care units, pediatric core hospitals, and tertiary emergency centers. Results: Among 3,967 pediatric OHCA patients, transport difficulty occurred in 106 (2.7%) (Table 1). Patients with transport difficulty had no significant difference in call-to-scene arrival time compared to those without the difficulty (9 vs 9 min, p= 0.290) but had longer scene time (16 vs 10 min) and total prehospital time (47 vs 31 min) (both p<0.001) (Table 2). ROSC before hospital arrival (6.6% vs 8.3%, p=0.650), 1-month survival (6.6% vs 13.1%, p=0.070), and favorable neurological outcome (3.8% vs 4.8%, p=0.810) did not significantly differ between groups. In exploratory analyses, observed 1-month survival rates were 12.9% for 1 call (reference), 15.0% for 2 calls (adjusted OR 1.15 [95% CI 0.82-1.58]), 11.2% for 3 calls (adjusted OR 0.82 [95% CI 0.42-1.49]), and 6.6% for ≥4 calls (adjusted OR 0.57 [95% CI 0.23-1.23]) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Transport difficulty was associated with prolonged prehospital time in pediatric OHCA. Despite no statistically significant association, the adjusted odds ratio for survival decreased as the requests increased. Further analysis with a larger sample size is needed to clarify this association.

articles.title: Abstract P1079: Hour-by-Hour Temporal Patterns in 30-Day Outcomes Following Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Japanese Registry Study
articles.abstract: Background: Previous Japanese studies have reported worse outcomes after nighttime pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). However, detailed hour-by-hour temporal patterns and their relationship to arrest etiology remain unclear. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that pediatric OHCA outcomes would exhibit distinct temporal patterns beyond conventional nighttime and that these patterns would differ according to arrest etiology. Aims: To evaluate hour-by-hour associations between emergency call time and outcomes after pediatric OHCA in Japan. Methods: We conducted a retrospective nationwide observational study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry (2005-2023). Pediatric OHCA patients (<18 years) with known emergency call time were included. Cases with transport time >120 minutes were excluded. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated hour-by-hour associations between emergency call time and 30-day outcomes using 12:00 PM as the reference hour. Models were adjusted for year, age, sex, witnessed arrest, dispatcher-assisted CPR instruction, bystander CPR, arrest etiology, and transport time. Subgroup analyses were performed according to arrest etiology and weekday/weekend status. Results: Among 31,386 pediatric OHCA patients, crude 30-day survival was 20.9% during daytime (09:00-16:59), 15.4% during transition periods (07:00-08:59 and 17:00-22:59), and 9.1% during nighttime (23:00-06:59). In hour-by-hour adjusted analyses relative to the 12:00 PM reference hour, adjusted odds of 30-day survival progressively declined overnight and during early morning hours, reaching the lowest value at 06:00 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.30, 95% CI 0.24-0.38) (Figure). Similar temporal patterns were observed for favorable neurological survival, with the lowest adjusted odds also at 06:00 (aOR 0.29, 95% CI 0.21-0.40). An additional decline in both survival and favorable neurological outcomes was observed around 17:00. These temporal patterns were more pronounced in non-cardiac OHCA than cardiac OHCA. Patterns were similar between weekdays and weekends, and transport time did not meaningfully differ across hours of the day. Conclusion: Pediatric OHCA outcomes demonstrated distinct hour-by-hour temporal patterns not explained by transport time or weekday/weekend differences. These findings may reflect temporal vulnerabilities in pediatric arrest recognition, family supervision patterns, and operational transitions within emergency and hospital systems.

articles.title: Abstract P1080: Early Calcium Administration During Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Introduction: Though national resuscitation guidelines recommend against routine use of calcium except in special circumstances, it is often given during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) for its vasoactive qualities. While observational studies have consistently shown associations between intra-arrest calcium and increased mortality, these studies failed to account for the timing of calcium administration, leading to high risk for resuscitation time bias. Aim: To examine the association of early calcium with outcomes from pIHCA. Research Question: Is early calcium associated with decreased odds of survival to hospital discharge or ROSC? Methods: This was a single-center retrospective study including patients ≤18 years old who had a pulseless IHCA from 2013-2023. The exposure was early calcium, defined as calcium administration within 5 minutes of CPR initiation. To ensure a similar timeframe for early calcium exposure across the cohort, patients who received CPR for <5 minutes were excluded. The primary and secondary outcomes were survival to hospital discharge and sustained ROSC, respectively. Logistic treatment-effects estimation utilizing inverse-probability weighting via a propensity score was used. A regression model was used to balance the groups with covariates selected a priori based on a patient’s propensity to receive early calcium: age, initial rhythm, illness category, interventions in place before arrest, presence of hyperkalemia, and presence of hypocalcemia. Because illness category, initial rhythm, and hyperkalemia did not achieve balance after weighting, they were included as covariates in the outcome model. Results: Of 242 patients, 64 (26%) received early calcium. In the univariate analyses, patients who received early calcium were more likely to be younger, have cardiac malformations, baseline central nervous system depression, hepatic insufficiency, and vasoactive infusions in place prior to arrest (Table 1). Early calcium administration varied by event location and time of event (Table 2). The median duration of CPR was longer in the early calcium cohort (27 minutes) compared with no early calcium (19 minutes; p=0.038). For the primary and secondary analyses using weighted cohorts, there were no differences in survival to hospital discharge (aOR 0.97, 95%CI 0.5-1.87, p=0.9) or ROSC (aOR 0.54, 95%CI 0.28-1.04, p=0.065; Table 3). Conclusions: In this weighted pIHCA cohort, there were no statistically significant differences in odds of survival to discharge or ROSC between patients who did and did not receive calcium in the first 5 minutes of CPR. Further work is needed to understand various time points of calcium administration and its effect on outcomes.

articles.title: Abstract P1081: Do Cognitive Biases Impact Adherence to Resuscitation Guidelines in Simulated Pediatric Cardiac Arrest?
articles.abstract: Introduction: Variation in outcomes after pediatric cardiac arrest may be driven by inconsistent adherence to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines. Time to defibrillation is a key metric for patients with presenting rhythm of ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VF/pVT), and delays >2 minutes are associated with a lower likelihood of survival. Interventions to improve resuscitation performance, such as CPR coaching, may offload cognitive demands on resuscitation team leaders. Excess cognitive loading has been associated with diagnostic error due to cognitive biases. Pertinent biases include the framing bias, in which the way information is initially presented impacts clinical decision-making, and the anchoring bias, which creates overreliance on initial impressions. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that cognitive biases influence resuscitation performance in simulated pediatric cardiac arrest. Specifically, events framed as non-cardiac in origin (septic shock in an oncology patient) would result in simulation teams being slower to defibrillate shockable rhythms versus events framed with a cardiac etiology (myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction). Methods: This study is a secondary analysis of a simulation-based study conducted at a quaternary children’s hospital to evaluate the impact of room design on resuscitation practices. Simulation teams of physicians, NPs, RNs, and respiratory therapists participated in two simulations with different clinical prompts both leading to cardiac arrest with initial rhythm of pVT. Team-based performance variables were abstracted from audio and video recordings including time stamps for cardiac arrest, initiation of compressions, first dose of epinephrine (if given), and defibrillation. Chest compression quality data were collected via Zoll OneStep Electrodes. Results: For all 38 simulations, average time to defibrillation was 3.4 minutes (95% CI = 3.0-3.8 mins). In 47% of simulations, epinephrine was given before defibrillation, despite the presence of a shockable rhythm. For myocarditis scenarios, defibrillation was the first intervention 58% of the time, versus 47% of the time for septic shock, though the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.51). In simulations where epinephrine was given first, time to defibrillation increased to 3.9 minutes (95% CI=3.1-4.7 min), versus 2.9 minutes (95% CI=2.6-3.3 min) for simulations where a shock was administered first (p = 0.011). Conclusions: Clinical framing in a simulated resuscitation may activate cognitive biases that impact adherence to PALS guidelines. Administering a dose of epinephrine as the first intervention resulted in a statistically significant delay in the time to appropriate defibrillation in simulated cardiac arrest with a presenting rhythm of pVT.

articles.title: Abstract P1082: Characteristics and Outcomes of Adult and Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Background: Adult and pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) have historically differed in baseline characteristics, etiologies, event features, interventions, and outcomes. Advances in arrest prevention and resuscitation practices may have narrowed these gaps, but contemporary comparisons are limited. We evaluated differences in characteristics and outcomes between pediatric and adult IHCA in a large national registry in North America. Methods: Using the GWTG-Resuscitation database, we identified index IHCA events requiring chest compressions for at least 1 minute between 2015 and 2024, excluding pandemic years 2020-2022. The exposure was age group (pediatric <18 years vs adult). Outcomes included survival to hospital discharge, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurological outcome (adult cerebral performance category [CPC] 1–2 or pediatric CPC 1–3). Generalized estimating equations were used for clustering by hospital and event year; pre-arrest factors were treated as mediators. Standard mean differences (SMDs) with SMD >0.1 or <-0.1 indicated meaningful differences. Results: The cohort included 161,162 adults and 3,749 children with IHCA. Adults had lower odds of survival to discharge (26% vs 46%; odds ratio [OR] 0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41-0.47), favorable neurological outcome (18% vs 33%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.46-0.57), and ROSC (73% vs 78%; OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.74–0.88) compared with children. Adults were more likely to present with VF/pVT (16% vs 10%, SMD -0.17), yet lower adult survival persisted after stratifying by initial rhythm: for non-shockable rhythms, survival was 22% vs 44% (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.48–0.52), and for shockable rhythms, 45% vs 52% (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78–0.97) for adults and children respectively. Children were more likely than adults to arrest in an ICU (69% vs 38%; SMD 0.66), receive calcium during CPR (44% vs 35%; SMD 0.18), and undergo ECPR (12% vs <1%; SMD 0.50). Adults more commonly received sodium bicarbonate (55% vs 48%; SMD 0.15) and amiodarone (20% vs 5%; SMD 0.49) during CPR. Conclusion: In this large IHCA registry, adults had approximately half the odds of survival to discharge and favorable neurological outcome compared with children, despite only modestly lower odds of ROSC. These survival differences were not explained by initial rhythm and occurred in the setting of marked differences in care setting, pre-arrest support, and resuscitation practices, highlighting age-specific targets to improve outcomes. Future directions include contrasting etiology of arrest and post-arrest care practices.

articles.title: Abstract P1083: Building a High-Impact Resuscitation Committee to Drive Systemwide Clinical Excellence
articles.abstract: Introduction: Medical emergencies require rapid, coordinated responses to optimize outcomes; however, variability in training, role clarity, and adherence to evidence-based practices are common. To address these gaps, a multidisciplinary Resuscitation Committee was established to oversee clinical support, quality improvement, and education for a hospital’s Medical Emergency Response Team. With executive sponsorship, committee structure was designed to ensure accountability, frontline engagement, and system-level reliability. Research Questions: This initiative aimed to determine whether a structured, interdisciplinary resuscitation committee could improve guideline adherence, team preparedness, and patient outcomes. We hypothesized that a formalized committee model integrating practice, education, and quality review would enhance resuscitation performance and support sustained improvement in survival outcomes. Methods: The committee operates using a three-arm framework: Practice, Clinical Support, and Quality. The Practice arm standardizes workflows, equipment, and code processes, with continuous refinement based on real event feedback. The Clinical Support arm provides structured onboarding, simulation-based training, and annual competencies to reinforce role mastery and team dynamics. The Quality arm reviews all resuscitation events through weekly multidisciplinary debriefs and bi-monthly trend analysis, incorporating metrics such as ROSC, survival to discharge, neurologic outcomes, and adherence to AHA guidelines. Results: Committee membership grew from 10 members in 2019 to 49 in 2025, reflecting increased institutional engagement. Survival to discharge improved from 20.8% in 2017 to 29.3% in 2024, representing a 40% increase from baseline, with rates consistently above 28% in past years. The institution received the American Heart Association Get With The Guidelines-Gold Award from 2020-2025. Conclusion: A structured, interdisciplinary resuscitation committee using a three-arm model can drive measurable improvements in resuscitation performance, guideline adherence, and patient outcomes. Integrating frontline clinical staff into shared governance enables sustainable system-wide change, improved operational efficiency, and enhanced emergency response reliability. This model is scalable and replicable for organizations seeking to strengthen resuscitation systems and achieve high-level clinical performance recognition.

articles.title: Abstract P1084: Relationships Among Excessive Responders & Survival of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Introduction/Background: Successful management of in-hospital cardiac arrests (IHCAs) depends on timely interventions, effective communication, and coordinated teamwork. Healthcare organizations commonly monitor outcomes using measures such as spontaneous circulation, survival to discharge (STD), and resuscitation guideline adherence. Review of IHCAs at a Level One Academic Trauma Center revealed variability in responder numbers. Resuscitation event critiques suggested that excessive responders during IHCAs created barriers to communication, role clarity, and overall workflow efficiency. Quality improvement efforts primarily focus on clinical interventions and documentation accuracy, with less attention given to how physical environments may influence patient outcomes during IHCAs.
