Research Question/Hypothesis: Is there a relationship between responder overcrowding during an IHCA and survivability? Goals/Aims: The aim of this study was to evaluate the relationship between responder overcrowding during IHCA event survival and STD. Methods/Approach: This retrospective study reviewed resuscitation event critiques from 1/1/2023 to 12/31/25. Patients who underwent an IHCA were included and those under the age of 18 years, outpatients, visitors, experienced more than one IHCA, and emergency department and operating room events were excluded. The Chi-Square Test for Independence evaluated the potential association between the number of appropriate responders (i.e., ≤ 13 responders) versus overcrowded (i.e., ≥ 14 responders) and survival of an IHCA and STD (i.e., Expired or Survived). Yates’ Correction for Continuity was reported for both outcomes. Results/Data: A Chi-Square Test for Independence indicated no significant association between survivability of an IHCA event and crowd status, χ 2 (1, n = 290 = 0.610, p = 0.435, phi = -0.055. A Chi-Square Test for Independence indicated no significant association between STD and crowd status, χ 2 (1, n = 290 = 2.934, p = 0.087, phi = -0.111. Conclusions: Although there were no significant associations between survivability of an IHCA and crowd status, this project demonstrated clinical significance. For example, qualitatively exploring emergency team responder perceptions of crowd status and the impact on IHCAs. Future research implications include additional factors that may impact survivability such as deviations from Advanced Cardiac Life Support and post-cardiac arrest care guidelines.

articles.title: Abstract P1086: Shock Trajectories and Practice Variation After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Retrospective Analysis of the Discover-IHCA Registry
articles.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest affects over 500,000 Americans annually and remains a major public health challenge. Post-cardiac arrest shock—defined as inadequate oxygen delivery to vital organs—occurs in over 70% of initial survivors and contributes substantially to mortality and organ dysfunction. While post-arrest shock following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has been extensively studied, data on in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is limited. Research Objectives: The objectives of this study are to characterize the epidemiology, treatment patterns, and trajectory of shock following IHCA, including progression/resolution, evaluate associations with organ dysfunction, vasopressor selection, organ support, and clinical outcomes Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with IHCA using the Discover-IHCA registry. Post-arrest variables included vasoactive medication use, organ support methods, and cardiac sequential organ failure assessment score (cSOFA). The primary exposure was post-arrest shock; the primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included organ dysfunction requiring organ support, survival at 24, 48 and 72 hours. We present descriptive statistics as means or medians where appropriate. Paired comparisons between pre- and post-arrest organ support were performed using McNemars where appropriate. A covariate-adjusted logistic regression model was also developed. Results: We included 955 adult patients across 69 hospitals. Of these, 339 (35.5%) were female. The majority (42.2%) of individuals were age > 70 (Table 1). Primary respiratory causes were the most common etiology of arrest (n = 316, 33.1%), followed by primary cardiac (n = 250, 26.2%). A total of 742 patients (77.7%) experienced post-arrest shock, defined as any use of vasopressor/inotrope (n = 666, 69.7%), mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump/impella) (n = 30, 3.14%), or initiation of VA-ECMO (n = 46, 4.82%). Norepinephrine was the most common vasopressor (n = 709, 74.2%). Comparison of pre- versus post-arrest organ support showed significant increases in multiple interventions (Table 2). Higher weighted cSOFA burden was associated with higher odds of in-hospital death (OR =1.95, 95% CI 1.73-2.19, p < 0.001) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Over three-quarters of patients with IHCA suffer post-arrest shock. Significant increases in organ support occur after IHCA. Higher cSOFA scores post-arrest was strongly associated with in hospital death. Future analyses will explore patient centered outcomes and variations in IHCA management.

articles.title: Abstract P1088: Predictors and Outcomes of Post-Intubation Cardiac Arrest in Critically Ill Adults
articles.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest following endotracheal intubation is a rare but catastrophic complication in critically ill patients. Data describing its incidence, predictors, and outcomes in large ICU populations remain limited. We evaluated the incidence, risk factors, and outcomes of early post-intubation cardiac arrest (PICA) in a large critical care cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database. Adult ICU patients undergoing endotracheal intubation were identified using procedure event records. The primary outcome was cardiac arrest occurring within 6 hours of the first recorded intubation. Secondary outcomes included cardiac arrest within 1 hour and 24 hours of intubation. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, pre-intubation laboratory values, hemodynamic parameters, and vasopressor use were extracted. A prespecified multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of PICA. Results: A total of 8,463 intubated ICU stays were identified. Post-intubation cardiac arrest within 6 hours occurred in 62 patients (0.73%), including 40 arrests within 1 hour (0.47%) and 103 arrests within 24 hours (1.22%). Patients experiencing PICA had higher pre-intubation lactate levels (4.42±3.18 vs 2.98±2.70 mmol/L, p<0.001), higher heart rates (117.0±22.2 vs 104.9±23.5 beats/min, p<0.001), lower minimum systolic blood pressure (91.4±26.1 vs 105.9±25.4 mmHg, p<0.001), higher creatinine levels (2.22±1.77 vs 1.72±1.73 mg/dL, p=0.030), and higher white blood cell counts (16.7±10.5 vs 13.7±10.4 х10 9 /L, p=0.032). Heart failure (43.5% vs 30.3%, p=0.033), sepsis (53.2% vs 31.6%, p<0.001), shock (17.7% vs 6.7%, p=0.001), and pre-intubation vasopressor use (33.9% vs 22.0%, p=0.036) were more common among patients who developed PICA.Hospital mortality was substantially higher among patients with PICA compared with those without PICA (82.3% vs 28.1%, p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, higher pre-intubation heart rate (adjusted OR 1.161 per 10 beats/min, 95% CI 1.020-1.306) and lower pre-intubation mean arterial pressure (adjusted OR 0.698 per 10 mmHg, 95% CI 0.560-0.869) were independently associated with PICA. Elevated lactate (adjusted OR 1.09 per mmol/L, 95% CI 0.99-1.17) and creatinine (adjusted OR 1.12 per mg/dL, 95% CI 0.98-1.24) demonstrated modest associations that did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: Post-intubation cardiac arrest occurred in approximately 1 in 137 intubated ICU patients and was associated with extremely high in-hospital mortality exceeding 80%. Pre-intubation tachycardia and hypotension independently identified patients at the highest risk, suggesting the hypothesis that hemodynamic optimization before intubation may be an important target for prevention.

articles.title: Abstract P2001: Generative Models for Synthesizing Cardiac Arrest Electrocardiograms With and Without Chest Compression Artifact
articles.abstract: Background: ECG rhythm assessment during resuscitation of ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia (VF/VT) out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) requires CPR interruption because CPR causes ECG artifacts. Ideally defibrillators would use artificial intelligence (AI) for binary (non-shockable vs. shockable) and 3-class (asystole [ASY] vs. organized [ORG] vs. shockable [VF/VT]) ECG classification during CPR to guide diagnosis and treatment. However, algorithm development is challenged by a paucity of OHCA ECGs, particularly during CPR. Goal: We built generative AI models to synthesize OHCA ECGs with and without CPR artifact to (1) determine whether classifiers trained with synthetic (artificial) ECGs can classify real (clinical) ECGs, and (2) compare performance between classifiers trained with real vs. synthetic ECGs. Methods: We performed a retrospective study of adult VF-OHCA from 2006-2021 in a metropolitan EMS system. Patients were randomized 80%/20% for training/test. Defibrillator pad ECGs clipped into 2.5-s segments were manually labeled by CPR and rhythm (ASY, ORG, VF, VT) by expert reviewers. Using training ECGs, we first developed generative adversarial networks (GAN) and diffusion models (DM) to synthesize ASY, ORG, and VF/VT ECGs with and without CPR. Then using (1) the real training ECGs, (2) GAN-generated ECGs, and (3) DM-generated ECGs, classifiers were trained for binary (ASY/ORG vs. VF/VT) and 3-class (ASY vs. ORG vs. VF/VT) rhythm prediction. Classifiers included 1-D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with ECG voltages as inputs and 2-D CNNs with ECG scalograms as inputs. To evaluate synthetic data utility, we compared classifiers trained with real vs. synthetic data in the test dataset using binary (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], F1 score) and 3-class (balanced accuracy [BAC]) metrics. Results: The cohort had 2011 patients with 1.03 million ECGs (60% with CPR). Classifiers were trained on real, GAN-generated, and DM-generated datasets of 816134 ECGs each (Figure). In the test dataset of 213664 ECGs from 402 patients, classifiers trained with synthetic data had good binary performance without CPR (AUC=0.97-0.99, F1=0.78-0.87) and with CPR (AUC=0.95-0.96, F1=0.84-0.86) (Table 1), and moderate 3-class performance without CPR (BAC=65-85%) and with CPR (BAC=62-84%) (Table 2). On average, classifiers trained with real data outperformed those trained with synthetic data by an AUC of 0.019 (vs. GAN) and 0.016 (vs. DM), F1 of 0.084 (vs. GAN) and 0.081 (vs. DM), and BAC of 4.4% (vs. GAN) and 6.1% (vs. DM). Conclusions: Generative models successfully synthesized ECGs with and without CPR. Classifiers trained on synthetic data had slightly reduced performance versus those trained on real data. The results suggest potential for on-demand synthesis of OHCA ECGs, enabling AI sandboxing and development of next-generation ECG algorithms.

articles.title: Abstract P2002: Artificial Intelligence Analysis to Detect Acute Coronary Occlusion During Active Ventricular Fibrillation in a Preclinical Model of Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Background: During ventricular fibrillation (VF), conventional ECG interpretation cannot identify acute coronary occlusion (ACO). Rapid detection of ACO during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) could facilitate targeted resuscitation and triage strategies. Hypothesis: Artificial intelligence (AI) analysis of VF waveforms can distinguish ischemic VF caused by ACO from non-ischemic VF without coronary occlusion. Methods: Female Yorkshire swine undergoing standardized VF OHCA experiments were classified as ischemic VF (I-VF) following proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion or non-ischemic VF (N-VF) induced without coronary occlusion. Lead II ECGs sampled at 250 Hz during the first 3 minutes of untreated VF were segmented into 10-second windows. Four AI models were developed: convolutional neural network (CNN), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and decision tree (DT). Model development used 4-fold cross-validation on 56 animals (20 I-VF, 36 N-VF) with oversampling of the minority class to address class imbalance. An independent, balanced holdout test set of 16 animals (8 I-VF, 8 N-VF) assessed generalizability. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (CI), and DeLong testing. Results: The CNN demonstrated superior discrimination compared with all other models in both the development and test datasets (all p<0.05 by DeLong testing). In the development dataset, the CNN achieved an AUC of 0.93 (95% CI 0.91-0.94), sensitivity of 0.84 (95% CI 0.79-0.87), and specificity of 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91). Performance remained robust in the independent test dataset, with an AUC of 0.91 (95% CI 0.88-0.94), sensitivity of 0.85 (95% CI 0.79-0.90), and specificity of 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.89). At a clinically relevant fixed sensitivity of 90%, specificity was 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.86) on the test set. Conclusions: AI-based analysis of VF waveforms can identify ACO during active VF with clinically meaningful accuracy in a porcine model of OHCA. If validated in human cohorts, this approach could support real-time triage, reperfusion decision-making, and personalized resuscitation strategies during VF cardiac arrest.

articles.title: Abstract P2003: Automated Video Review of Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Using Multimodal Artificial Intelligence
articles.abstract: Introduction: Video review is a powerful resource in quality improvement and research of high mortality rates of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs). Manual review is time and resource-intensive, limiting implementation at scale. Hypothesis: Automating the video review process is feasible using Artificial Intelligence (AI). Aim: We assessed the feasibility and accuracy of Google’s Gemini AI in reviewing cardiac arrest resuscitation simulations in the Emergency Department (ED). Methods: Eight pediatric OHCA simulation videos with identical scenarios were reviewed by trained investigators and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro model. Data points were extracted blinded to study results. Inter-rater reliability of reviewers was 0.78. Simulations included a team leader, charting nurse, medication nurse, and four research actors (CPR provider/coach, bedside nurse, airway provider). Videos were captured with a GoPro Hero 12 Black camera and compressed using HandBrake to optimize AI processing. AI was instructed to act as a clinical expert in cardiac resuscitation, tasked with reviewing technical and non-technical aspects of care. Human reviewers and AI were given definitions of each critical event, Concise Assessment of Leader Management (CALM) tool, and teamwork assessment (TEAM) tool. Technical variables included critical event timestamps (cardiac arrest recognition, compression initiation, pulse/rhythm assessment/identification). Non-technical variables included TEAM and CALM scores. Human vs AI results were compared using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) values and Bland Altman plots. Results: AI demonstrated excellent agreement with humans on technical variables (ICC ≥0.94). A total of 142 timestamps were included, with 9 events (6.3%) discordant between human and AI. Time to critical events showed a mean difference of -2.32 seconds with limits of agreement from -12.76 to +8.12 seconds (Figure 1), reflecting expected variability across clinical actions. Non-technical variable agreement was moderate. TEAM scores showed a mean difference of 7.25 points (range 1.83 to 12.67) (Figure 2); CALM scores showed a mean difference of 1.12 points (range -7.15 to 9.40) (Figure 3). ICC for non-technical variables were poor (TEAM: 0.022, CALM: 0.31). Conclusions: AI showed excellent concordance for technical metrics but requires refinement for non-technical variables. Results support automating video analysis of cardiac resuscitation to improve efficiency and scalability.

articles.title: Abstract P2004: A Numerical Autopsy for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Reclassifying Unknown Etiologies from Electronic Health Records
articles.abstract: Introduction: The cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) often remains unknown because most patients die before comprehensive diagnostic evaluation can be performed. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that healthcare data can be leveraged to infer plausible causes that are not captured by conventional investigations. Aims: The aims of our study was to develop and assess a “numerical autopsy” framework that infer probabilistic etiologic profiles for unexplained OHCA using longitudinal healthcare data. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population based study linking the Paris Cardiac Arrest Center registry with the French National Health Insurance database. Adults with non-traumatic OHCA occurring between May 2011 and May 2020 were included. Five-year pre-arrest hospital diagnoses, outpatient drug dispensations, procedures, and registry variables were aggregated into 393 standardized features. A calibrated multiclass Light Gradient Boosting Machine model was trained on clinically adjudicated cases to predict six etiologic categories: cardiac ischemic, cardiac other, hypoxic, embolic, neurologic, and other. Cases with initially unknown etiology were reclassified only when the highest predicted probability was ≥ 50%. Results: Among 22,170 eligible patients, 3,353 had an adjudicated etiology and 18,817 remained unexplained after standard evaluation. On a held-out random test set, the model achieved a log-loss of 1.07, an overall one-vs-rest AUROC of 0.79, a F1-score of 0.37, and 63% accuracy. Temporal validation showed similar performance, with log-loss of 1.04, AUROC of 0.81, and macro F1-score of 0.36. After numerical autopsy, the proportion of unknown etiologies decreased from 84.9% to 53.1%. Ischemic etiologies increased from 7.5% to 20.2%, and hypoxic etiologies from 3.0% to 21.4%. Explainability analyses showed clinically coherent patterns, including respiratory variables among hypoxic reclassifications and cardiovascular variables among cardiac reclassifications. Conclusions: Numerical autopsy provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware approach to reclassifying unexplained OHCA using routine longitudinal healthcare data. It does not replace clinical adjudication or post-mortem investigation but may support etiologic surveillance and prevention-oriented review when conventional diagnostic information is incomplete.

articles.title: Abstract P2005: Contrastive Language and Image Reasoning - A Novel Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Post-Anoxic Brain Injury Prognostication
articles.abstract: Anoxic brain injury (ABI) classification after cardiac arrest is critical to determining eligibility for neuroprotective therapies such as therapeutic hypothermia. Subjectivity in determining injury severity on diagnostics such as CT confound and delay accurate classification and prognostication. The current standard for objective CT-based ABI classification relies on manual gray-white matter ratio (GWR) measurement, which is time-intensive and limited by variability across CT scanners, hindering its utility for time-sensitive decision-making in the early post-arrest window. In this study, we introduce contrastive language and image reasoning with masked autoencoders (CLAIR), a novel multimodal framework integrating head computed tomography (CT) imaging with non-imaging clinical patient information through a cross-attention mechanism and contrastive learning approach to predict dichotomized cerebral performance category (CPC) score in patients after cardiac arrest. We benchmarked CLAIR against manual measurements and an automated, CT only-based masked autoencoder approach (CT-MAE) in a retrospective study of 208 patients with CT scans obtained within the first 24 hours of arrest. Manual GWR and CT-MAE achieved comparable overall discriminative performance (AUC-ROC: 0.87 and 0.80, respectively); however, manual GWR was limited by low specificity (0.54), with important implications for withdrawal-of-care decisions, while CT-MAE offered the advantage of full automation without sacrificing accuracy. Critically, neither imaging-only approach alone achieved sufficient predictive performance to independently guide clinical decision-making. In contrast, CLAIR achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.94 (CI: 0.90-0.97) when trained on multiplanar CT reconstructions combined with non-imaging clinical data, significantly outperforming CT-based imaging-only methods (p = 0.03) and surpassing the manual GWR clinical standard. To further evaluate clinical utility of CLAIR, we conducted a structured clinical assessment comparing CLAIR against two clinicians, a senior neurology resident and an attending neurointensivist, across a series of tests simulating varying levels of information availability during the post-arrest course. Clinicians assisted by CLAIR predictions made fewer prognostic errors than in their non-assisted assessments. Our results suggest that CLAIR can contribute value as a clinical assistive tool aiming at reliable ABI classification for post-cardiac arrest patients, potentially enabling more timely clinical decision-making, family counseling, and resource allocation.

articles.title: Abstract P2006: Automated Classification of Shock-Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation Subtypes
articles.abstract: Background: Refractory ventricular fibrillation (R-VF) out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients—pragmatically defined as those requiring ≥3 shocks—experience lower likelihood of resuscitation and survival compared to non-refractory patients. R-VF subtypes can further stratify patients by prognosis which could help guide treatment. Specifically, incessant R-VF (shocks fail to terminate VF) fare worse than recurrent R-VF (shocks terminate VF but VF recurs); hence incessant R-VF outcomes may be improved with targeted, alternative treatment strategies. However, identification of incessant R-VF has been limited to retrospective studies requiring post-hoc ECG rhythm review, challenging real-time implementation of a targeted strategy. We evaluated whether a deep learning-based rhythm classification algorithm designed for real-time use can determine shock response to classify patients by R-VF subtype as a means to consider clinical implementation of subtype-specific therapies. Objective: We evaluated automated classification of individual VF shock responses and patient-level R-VF subtypes using a “see-through-CPR” rhythm identification algorithm. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult VF-OHCA from 2006-21 from a metropolitan EMS system using continuous defibrillator ECG recordings. The gold standard annotation used a previously-published, 2-person review of immediate post-shock rhythm to determine shock-specific response (incessant vs. recurrent) and consequent patient-level classification (incessant only, recurrent only, or mixed). These annotations were compared with predictions from a previously-described deep learning rhythm classifier. Data were split into training and test sets. We selected a VF probability cut point that maximized F1 score in the training set for classifying shock-specific R-VF subtypes, and calculated accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of the automated algorithm relative to the gold standard annotations. Results: Among 1790 VF patients, median age was 62, 392 (22%) were female, 999 (56%) were refractory, and 760 (43%) survived with favorable status. Based on the gold standard annotations, R-VF shock-specific response was incessant in 35% and recurrent in 65% of shocks, producing patient-level classification of 16% incessant only, 46% recurrent only, and 37% mixed. Among the R-VF test set, the algorithm achieved a shock-specific accuracy of 93% (Table 1) and a patient-level 3-category accuracy of 88% (Table 2), with an incessant classification sensitivity of 0.81 (43/53) and specificity of 0.98 (276/282). Conclusions: An automated “see-through-CPR” rhythm identification algorithm can evaluate shock-specific rhythm response to achieve classification of R-VF subtypes including incessant R-VF, providing the potential to guide differential treatment strategies in real-time.

articles.title: Abstract P2007: Data-Driven ECG Features for Prediction of Out-of-Hospital Rearrest
articles.abstract: Introduction: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) affects up to half of patients who achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and is associated with worse outcomes. Predicting rearrest may enable preemptive EMS interventions. Evidence to date indicates clinical ECG features provide modest, time-dependent prediction of rearrest, performing better as rearrest approaches, potentially too late for intervention. Machine learning-based feature extraction may capture ECG signatures not detected by clinical measures. Goal: We evaluated a data-driven approach for rearrest prediction using ECG waveform data. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult OHCA patients treated by urban Emergency Medical Services (EMS) between 2018 and 2024 who achieved ROSC. We developed and evaluated a machine learning model to predict rearrest using a 5-minute ECG segment spanning the 6 to 1 minute period before rearrest. Patients were randomized 80/20% into training and test sets. ECGs were divided into 15-second segments and transformed into scalograms ( Figure 1 ). Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the training data, and the top 20 principal components (measured by variance captured) were used as inputs to an XGBoost classifier. Hyperparameters were optimized using a grid search with 10-fold cross-validation. To provide a comparative baseline versus the data-driven model, a clinical model was also developed using heart rate, heart rate variability, and QRS duration as inputs for logistic regression. Performance was evaluated by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results: Of the 1,247 OHCA patients who achieved ROSC, 526 (42%) experienced rearrest. The AUROC of the data driven model and the clinical model were 0.48-0.65 and 0.49-0.74, respectively. The data-driven model demonstrated relatively stable predictive performance across the entire evaluated pre-rearrest ( Figure 2 ). In contrast, the clinical model showed greater temporal dependence, with AUROC values improving as rearrest approached. At earlier timepoints, the data-driven approach’s AUROC point estimates exceeded the clinical model’s, whereas the clinical model AUROC point estimates were higher closer to rearrest. Conclusion: Rearrest prediction did not differ between machine learning versus clinical ECG measures, though these models differed with regard to time-dependent prediction. Machine learning-based feature extraction may complement conventional ECG models to predict impending rearrest, enabling earlier and more robust identification of patients at risk.

articles.title: Abstract P2009: Hydrogen Gas Inhalation Enhances Transfusion-Based Resuscitation Efficiency and Attenuates Organ Injury After Hemorrhagic Shock
articles.abstract: Background: Hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation cause ischemia-reperfusion injury, endothelial glycocalyx degradation, vascular dysfunction, and organ injury. Although transfusion is essential, strategies that improve resuscitation efficiency and reduce blood product requirements are needed. The effect of hydrogen gas (H 2 ), which has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, during transfusion-based resuscitation remains unknown. Hypothesis: H 2 inhalation would reduce transfusion requirements without compromising hemodynamic or metabolic recovery and would attenuate endothelial and organ injury. Methods: Twenty male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent pressure-controlled hemorrhagic shock. Blood was withdrawn to maintain mean arterial pressure at 30-35 mmHg for 60 minutes, followed by shed-blood transfusion over 60 minutes to achieve predefined hemodynamic targets. Animals were randomized to control gas or 1.3% H 2 gas inhalation, which was initiated 15 minutes before resuscitation and continued throughout resuscitation. Hemodynamics, arterial blood gas variables, lactate, transfusion volume, and plasma syndecan-1 were evaluated during the acute resuscitation phase. Animals were followed for 24 hours, after which blinded histopathological scoring of kidney, small-intestinal, and liver injury was performed. Results: Shed blood volume was similar between the H 2 and control groups (10.8 vs 10.4 mL; P=0.64), whereas transfused blood volume was significantly lower with H 2 (4.7 vs 6.9 mL; P<0.02). Despite receiving less transfusion, H 2 -treated rats maintained post-resuscitation hemodynamics and arterial blood gas parameters comparable to controls throughout the acute observation period, indicating that reduced transfusion did not compromise circulatory stabilization. Lactate did not increase after resuscitation in the H 2 group, and lactate normalization occurred more frequently with H 2 than with control gas (67% vs 38%; P=0.23). Plasma syndecan-1 after resuscitation was lower with H 2 , consistent with attenuated endothelial glycocalyx shedding (900 vs 1140 pg/mL; P<0.01). H 2 also reduced renal tubular injury (Paller score, 4 vs 9; P<0.01) and intestinal mucosal injury (Chiu-Park score, 0.5 vs 4; P<0.01). Liver injury scores were lower with H 2 , although the difference was not statistically significant (2.0 vs 6.5; P=0.24). Conclusions: H 2 inhalation improved transfusion-based resuscitation efficiency by reducing transfusion requirements while preserving hemodynamic stability and lactate clearance. Attenuation of endothelial glycocalyx shedding and kidney and intestinal injury suggests that H 2 may be a promising, resource-sparing adjunct for hemorrhagic shock resuscitation.

articles.title: Abstract P2010: Neurophysiological and Molecular Remodeling in the Hippocampus Following Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Introduction: Brain injury is a major contributor to post-cardiac arrest (CA) morbidity and mortality, yet the synaptic and molecular mechanisms governing these outcomes remain poorly understood. We have previously shown that Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a regulator of mitochondrial fission, is activated in the heart immediately following resuscitation and is an important determinant of myocardial function. Drp1 is also critical for maintaining normal synaptic function, but its relationship to post-CA neurophysiology is unknown. Here, we evaluated acute post-CA changes in synaptic physiology and Drp1 expression at the CA3-CA1 synapse of the hippocampus, a region with well-characterized ischemic vulnerability and a central role in activity-dependent plasticity, at 3 and 7 hours (h) post-CA. Methods: In an established murine model of CA, we characterized the neurophysiology of the CA3-CA1 synapse using field electrophysiological recordings, at 3h and 7h post-CA to characterize the input-output relationship, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) and short-term and long-term potentiation (PPF). We also evaluated changes in total Drp1 and Drp1 phosphorylation, and total CaMKII and CaMKII T286 phosphorylation, in the hippocampus and in the heart, at 3h and 7h post-CA. Results: In the hippocampus, we observed impairment in baseline transmission as seen in the input-output curve at the CA1-CA3 synapse (p<0.05) as well as in synaptic functions, such as short-term potentiation (p<0.01) and long-term potentiation, LTP (p<0.0001) at both 3h and 7h post-CA, congruent with loss of postsynaptic function. Additionally, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) was only impaired at 7h post-CA (p<0.05), indicating the generalization of injury to presynaptic sites. We also measured total Drp1 and Drp1 phosphorylation at these timepoints, and our results demonstrate that inactivating Drp1-S637 phosphorylation is downregulated in the heart (p<0.05) at 3h and 7h post-ROSC. However, in the hippocampus, activating Drp1-S616 phosphorylation is upregulated only at 7h (p<0.01), indicating increase in mitochondrial fission markers at 3h and 7h in the heart but only at 7h in the brain. We also evaluated total CaMKII protein and CaMKII T286 phosphorylation in the hippocampus at both timepoints, and saw a decrease in total CaMKII protein (p<0.05) at 3h and 7h post-ROSC. Conclusion: Post-CA injury in the hippocampus is dynamic and progressive in the hours following resuscitation, in contrast to the more acutely injured heart. These findings demonstrate that the brain and heart follow unique post-CA timelines, suggestive of distinct windows of organ specific opportunity for therapeutic intervention.

articles.title: Abstract P2011: Automated Endovascular Aortic Occlusion Mitigates Cerebral Ischemia and Eliminates Rearrest in a Porcine Model of Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Background: Traditional cardiac arrest resuscitation relies heavily on high-dose epinephrine to achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and on continued vasopressors to support hemodynamics after ROSC. Despite high doses of vasopressors, many patients continue to re-arrest after ROSC and have substantial cerebral ischemia. We evaluated whether automated, titratable endovascular partial aortic occlusion to offset epinephrine requirements could mitigate secondary injury, eliminate post-ROSC rearrest, and preserve cerebral perfusion compared to standard vasopressor-based management. Methods: Ventricular fibrillation was induced in 20 anesthetized Yorkshire swine. Following a 5-minute no-flow injury phase, mechanical CPR and automated Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS)-guided resuscitation were initiated. Animals achieving ROSC were randomized to automated critical care for 12 hours (Control, n=10) or endovascular perfusion augmentation for critical care (EPACC, n=6) for 6 hours, followed by an additional 6 hours of automated critical care. Automated critical care used MAP, CVP, fluid responsiveness, lactate, and urine output as input variables for determining the need for weight-based crystalloid boluses and titration of epinephrine and vasopressin. Automated aortic balloon-augmentation created a goal blood pressure gradient of 10 mmHg across the balloon within Zone 1 of the descending thoracic aorta. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed on all surviving animals at 12 hours after ROSC. Results: A total of 12 animals survived to MRI evaluation (EPACC, n=6; Control, n=6); 4 control animals expired early due to re-arrest. Automated balloon support achieved a 100% survival rate and eliminated rearrests, compared with 40% early mortality and a significant rearrest rate in the control group (p = 0.03). While macro-hemodynamics (mean arterial pressure, carotid blood flow) and total epinephrine and fluid requirements were comparable between groups, laser Doppler flowmetry demonstrated significantly higher cerebral microvascular perfusion in the EPACC group during the first hour after balloon deflation (p < 0.05). MRI revealed smaller cerebral infarct volumes and superior sum ASPECTS in the EPACC group compared to Controls (Figure 1, p < 0.05). EPACC animals exhibited a minor, non-significant increase in peak creatinine. Conclusions: Automated, dynamic endovascular aortic occlusion successfully bridged the post-ROSC "hemodynamic cliff," preventing rearrest and significantly reducing cerebral infarction. These data demonstrate that second-to-second automated titration of afterload provides neuroprotection and preserves micro-perfusion during the early post-ROSC phase.

articles.title: Abstract P2012: Nicolas Segond M.D. Ph.D.
articles.abstract: Introduction: The potential impact of Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains controversial. Little is known about the potential survival benefit of REBOA combined with head-up cardiopulmonary resuscitation (AHUP-CPR). Research question: The primary study objective was to compare the 24-hour survival after conventional (C) CPR+REBOA, AHUP-CPR alone, or AHUP-CPR+REBOA. Additional survival and hemodynamic outcomes were assessed. Methods: This was an experimental, prospective, controlled, randomized study. After isoflurane anesthesia, preparation and induction of ventricular fibrillation (VF), Yorkshire pigs were randomized in three groups: C-CPR+REBOA, AHUP alone and AHUP+REBOA. After 10 minutes of untreated VF, 18 minutes of C-CPR or AHUP-CPR (combination of an impedance threshold device, active compression-decompression and progressive head and thorax elevation) was provided. REBOA was inflated after 15 min (Figure 1) of CPR. Using Kaplan-Meier and a log-rank tests, 24-hour survival was compared between groups. Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurologic function at 24 hours (FN-24, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2) were assessed. Decompression aortic blood pressure (DBP), coronary perfusion pressure (CorPP), end-tidal CO2 (EtCO 2 ) and cerebral oximetry (rSO 2 ) before (14min) and after (17min) REBOA inflation were measured. Results: With 10 pigs per group, ROSC rates were 20% with C-CPR+REBOA, 60% with AHUP alone, and 90% with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.008), respectively. Differences in 24h survival were also significantly different between groups (0% C-CPR+REBOA, 30% AHUP alone, and 30% AHUP+REBOA; log-rank p = 0.008; Fig. 2). Median (Q1; Q3) survival times were 0 h (0; 0) with C-CPR+REBOA, 4.25 h (0.0; 19.5) with AHUP alone, and 7.5 h (6.0; 20.0) with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.002). FN-24 was 0% with C-CPR+REBOA, 30% with AHUP alone and 30% with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.15).Detailed hemodynamic data are presented in Table 1. Before REBOA inflation (14 min of CPR), EtCO2 differed significantly among the three groups (p < 0.001). After REBOA inflation (17 min of CPR), DBP, CorPP, and EtCO2 differed significantly among the three groups (p = 0.04, p = 0.03, and p < 0.001, respectively). Conclusion: In this preclinical study, AHUP-CPR alone or with REBOA, significantly increased 24-hour survival rate and hemodynamics compared with C-CPR+REBOA.

articles.title: Abstract P2013: Oxygen Without Benefit: Post-Cardiac Arrest Hyperoxia Results in Systemic Metabolic Failure Despite Preserved Arterial Oxygenation
articles.abstract: Background: Oxygen administration following cardiac arrest (CA) is associated with cardiac dysfunction, brain injury, and poor survival. These injuries are driven in part by mitochondrial injury, but the metabolic consequences of post-CA hyperoxia remain incompletely understood. We hypothesized that post-CA hyperoxia produces histotoxic dysoxia — impaired cellular oxygen utilization despite adequate arterial oxygenation. Methods: In a murine model of CA, mice underwent 12 minutes of asystole followed by CPR. Beginning 30 minutes post-resuscitation, mice were exposed to 30% O 2 for 6 hours. Systemic metabolic parameters, including core body temperature, whole-body oxygen consumption (V̇O 2 ), and arterial blood gas values (pH, PO 2 , SaO 2 ) were assessed. Results: Post-CA exposure to 30% O 2 induced a systemic metabolic crisis characterized by hypothermia (35.0±0.3 vs. 37.3±0.1°C, p<0.005, n=3-4) and markedly suppressed V̇O 2 (2.1±1.0 vs. 9.1±1.3 mL/kg/min, p<0.001, n=5) compared to sham animals receiving identical oxygen treatment. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated severe acidosis (pH 6.91±0.03 vs. 7.19±0.01, p<0.001, n=8-10). Notably, arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 were preserved and did not differ from sham (p>0.05, n=8-10), indicating that metabolic injury occurred independently of arterial hypoxemia. Conclusions: Post-CA hyperoxia produced systemic hypothermia, suppressed whole-body oxygen consumption, and severe acidosis. Despite normal arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 , these findings indicate a failure of cellular oxygen utilization rather than delivery. This pattern is consistent with histotoxic dysoxia and implicates mitochondrial dysfunction as a central mechanism of post-resuscitation metabolic injury.

articles.title: Abstract P2014: Pharmacological Inhibition of cGAS Attenuates the Early Post-Resuscitation Transcriptomic Inflammatory Response in a Porcine Model of Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: Objective: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS) is characterized by a rapid, dysregulated inflammatory response that exacerbates organ injury and undermines recovery. Extracellular vesicle-encapsulated mitochondrial DNA has recently been identified as a potent stimulus of post-resuscitation immune cell activation via the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Whether pharmacological cGAS inhibition can attenuate the post-resuscitation inflammatory response in vivo is unknown. Accordingly, we tested the hypothesis that cGAS inhibition attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) after cardiac arrest. Methods: Swine (n=14) underwent 7 minutes of ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest and subsequent resuscitation. After return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), animals were randomized to receive a small molecule inhibitor of cGAS (G140; 0.1 mg/kg IV; n=7) or vehicle (n=7) at 15 minutes post-ROSC. PBMCs were isolated at baseline and 4 hours post-ROSC for bulk RNA sequencing. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (adjusted p<0.05). Results: PBMCs from vehicle-treated animals exhibited 3,145 DEGs at 4 hours post-ROSC compared with baseline, reflecting widespread transcriptomic activation. G140-treated animals exhibited only 719 DEGs (77% reduction vs. vehicle; Figure, A ). Expression of cGAS itself was unchanged, consistent with pharmacological inhibition of enzymatic activity rather than gene expression. However, TBK1, the kinase immediately downstream of STING that phosphorylates IRF3, was significantly downregulated in G140-treated animals (log 2 FC=–0.39, p_adj=0.04). Additional genes within the cGAS-STING and innate immune signaling pathways were suppressed in G140- vs. vehicle-treated animals, including NLRP3, IL-15, TNFRSF11A, CCL14, and CCL21 ( Figure, B ). Conclusion: Systemic cGAS inhibition with G140 administered shortly after ROSC markedly attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in porcine PBMCs. These findings support cGAS-STING as a tractable therapeutic target and provide rationale for further evaluation of cGAS inhibition as a targeted immunomodulatory strategy in PCAS.

articles.title: Abstract P2015: Hydrogen Peroxide-Induced Pyroptosis in Cardiomyocytes is Regulated by NAMPT and NAD
articles.abstract: Introduction: The role of pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death, in cardiac injury following cardiac arrest is unknown. Related to pyroptosis, our prior work has shown that both oxidant injury and intracellular NAD levels result in significant cardiac injury and protection respectively. A better understanding of how oxidant stress and NAD metabolism affect cardiomyocyte injury and pyroptosis could identify new targets for cardiac arrest care. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that cardiac oxidant exposure induces NAD depletion and pyroptosis, which can be rescued by replenishment of cellular NAD. Methods: H9C2 cardiomyocytes were exposed to H 2 O 2 to create oxidative stress. Cell morphological change was observed under microscope, and cell viability was measured by CCK8 kit based on intracellular LDH activity. The expressions of GSDMD and GSDME and their N-terminal fragments were assessed by Western blot analysis. Intracellular NAD content was measured by assay kit. Results: H 2 O 2 induced a dose-dependent death of H9C2 cardiomyocytes, which plateaued at 1 mM and this death was related to NAD + depletion. H9C2 cells exhibited characteristic morphological changes of pyroptosis, such as cell swelling and rupture of the cell membrane, and release of LDH. Supplement with 1 mM NAM, a NAD + precursor, partially rescued viability in H 2 O 2 -treated cells from 54.9 ±1.7% to 81.7 ± 2.2% at 4h (p<0.01). The Nampt inhibitor FK866 (1 μM), which blocks NAD synthesis, totally nullified the protective effect of NAM on cell viability. The pan-caspase inhibitor Z-vad (100 μM) blocked the typical morphology of pyroptosis induced by H 2 O 2 . NAM also restored NAD + concentrations. To determine which gasdermin is involved in oxidant-induced cell death, cardiomyocytes were treated with 1 mM H 2 O 2 for up to 5 hrs. Both GSDME and its Asp270 cleavage N-terminal fragment were observed, and GSDME-N expression peaked after 2h exposure to H 2 O 2 . It was blocked by treatment with NAM or a caspase 3 inhibitor, but not by the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950. Although GSDMD was cleaved after 2h exposure, there was no expression of the cleaved GSDMD (Asp275) N-terminal fragment. Conclusion: Cardiac oxidant injury, known to occur during cardiac arrest, can result in pyroptotic cell death that is mediated by caspases and can be rescued by NAD precursor treatment.

articles.title: Abstract P2016: Physiological Effects of a Flow-Modulating Device During Prolonged Manual Ventilation in a Swine Model
articles.abstract: Introduction: In austere settings, prolonged bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation may be required before advanced airway support is available. Excessive inspiratory flow, elevated airway pressures, and inconsistent tidal volumes during sustained manual ventilation increase the risk of lung injury and provider fatigue. Sotair is a flow-modulating accessory designed to improve ventilation safety during prolonged manual ventilation. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that Sotair would improve ventilation safety by limiting excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume delivery while maintaining physiologic stability compared to ventilation with a sham device. Methods: Twenty-two juvenile domestic swine (mean weight 52 ± 4 kg) were enrolled and assigned to 6-hour (n=8) or 24-hour (n=14) ventilation cohorts in a non-survival model of prolonged manual overventilation. Animals underwent intubation, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, hourly arterial blood gas sampling, and prolonged manual ventilation with a BVM system using either an active Sotair or sham device. Respiratory rate was titrated to end-tidal CO 2, and sham ventilation was delivered with forceful manual respirations to model excessive ventilation conditions. Airway flow, peak airway pressure, and tidal volume were continuously recorded, and gross lung injury was assessed at necropsy. Longitudinal physiologic data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations and mixed-effects regression models. Results: Twenty-one animals were analyzed after protocol violation: 8 in the 6-hour cohort (4 sham, 4 Sotair) and 13 in the 24-hour cohort (7 sham, 6 Sotair). Across 124,350 breaths over 360 observation hours, Sotair significantly reduced average inspiratory flow (–46.63 L/min), peak airway pressure (–33.04 cmH 2 O), and tidal volume (–312.52 mL) compared with sham ventilation (all p<0.001). In the 24-hour cohort, Sotair was associated with improved oxygenation stability, including higher ABG-derived arterial oxygen saturation at 24 hours compared with sham (+3.34%, p=0.031), lower continuous pulse oximetry-derived oxygen saturation coefficient of variation (1.73% vs 4.26%, p<0.0001), and lower partial pressure carbon dioxide coefficient of variation (12.01% vs 15.29%, p<0.0001). Gross lung injury scores did not differ significantly between treatment groups overall, although injury severity was greater in 24-hour than in 6-hour animals independent of device assignment (p=0.003). Conclusions: Flow modulation using Sotair reduced excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume during prolonged manual ventilation while maintaining physiologic stability. Although gross injury outcomes were not significantly different between groups, these findings support further evaluation of Sotair as a low-resource adjunct for prolonged field care and austere settings.

articles.title: Abstract P2017: Cadaveric Evaluation of Supraglottic Prehospital Ventilation Esophageal Pressure and Gastric Venting
articles.abstract: Background: During prehospital airway and ventilatory emergencies including respiratory emergencies, airway compromise, and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), ventilation delivered by prehospital providers often exceeds recommended airway pressures and ventilation rates. Elevated inspiratory pressures increase intrathoracic pressure, impair venous return, and promote gastric insufflation, increasing the risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) are widely used in emergency medical services because they can be placed rapidly and have high first-pass success rates. However, limited physiologic data describe how SGA design affects esophageal pressure transmission under high-pressure ventilation conditions typical of prehospital resuscitation. Hypothesis: Second-generation SGAs with dual gastric channels will reduce gastric insufflation and distention, reflected by lower esophageal pressures, compared with single-channel devices under conditions simulating cardiac arrest ventilation. Goal: This study compared esophageal pressure transmission and gastric venting among SGAs during pressure-controlled ventilation simulating prehospital cardiac arrest. Methods: In a controlled cadaveric study, fresh unfixed human cadavers were ventilated with multiple SGAs; an endotracheal tube served as the reference standard. Pressure-controlled ventilation was delivered at inspiratory pressures of 20, 30, 40, and 50 cmH 2 O to replicate prehospital ventilation extremes. Distal esophageal pressure was measured continuously through a cannula inserted through the abdominal wall into the stomach and secured in the distal esophagus. Airway placement was confirmed bronchoscopically, and airflow through gastric channels and oropharyngeal leak pathways was assessed. Results: As inspiratory pressure increased, esophageal pressure rose across all devices. Dual-channel second-generation SGAs transmitted lower esophageal pressures than single-channel and first-generation devices, indicating reduced gastric insufflation and distention under high-pressure ventilation. Conclusion: SGA design significantly influences esophageal pressure transmission during cardiac arrest ventilation. Dual-channel second-generation SGAs reduce esophageal pressurization, suggesting a mechanism to mitigate gastric distention during CPR. These findings have direct implications for OHCA airway strategy, supporting device selection and ventilation approaches that minimize hyperventilation and its downstream hemodynamic consequences during resuscitation.

articles.title: Abstract P2018: Effects of Positive-End Expiratory Pressure on Capnography and Hemodynamics During Mechanical Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Swine
articles.abstract: Introduction: During CPR, chest compressions induce oscillations in the capnogram that can be quantified as the Capnogram Oscillation Magnitude (COM) and the Airway Opening Index (AOI). These metrics are hypothesized to reflect airway patency and effective ventilation. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) may modulate capnographic waveform morphology during CPR, though the relationship between PEEP, COM, AOI, and hemodynamics remains poorly understood. Aim: We examined the effect of titrated PEEP on capnographic waveform morphology, including COM, AOI, and peak end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) during mechanical CPR in a pilot study using a swine model of ventricular fibrillation (VF) cardiac arrest. Methods: Four swine underwent 8 minutes of untreated VF followed by 60 minutes of mechanical CPR. Animals were intubated and ventilated at 10 breaths/min with fraction of inspired oxygen of 1.0. PEEP was sequentially titrated across 6-minute epochs of 0, 5, and 10 cmH 2 O in repeated cycles during CPR. 6 doses of epinephrine (0.02 mg/kg) were administered beginning at minute 14 and repeated every 4 minutes. Continuous capnography and aortic blood pressure were recorded throughout. A custom MATLAB algorithm was used to calculate COM and AOI. Results: Across 4 animals, we observed that stepwise increases in PEEP from 0 to 5 to 10 cmH2O were associated with longer time to peak ETCO2 within ventilation cycles (Figure 1). We observed no overall changes in aortic pressure or ETCO2 with PEEP titrations, but these did gradually decrease over the course of resuscitation (Figure 2). Conclusion: In this preliminary swine model of cardiac arrest, increasing PEEP appeared to influence capnographic waveform morphology during mechanical CPR, particularly the time to peak ETCO2 after a ventilation. Aortic blood pressure and overall ETCO2 remained largely stable during stepwise PEEP titration, but decreased over the course of resuscitation. This association may indicate that at higher PEEP levels cardiac output exceeds ventilation, resulting in the prolonged time to peak ETCO2. Ongoing analysis will quantify the dose-dependent effects of PEEP on ventilation metrics (AOI, COM, and peak ETCO2), along with indicators of cardiac output (aortic blood pressure and the area under the capnography waveform curve). These findings may inform PEEP as a modifiable ventilation parameter during CPR to optimize airway management and resuscitation outcomes.

articles.title: Abstract P2019: Mental Health Outcomes After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population-Based Cohort Study Comparing Adult Survivors with Other Critically Ill Patients
articles.abstract: Background: Psychiatric morbidity is common after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet whether survivors carry excess risk relative to other critically ill patients or instead share post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) mechanisms remains unclear. Hypothesis: OHCA survivors experience excess new-onset mental health and addictions (MHA) risk compared with matched critical illness survivors, beyond what is explained by pre-existing psychiatric history and sociodemographic vulnerability. Methods: Population-based retrospective cohort study (ICES, Ontario, Canada; 2007-2022). Adults surviving ICU admission for non-traumatic OHCA were matched to non-OHCA critical illness survivors by age (±3 years) and admission date (±3 days). Primary outcome: time to first new-onset MHA diagnosis within 15 years of discharge, from validated physician-coded inpatient, emergency department (ED), and outpatient records. We fit flexible parametric (Royston-Parmar) survival models with death as a competing risk and used logistic regression to compare inpatient versus outpatient care intensity, adjusting for sex, comorbidities, prior healthcare use, and neighbourhood marginalization. Results: Among 6,034 OHCA survivors matched to 16,461 controls (mean follow-up 4.7 years), 2,740 OHCA survivors (45.4%) received a new MHA diagnosis: anxiety/mood (33.9%), substance-related (7.8%), and psychotic disorders (2.7%); 20.0% required inpatient psychiatric admission. Incidence peaked within six months post-discharge. Composite MHA hazard was similar between cohorts (aHR 0.95; 95% CI 0.89-1.02). OHCA survivors had lower hazards for outpatient anxiety/mood (aHR 0.91), psychotic (0.74), and behavioural disorders (0.62); any inpatient psychiatric admission (0.85); inpatient mood disorders (0.69); and deliberate self-harm (0.73). The strongest predictor of new MHA outcomes was pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (aHR 2.22; 95% CI 1.97-2.49); high pre-arrest ED use, younger age, female sex, and residence in racially marginalized or high-density neighbourhoods also independently predicted risk. Conclusions: Contrary to our hypothesis, OHCA survivors did not exhibit excess MHA risk versus matched critical illness survivors and showed lower hazards across several subcategories, suggesting shared post-ICU rather than arrest-specific psychiatric mechanisms. Nevertheless, nearly half developed a new MHA diagnosis, concentrated in the first six months and driven chiefly by pre-existing psychiatric history. These findings support integrating OHCA survivors into unified post-ICU mental health pathways, with early screening and targeted outreach for those with prior psychiatric diagnoses, high ED use, or residence in disadvantaged communities.

articles.title: Abstract P2020: Adolescent and Young Adult Survivors’ and Parent Co Survivors’ Lived Experiences of Pediatric Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivorship
articles.abstract: Background: Survival following pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has improved, yet there is a paucity of research about the long-term outcomes and experiences of survivors and their families. Understanding their experiences will help shape survivor- and co-survivor-centered interventions and outcomes that focus on long-term recovery and well-being. Research Question: What is the lived experience of adolescent/young adult survivors (AYA) of OHCA and their parent co-survivors in survivorship? Aims: This study primarily sought to: (1) gain a deeper understanding of AYA survivors’ and their parents’/legal guardians’ perceptions of life after a CA in survivorship and (2) understand how survivors’ and co-survivors’ needs have changed over time since arrest. Methods: The study was conducted at a large pediatric healthcare system in Southern California using a qualitative phenomenological design. Participants were recruited using purposive, snowball, and convenience sampling. Eligible AYA were aged 10 to 24 years, English-speaking, experienced OHCA between ages 10-18, survived greater than 6 months post-arrest, and were able to verbally articulate their experiences. Parents/legal guardians of eligible AYA were also invited to participate. Each participant completed two semi-structured interviews between October 2025 and March 2026, which were audio-recorded and transcribed. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis informed by the hermeneutic circle. Coding was performed independently by two researchers, resolving discrepancies through consensus. Recruitment continued until thematic saturation was achieved. Results: Nine participants, including both survivors (n=3, 33.3%) and co-survivors (n=6, 66.6%), participated. Survivors were aged 18 to 24 years, and co-survivors were aged 40 to 59 years. Four (44.4%) self-identified as Hispanic or Latino. Five (55.5%) identified as White, two (22.2%) as Asian, and two (22.2%) as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander. Among participants, four (44.4%) preferred “she” as their gender pronoun, three (33.3%) preferred “he,” and two (22.2%) preferred not to state. Five overarching themes about survivorship were identified: survivorship (a) is a new normal, (b) means being there, (c) is a physical embodiment, (d) means letting go, and (e) is what meaning we want to give it. Survivors emphasized challenges with self-concept and social reintegration, which is critical in their development stage. Parents described persistent anxiety, adjustment challenges, and advocacy burdens. Both groups highlighted discordance between acute care received and long-term support. Conclusions: AYA survivors of OHCA and their parents experience enduring psychosocial and functional impacts. Findings underscore the need for structured, family-centered, and individualized support throughout survivorship.

articles.title: Abstract P2021: Temporal Trends in Hospitalization and Survival After Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Insights from the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES)
articles.abstract: Background: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major public health challenge, with persistent variation in outcomes across demographic and clinical subgroups. Evaluating recent trends in hospitalization and survival may identify disparities and inform targeted improvements in resuscitation systems of care. Methods: We conducted a retrospective trend analysis using the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) from 2019-2024. We evaluated temporal changes in (1) proportions of hospitalized OHCA patients across demographic and clinical characteristics and (2) survival to hospital discharge stratified by hospitalization-related factors.Generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution and log link were applied separately for each subgroup, with calendar year modeled as a continuous predictor and population at risk included as an offset. Deviance-based corrections accounted for overdispersion. Annual percentage changes with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated, with p<0.05 indicating statistical significance. Results: Significant shifts in OHCA hospitalization patterns were observed. The proportion of hospitalized female patients declined by 0.60% per year (95% CI, –0.76% to –0.45%; p<0.0001), while male hospitalizations increased by 0.37% per year (95% CI, 0.28% to 0.46%; p<0.0001). Hospitalizations among Black patients decreased modestly (–1.30% per year; 95% CI, –2.56% to –0.03%; p=0.045), whereas Hispanic/Latino patients demonstrated a substantial increase (4.94% per year; 95% CI, 2.17% to 7.79%; p=0.0004).Clinically, the proportion of patients achieving sustained return of spontaneous circulation declined (–2.58% per year; 95% CI, –4.41% to –0.72%; p=0.0066), while hospitalizations without sustained ROSC increased modestly. The proportion pronounced dead in the emergency department decreased significantly (–6.26% per year; 95% CI, –10.24% to –2.10%; p=0.0035).Despite these shifts, no subgroup demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in survival to discharge. Overall survival increased by 1.54% per year (95% CI, –2.18% to 5.39%; p=0.42), with similarly non-significant findings across arrest characteristics and hospitalization factors. Conclusions: From 2019 to 2024, OHCA hospitalization patterns shifted across demographic and clinical subgroups, with persistent disparities and declining sustained ROSC. Despite these changes, survival to hospital discharge has not significantly improved. These findings highlight ongoing inequities and underscore the need for targeted, system-level interventions to improve OHCA outcomes.

articles.title: Abstract P2022: Functional Recovery After Cardiac Arrest Understanding Paths and Potential
articles.abstract: Introduction: Survivorship after cardiac arrest includes cognitive, emotional, and physical aspects of recovery. Domain specific recovery trajectories are individualized and under-reported in the literature. Understanding recovery capacity is critical for optimizing goal setting when counseling patients and their caregivers. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of comatose cardiac arrest survivors enrolled in our single-center acute brain injury repository between 2/5/2022 and 12/11/2025. We excluded patients who died prior to hospital discharge or who had no follow up modified Rankin Scale score (mRS). Patients were followed prospectively, and mRS was determined using patient and family interviews. Patients discharged alive with at least one follow-up mRS at any of the four time-points (3-month, 6-month, one year, two years) were included in the analysis. Good outcome was defined as mRS 0-3; longitudinal mRS changes were assessed with a Sankey plot. Results: Among the 56 patients [mean (SD) age 57.7 (16.8) years] included, 89.3% (n=50) were out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The most common arrest etiology was cardiac (n = 36, 64.3%), of which the majority (n = 26, 72.2%) had a shockable rhythm, followed by respiratory (n = 15, 26.8%). Median (IQR) length of stay was 14 (9-22) days. The most common discharge locations were home (n=31, 55.4%) and short-term rehabilitation (n=14, 25%). Median (IQR) number of mRS assessments was 2 (2-3). Good outcome increased from 23 patients at three months to 26 patients at one year. There was one patient with poor outcome at one-year (mRS 4) who improved to good outcome at two years (mRS 0). In a sub-analysis of patients with an mRS at both 3-months and 1-year (n=11), 4 (36.4%) patients with mRS 2-3 improved to mRS 0-1. Conclusion: Functional neurologic recovery following cardiac arrest varies over time. Understanding recovery trajectories and factors associated with improvement are critical to maximizing survivorship potential. Our preliminary findings convey that recovery can be delayed, and possible up to two years following arrest.

articles.title: Abstract P2023: Hospital Readmission and Mortality in Cardiac Arrest Survivors Discharged with Favorable Neurologic Outcome
articles.abstract: Introduction: Even among cardiac arrest survivors discharged with favorable neurologic outcomes, the risk of subsequent cardiac and non-cardiac complications, hospital re-admission, and mortality remains substantial. A better understanding of the causes and predictors of post-discharge re-admission and death is essential to developing targeted follow-up strategies, optimizing long-term recovery, and improving cardiac arrest survivorship. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of cardiac arrest survivors enrolled in a single center cardiac arrest recovery program (CARP) between 1/19/2024 and 5/9/2026. The CARP program follows all in-hospital (IHCA) and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients from index hospitalization admission to discharge, at which point those who awaken and were following basic commands were enrolled. Enrollment included an evaluation for psychological and cognitive symptoms, as well as post-discharge neurology clinic appointment (on average three months post-discharge). Amongst enrolled patients, hospital re-admissions and mortality occurring prior to post-discharge neurology clinic visit were tracked. Results: Of 105 enrolled patients, 34 (32.4%) underwent hospital readmission. The median [interquartile range] time from index cardiac arrest discharge to re-admission was 16 [8-99.8] days. Eight (7.6% of all patients, 24% of re-admitted patients) died at a median of 71.5 [20-160] days from index hospital discharge. The most common cause of death was withdrawal of life sustaining therapy (50%, n=4), followed by recurrent arrest without ROSC (25%, n=2). Amongst those who survived the readmission, the median [IQR] length of stay was 4 [2-10] days and the most common admission diagnoses included cardiopulmonary dysfunction (n=13, 38.2%) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (n=11, 32.4%). Patients requiring readmission were more likely to have suffered an IHCA, were younger, had longer length of stay, and were less likely to be discharged home (Table 1). Conclusion: Cardiac arrest survivors experience a heightened risk for readmission and mortality, even after discharge with good neurologic outcome. The most common causes for readmission were cardiopulmonary and neurologic symptoms. Further work to help identify those at highest risk for readmission and to evaluate the impact of a nurse navigator on readmission rate and mortality should be prioritized.

articles.title: A “Significant” Shift in Statistical Interpretation in Ecology and Evolution: A Helpful Guide for Authors and Reviewers
articles.abstract: “Statistical significance”, wherein the deviation of some measure of a sample population is greater than an expected threshold (usually p > 0.05) is a concept and practice strongly embedded in the life sciences. However, the use of “statistical significance” has been deprecated by the American Statistical Association (ASA), and that news has been slow to spread across disciplines. The result of this misuse is that many authors are wrongfully claiming “no effect” of a variable when p > 0.05 or confidence intervals (CIs) overlap zero. To ensure scientific rigor in Ecology and Evolution, we offer this brief guide to authors and reviewers and strongly encourage authors to use the ASA statement on p‐values. The ASA suggests that authors report effect sizes and attendant error in ways that let users judge support for the hypotheses represented in a model, avoiding the binary “true or false” of p = 0.05 or overlapping CIs. Furthermore, we encourage authors to acquaint themselves with numerous other common mistakes in statistical interpretation highlighted by the ASA and subsequent authors. By incorporating these principles into statistical reporting and results, information and patterns that might otherwise be overlooked remain available for readers to evaluate. We recognize that changes in reporting practices will not occur overnight, so our aim is to help authors adopt ASA principles: to that end we describe potential problems and offer guidelines for authors and reviewers to follow, to avoid incorrect statistical interpretations and spurious conclusions.

articles.title: Broad‐Scale Landscape Structure and Fine‐Scale Microhabitat Jointly Shape the Distribution of the Jeju Salamander, Hynobius quelpaertensis
articles.abstract: Species distribution models often assume that species occupy all environmentally suitable space, but low-dispersal amphibians may track landscape structure that has persisted over long periods as well as current local conditions. We examined how broad-scale landscape structure and fine-scale microhabitat jointly shape the distribution of the Jeju salamander, Hynobius quelpaertensis, on Jeju Island, Republic of Korea. Using 85 spatially thinned occurrence records and 10,000 background points sampled on land, we compared a broad-scale predictor set (terrain at ≥ 1 km, drainage position and long-term climate, used as a proxy for a long-term topographic-hydrological template) with a fine-scale set (microtopography, wetness, insolation and canopy). Weighted elastic-net models were evaluated by spatial block cross-validation with block-bootstrap confidence intervals, and a generalized additive model (GAM) with broad-scale suitability as an offset tested whether microhabitat refined occupancy within broadly suitable space. The broad-scale and fine-scale models discriminated occurrences equally well (ROC AUC = 0.79 and 0.78), but the broad-scale model was better calibrated (Tjur's R 2 = 0.16 vs. 0.12), and the combined model performed best (ROC AUC = 0.81; Tjur's R 2 = 0.20). Both sets identified drainage position: occurrence increased with upstream drainage area and local wetness and was higher in hollows and valley bottoms. Within the broad-scale core, fine-scale smooth terms doubled Tjur's R 2 (0.14 to 0.28): occurrence rose with canopy shade and valley depth and declined on exposed south-facing slopes, although the gain in discrimination was uncertain. Areas suitable only at the fine scale covered 24% of the island but had one-sixth the presence rate of areas suitable at both scales. Valley drainage structure thus sets the template for the distribution of H. quelpaertensis, and shaded, moist microhabitat refines occupancy within it. Conservation should maintain drainage networks together with their forest cover, and candidate unoccupied areas should be surveyed in the field.

articles.title: Comparative Chloroplast Genomics Reveals Phylogenetic Relationships Among Korean Dioscorea Species
articles.abstract: Crop wild relatives represent important sources of genetic variation for crop improvement, particularly as climate change and increasing global food demand require the development of more resilient and productive crop varieties. However, genomic information on many wild Dioscorea species in East Asia remains limited. In this study, we sequenced and assembled the complete chloroplast genomes of six Dioscorea species native to Korea, including the first reported complete chloroplast genome of D. coreana. The assembled genomes exhibited a conserved quadripartite structure with similar gene contents and GC compositions across species. Despite this overall conservation, comparative analyses revealed localized sequence variation, particularly in noncoding regions. Several loci, including ndhF and ycf1, exhibited increased nucleotide diversity, indicating their potential as informative markers. In addition, simple sequence repeats were composed mainly of A/T‐rich motifs and predominantly distributed in the large single‐copy region. Phylogenetic analysis based on concatenated chloroplast protein‐coding gene sequences provided a well‐resolved framework for the studied taxa and clarified the relationships among Korean Dioscorea species. Furthermore, the close genetic relationship between cultivated yam and its wild relatives was supported. These results provide new genomic data for previously underrepresented Korean taxa, including the first chloroplast genome of D. coreana, and offer a basis for future studies on genetic diversity, species identification, and the utilization of wild germplasm.

articles.title: Conservation Implications of High Population Genetic Structure Detected in a Parasitic Fluke of Diamondback Terrapins
articles.abstract: Parasites are increasingly utilized as surrogates for investigating host ecology. Digenean trematodes (“flukes”) have been identified as promising bioindicators because they have obligate multi‐host life cycles that often include an abundant and accessible gastropod intermediate host and one or more vertebrate definitive hosts. Definitive vertebrate hosts are typically the mechanism for dispersal by flukes, thus driving congruent patterns in population genetic structure between host and parasite. This suggests that flukes can function as surrogates for understanding dispersal of their vertebrate hosts. Here, we investigated the terrapin fluke Pleurogonius malaclemys as a surrogate for its definitive diamondback terrapin host Malaclemys terrapin. This parasite is reliant on its intermediate host, the eastern mudsnail Ilyanassa obsoleta, as well as terrapin final hosts. We hypothesized that there would be high population genetic structure across fluke populations, reflecting the limited dispersal rates and low population connectivity of terrapin hosts. Specimens of Pleurogonius malaclemys were sampled from mudsnails (internal first‐intermediate and external cyst stages) and from terrapins (adult stage) across their co‐occurring range from Massachusetts to northeast Florida. Fluke mitochondrial DNA was extracted and sequenced, and a 620 bp fragment was used for population genetics analyses. Asexually reproducing larval fluke stages were rare within mudsnails (often 0%, but never exceeding 3.85%), while external cysts were common on mudsnails (up to 74%). About 45% of terrapins from southern New Jersey harbored adult flukes. Genetics analyses revealed high diversity and population genetic structure in flukes, broadly consistent with reported patterns for terrapins. Our study provides baseline genetic data and a foundational understanding of the biogeography and diversity of the terrapin fluke, thereby identifying a promising surrogate for terrapin population ecology and subsequent conservation efforts.

articles.title: Relationship Between Predicted Habitat Suitability and Population Density of Game Mammals Under a Sharply Continental Climate
articles.abstract: This study evaluates the relationship between MaxEnt-predicted habitat suitability and departmental estimates of population density for 14 game mammal species in the Pavlodar Region. Model performance varied substantially among species (Test AUC = 0.538–0.992; TSS = 0.220–0.984), and extremely high AUC values for some species with small samples were interpreted cautiously. For 41 territorial units, habitat suitability was aggregated as the mean MaxEnt value within each polygon and compared with density using Spearman's rank correlation. Spearman's r s ranged from 0.288 to 0.738; in the initial analysis, a statistically significant positive relationship was detected for 13 of the 14 species, whereas the relationship was not statistically significant for the steppe polecat (r s = 0.288; p = 0.068). Residual spatial autocorrelation assessed with Moran's I was non-significant for 11 species; for wolf, bobak marmot, and roe deer, an additional spatially constrained permutation analysis was performed. After this analysis, the relationship remained significant for wolf (r s = 0.714, p = 0.0007) and roe deer (r s = 0.488, p = 0.0198), whereas for bobak marmot it remained positive but was not statistically significant after accounting for spatial structure (r s = 0.467; p = 0.0615). The results indicate that habitat suitability reflects the environmental potential of an area but is not a direct measure of population density.

articles.title: Siblings in Flight: Unravelling Reproductive Barriers Between Two Butterfly Sister Species
articles.abstract: Understanding how reproductive isolation is maintained between closely related taxa is a central question in evolutionary biology. Here, we investigate the mechanisms underlying divergence and isolation between two sister butterflies, Erebia palarica and Erebia meolans, which occur in sympatry in the Cantabrian Mountains (N Spain) and in allopatry elsewhere. Using an integrative approach, we combine genetic, genome synteny and cytogenetic analyses, Wolbachia screening, and geometric morphometrics to assess their evolutionary history and elucidate potential reproductive barriers between these species. The phylogeographic pattern suggests that both species diverged in allopatry, coming into secondary contact along the Cantabrian Mountains after the last glacial maximum. Both mitochondrial and nuclear markers recover reciprocal monophyly, indicating the absence of recent hybridisation. The identical chromosome numbers in both species (2n = 28), the absence of major chromosomal rearrangements or straightforward genitalia differentiation, and the presence of the same Wolbachia strain in all infected individuals suggest that neither chromosomal rearrangements nor Wolbachia‐induced incompatibilities contribute to their reproductive isolation in sympatry. In contrast, morphometric analyses show a significant divergence in wing size consistent with asymmetric character displacement: sympatric populations of E. palarica exhibit larger wings relative to both allopatric conspecifics and sympatric E. meolans, whereas E. meolans shows little size variation across northern Spain. Our findings point to wing size divergence in E. palarica as a response to sympatry with E. meolans. Overall, this study provides novel empirical evidence for morphometric character displacement in the family Nymphalidae, highlights the importance of multidisciplinary approaches for understanding species differentiation, and sets a framework for future genomic studies of speciation and reproductive isolation between closely related taxa.

articles.title: Thermoregulatory strategy shapes physiological responses to dormancy in animals: A meta‐analysis
articles.abstract: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Dormancy allows animals to persist through prolonged periods of unfavourable environmental conditions by entering states of extreme metabolic depression. However, physiological responses to dormancy vary substantially across taxa and can involve changes in redox balance, immune function and endocrine adjustments. A key unresolved question is whether this variation reflects fundamental differences in how endotherms and ectotherms regulate metabolic depression and subsequent reactivation, with implications for understanding animal life histories and responses to climate change. Here, we conducted a meta‐analysis to test whether physiological responses to dormancy differ between endothermic and ectothermic animals. We synthesised 2464 effect sizes from 106 studies across 57 species, quantifying redox, immune and glucocorticoid status during dormant and arousal states relative to active, non‐dormant state, under cold‐ and heat‐induced dormancy.
