Defect-Initiated Anisotropic Oxidation in Two-Dimensional GaSe
articles.abstract: Oxidation governs the stability and functional conversion of two-dimensional semiconductors, yet its propagation through layered crystals remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the thickness-dependent oxidation of GaSe using optical spectroscopy, cross-sectional microscopy, and first-principles calculations. Experiments reveal concurrent top-down and edge-initiated oxidation, accompanied by Se redistribution and transient Ga2Se3 formation. Calculations identify Se vacancies as favorable sites for O2 adsorption and activation, which weaken neighboring Ga–Se bonds and promote oxygen incorporation. Molecular O2 faces a 4.03 eV barrier when penetrating a monolayer Ga2O3 model, compared with 0.54 eV along a GaSe van der Waals gap. This contrast supports interlayer diffusion as a plausible pathway for lateral oxidation, consistent with the pronounced thickness dependence and spatial anisotropy observed experimentally. Oxidation also yields a progression from p-type GaSe through ambipolar Ga2O3/GaSe heterostructures to n-type Ga2O3, whose devices retain stable characteristics after 300 °C air annealing.

articles.title: Emergent Giant Topological Hall Effect at the van der Waals Ferromagnet/Topological Insulator Interface
articles.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) magnet-based heterostructures provide a vital platform for manipulating magnetic ground states and hosting complex spin textures. The topological Hall effect (THE) is a powerful tool for probing these textures in such systems. However, achieving a sizable THE in 2D vdW ferromagnets remains challenging due to the absence of broken inversion symmetry and sufficiently strong spin–orbit coupling (SOC). Here, we report an emergent giant topological Hall resistivity of 6.9 μΩ·cm at 10 K by interfacing the 2D ferromagnet Fe3GeTe2 (FGT) with the topological insulator BiSbTeSe2 (BSTS). Systematic temperature- and thickness-dependent studies suggest the origin of this pronounced signal to be the interfacial Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI). Furthermore, temperature-field mapping reveals the coexistence of two distinct phases that we identify as having opposite topological charge. Our results establish these vdW ferromagnet/topological insulator heterostructures as a robust platform for enhanced interfacial THE, opening new avenues for high-efficiency topological spintronics.

articles.title: Photoinduced Carrier Doping of α-RuCl3 through Interlayer Charge Transfer
articles.abstract: Controlling doping density in correlated quantum materials offers a route to tuning their electronic states, but chemical doping can introduce disorder and limits dynamic control. Here, we demonstrate optically tunable electron doping of the layered Mott insulator α-RuCl3 through photoinduced interlayer charge transfer in MoS2/α-RuCl3 heterostructures. Photoluminescence and transient absorption measurements support electron transfer to α-RuCl3, leaving holes in MoS2. The layer-separated carrier population persists for more than 100 ps with an estimated doping density tunable through the excitation fluence. Selective excitation of α-RuCl3 further reveals hole transfer to MoS2. Transient absorption microscopy yields an early time effective hole diffusion coefficient of approximately 100 cm2 s–1 in the heterostructure, supporting a predominantly unbound carrier population. These results establish photoinduced charge transfer as a means of dynamically controlling carrier doping in α-RuCl3, providing a route toward optical manipulation of correlated electronic states.

articles.title: Photoluminescence-Driven Quasi-BICs in Photonic Nanomembranes for Active Refractometric Sensing
articles.abstract: Quasi-bound states in the continuum (quasi-BICs) offer a powerful platform for refractometric sensing by combining narrow resonances with strong electromagnetic confinement, promising high spectral resolution and large figures of merit (FOM). In practice, however, these advantages are often compromised by stringent angular alignment in passive transmission/reflection interrogation. Here, we demonstrate an active sensing platform that couples the defect-related photoluminescence (PL) of a freestanding silicon nitride nanomembrane to quasi-BIC modes. The substrate-free architecture suppresses radiation leakage and sustains tightly confined high-Q resonances, while emission-based readout bypasses stringent angular alignment. The resulting PL resonances exhibit line widths of 0.17 nm (Q ≈ 4000) in air and 0.26 nm in water. In aqueous sensing, the platform achieves a FOM of 250, substantially exceeding representative values reported for passive quasi-BIC sensors in the visible regime. This synergy translates the high-Q advantage of quasi-BICs into a practical active platform for high-performance refractometric and surface-binding sensing.

articles.title: Ultralow-Loss Femtosecond Laser Slicing of Lithium Niobate Enabled by Anisotropic Thermal Dissipation-Guided Vector Scanning
articles.abstract: Lithium niobate (LiNbO3) crystals have been widely used in photonic and electronic devices owing to their outstanding intrinsic optoelectronic properties. However, fabricating hundreds-of-micrometer-thick LiNbO3 wafers remains dominated by diamond wire sawing, which causes substantial material loss. Although ultrafast laser processing offers a promising alternative, the intrinsic noncentrosymmetric lattice, spontaneous polarization, and anisotropic photothermal response of LiNbO3 severely hinder high-quality laser cutting. Here, a thermal dissipation-guided vector scanning technology is proposed to realize ultrafast laser slicing of LiNbO3 crystals for the first time. By tailoring the scanning direction according to the anisotropic thermal dissipation, we achieve crystal exfoliation with an ultrathin subsurface damage layer of 10 μm and an exceptionally high-quality separation surface. The results establish vector scanning technology as an innovative route for high-quality femtosecond laser processing and low-damage separation of anisotropic crystals.

articles.title: Ultrathin SrTiO3 Capping Stabilizes the Surface Chemistry of Brownmillerite Ferrites during Reduction
articles.abstract: Redox processes in oxides are central to materials synthesis and functionality, but their control is often hindered by surface instabilities. Using ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, we show that a nominally 1 nm-thick SrTiO3 (STO) cap markedly enhances the surface stability of La0.05Sr0.95FeO2.5-δ (LSFO) thin films during H2 reduction by suppressing the formation of a secondary metallic Fe0 phase. Kinetic analysis indicates that the STO cap reduces the effective Fe0 formation rates by more than 6-fold at both 250 and 350 °C. These findings highlight ultrathin capping layers as an effective strategy for stabilizing oxide surfaces during redox.

articles.title: Antagonistic second-messenger signalling coordinates Pseudomonas aeruginosa surface colonization and virulence
articles.abstract: Second messengers cAMP and c-di-GMP regulate surface behaviours and virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Here, the authors show how the bacteria switch between attachment and surface movement by coordinating the two signalling systems, allowing distinct bacterial populations to work together to colonise and damage human airway tissue.

articles.title: CO2 responsive nanoscopic and macroscopic materials directed by peptides
articles.abstract: Stimuli responsive assemblies can offer precise control over behaviour, but use of gases for this control is rare. Here, the authors report the use of carbon dioxide for tuneable nanoparticle response, directed by changes in peptide structure.

articles.title: Coupling electrolyte mechanical reinforcement and interfacial stress relaxation for near-ambient sulfide all-solid-state lithium metal batteries
articles.abstract: All-solid-state lithium metal batteries can suffer from dendrite growth and interfacial stress at low pressures. Here, authors couple a self-polymerizable composite sulfide electrolyte with a porous carbon current collector, enabling stable near-ambient condition cycling at high areal loading.

articles.title: Fully Integrated Deep-Ocean Flexible Temperature–Depth Sensor with Neural Network Compensation
articles.abstract: Marine pressure monitoring helps reveal ocean dynamics and assess human impacts. This work reports a self-contained low-power flexible marine temperature depth (FMTD) sensor featuring wide range, high precision and restrained temperature drift.

articles.title: Nanofluid wetting of Cu enables thin lithium negative electrodes for high-energy and long-cycling lithium metal batteries
articles.abstract: Lithium metal batteries face trade-offs between energy density and cycling life owing to lithium processability and plating challenges. Here, authors develop a nanofluid-wetting method to fabricate thin Li foils down to 800 nm, which enables anode-lean pouch cells with 498 Wh kg–1 / 1,142 Wh L–1 and stable cycling over 250 cycles.

articles.title: Selective depolymerization of poly(ethylene terephthalate) for economical closed-loop recycling of mixed textiles
articles.abstract: Recovering polymerization-grade monomers from waste textiles remains challenging. Here the authors report that the depolymerization of PET from thermally treated mixed textiles via methanolysis can be achieved in a rapid yet highly selective manner under mild conditions.

articles.title: Topological Josephson trijunctions as a Majorana source and path
articles.abstract: Majorana bound states (MBSs) are zero-energy localized states in topological superconductors, obeying non-Abelian braiding statistics. Manipulation of mobile MBSs, encompassing their on-demand generation, propagation, and fusion, is essential for braiding MBSs and operating topological qubits. We show that the manipulation is enabled by a trijunction formed on a topological insulator in a perpendicular magnetic field, where three Josephson junctions meet. While the superconducting phases at the trijunction center evolve to cross a boundary between topological and non-topological phase domains, the trijunction offers two distinct dynamics, source/sink and path, depending on the phase boundaries. At a source/sink boundary, two MBSs are pairwise generated at the center, and one of them is ejected to a Josephson junction. The reverse, pair annihilation by collision of two MBSs, can also happen. At a path boundary, an MBS moves from a Josephson junction to the trijunction center or vice versa, without involving other MBSs. Exploiting the two dynamics, fusion and braiding of MBSs can be operated in a trijunction network. We illustrate this with a double trijunction setup, where non-Abelian state evolutions associated with MBSs can be manipulated without dynamical control of the setup and detected by Josephson emission spectroscopy. Manipulating Majorana bound states is a key requirement for topological quantum computation. Here, the authors propose a topological insulator Josephson trijunction in a magnetic field that enables the generation, transport, and fusion of Majorana bound states through static control of superconducting phases.

articles.title: WASH orchestrates phagosomal maturation and bacterial killing in neutrophils through syntaxin 19-mediated lysosomal fusion
articles.abstract: Neutrophil phagocytosis is crucial for combating infections, yet the actin-mediated regulation of vesicular trafficking during late phagosomal maturation remains obscure. Using neutrophils lacking the actin nucleation regulator Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome Protein and Scar Homolog (WASH), we identify a mechanism linking actin remodeling, lysosomal fusion, and bacterial killing. Although WASH is dispensable for particle internalization, WASH deficiency impairs lysosome-phagosome fusion and intracellular bacterial killing. Lysosomes from WASH-deficient neutrophils show decreased association with actin comets and impaired dynamics. Rac1 activation rescues lysosomal trafficking but not phagosomal maturation. Mass spectrometry of phagolysosomes and TR-FRET identify atypical syntaxin 19 (STX19) as a WASH binding partner, and WASH recruits STX19 to phagosomes. Reconstituting WASH in primary neutrophils rescues phagocytosis, STX19 interference impairs phagosomal maturation, while STX19 overexpression enhances it. WASH is thus a central mediator of phagosomal maturation through STX19-mediated membrane fusion and actin-driven lysosomal dynamics, revealing how dysregulated trafficking contributes to immunodeficiency. How actin regulates late phagosomal maturation and microbial killing in neutrophils remains unclear. The authors here show that WASH drives actin-dependent lysosomal dynamics and STX19 recruitment to phagosomes, enabling lysosome fusion and bacterial killing.

articles.title: Bringing Rapid Reperfusion to More Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
Discontinuing Statins in Older Adults without Cardiovascular Disease
articles.abstract: BackgroundWhether discontinuing statin therapy in older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease affects the time to a first cardiovascular event is not well characterized.MethodsWe conducted an international, open-label, randomized, controlled trial that enrolled adults at least 70 years of age who were taking statins for primary prevention. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either discontinue or continue statin therapy and other lipid-lowering therapies. The primary outcome was a composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal ischemic stroke, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. The primary analysis assessed noninferiority on the basis of the between-group difference in restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years, with a noninferiority margin of -5.2 weeks.ResultsA total of 1880 participants underwent randomization: 938 were assigned to the discontinuation group and 942 to the continuation group. The mean age of the participants was 77.5 years, and 46.9% were women. The between-group difference in the restricted mean event-free survival time at 2 years was -2.0 weeks (95% confidence interval, -3.7 to -0.3; PConclusionsAmong older adults with at least two chronic conditions but no known cardiovascular disease, discontinuation of statin therapy was noninferior to continuation with respect to major cardiovascular events or death from any cause at 2 years. (Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation; STREAM ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05178420.).

articles.title: Early Days, Late Nights
Equity in Maternal–Fetal Medicine — Technological Advances and a Potential Path Forward
Hyperaldosteronism Remission after Extended Aldosterone Synthase Inhibition
Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke
articles.abstract: BackgroundWhether intensive blood-pressure control reduces cardiovascular risk after cerebrovascular events remains uncertain.MethodsIn this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, we assigned participants with elevated blood pressure and previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack to receive intensive treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or to receive standard treatment targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure.ResultsA total of 4368 participants were enrolled, with 2172 assigned to intensive treatment and 2196 to standard treatment. The mean (±SD) age of the participants was 63.9±11.2 years, and 2093 (47.9%) were women. During the follow-up period, excluding the first 3 months, the mean systolic blood pressure was 122.0±11.5 mm Hg (median, 119.6 mm Hg) in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2±9.7 mm Hg (median, 135.0 mm Hg) in the standard-treatment group, with a between-group mean difference of 13.1 mm Hg (95% confidence interval [CI], 12.5 to 13.8). Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, a primary-outcome event occurred in 236 participants (10.9%; 3.25 events per 100 person-years) with intensive treatment and in 297 (13.5%; 4.11 events per 100 person-years) with standard treatment (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P = 0.007). The composite renal outcome (sustained reduction of ≥50% in the estimated glomerular filtration rate or progression to end-stage renal disease) was more common with intensive treatment. The overall incidence of serious adverse events was similar in the two groups.ConclusionsAmong participants with previous ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg resulted in a lower incidence of major cardiovascular events than targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-STROKE ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04036409.).

articles.title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
articles.abstract: BackgroundUncertainty persists regarding the effects of intensive blood-pressure lowering in patients with type 2 diabetes.MethodsIn this multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted in Brazil, patients with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and high cardiovascular risk received intensive therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg or standard therapy targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary end point was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure.ResultsOf the 9476 ethnically diverse patients who were enrolled, 4745 were assigned to receive intensive therapy and 4731 to receive standard therapy. The mean (±SD) age was 64.7±8.2 years, and 5871 of the patients (62.0%) were women. The mean systolic blood pressure during follow-up (with exclusion of the first 3 months) was 121.8±10.8 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and 135.4±8.2 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. During a median follow-up of 4.0 years (interquartile range, 3.9 to 4.0), a primary-outcome event occurred in 286 patients (6.0%; 1.65 events per 100 person-years) in the intensive-therapy group and in 315 patients (6.7%; 1.83 events per 100 person-years) in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; 95% confidence interval, 0.77 to 1.06; P = 0.20). Serious adverse events occurred in 706 patients (14.9%) with intensive therapy and in 693 patients (14.6%) with standard therapy.ConclusionsAmong patients with type 2 diabetes, targeting a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg, as compared with less than 140 mm Hg, did not reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events. (Funded by Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and the Brazilian Ministry of Health; OPTIMAL-DIABETES ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04040634.).

articles.title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 is hypothesized to be a therapeutic target for patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Whether neutralizing interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody, reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events remains unknown.MethodsWe conducted a multinational, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving adults with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation (defined by a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein [CRP] level of ≥2 mg per liter). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ziltivekimab (15 mg once monthly) or placebo. The primary efficacy end point was a 3-point major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE). This composite end point included death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke.ResultsA total of 6376 patients were included in the full analysis population: 3184 were assigned to receive ziltivekimab and 3192 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 69.4 years, and 27.5% were women. At 24 months, the between-group difference in the median percent change in the levels of inflammatory biomarkers among patients receiving ziltivekimab as compared with those receiving placebo was -76 percentage points for free interleukin-6 and -64 percentage points for high-sensitivity CRP. During a median follow-up of 33 months, a primary end-point event occurred in 561 patients (17.6%) in the ziltivekimab group and in 565 patients (17.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 1.11; P = 0.84). Serious adverse events occurred in 54.6% of the patients in the ziltivekimab group and in 54.8% of those in the placebo group; serious infections occurred in 20.4% and 17.9%, respectively.ConclusionsAmong patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and cardiovascular inflammation, a strategy of lowering interleukin-6 levels with ziltivekimab did not result in a lower risk of cardiovascular events than placebo. (Funded by Novo Nordisk; ZEUS ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05021835.).

articles.title: Lung Hernia with a Chest-Wall Hematoma
Mass Surveillance with Artificial Intelligence — A New Determinant of Health?
Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
articles.abstract: BackgroundPelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). However, the effect of pelacarsen on cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain.MethodsWe conducted an international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg per deciliter. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen (80 mg) administered monthly or matching placebo. The primary end point was a major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization.ResultsA total of 8350 patients underwent randomization, with 8322 included in the efficacy analysis; 4157 patients were assigned to receive pelacarsen, and 4165 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 59.7 years, and 27.0% were women. The median lipoprotein(a) level at baseline was 236 nmol per liter. At 12 months, the lipoprotein(a) level was 64.4 nmol per liter in the pelacarsen group and 233.4 nmol per liter in the placebo group. The median follow-up was 4.7 years. A primary end-point event occurred in 511 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 503 (12.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90 to 1.15, P = 0.76). Among patients with a baseline lipoprotein(a) level of at least 90 mg per deciliter, a primary end-point event occurred in 402 of 3266 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 403 of 3274 (12.3%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15; P = 0.99). Serious adverse events occurred in 1553 of 4166 patients (37.3%) who received pelacarsen and in 1709 of 4154 (41.1%) who received placebo.ConclusionsPelacarsen did not result in a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo at a median follow-up of 4.7 years. (Funded by Novartis; Lp[a]HORIZON ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04023552.)See also in NEJM Evidence: Extended Analyses of Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).

articles.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
articles.abstract: BackgroundIn patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with the use of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation can be performed to establish reperfusion. Data comparing prehospital ECPR with conventional care regarding survival until hospital discharge among patients who are 50 years of age or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest are limited.MethodsIn a nationwide, nonrandomized study conducted in the Netherlands, we evaluated the outcomes in young adults who were attended by Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) that were equipped to deliver prehospital ECPR (intervention group) as compared with those attended by HEMS without ECPR capability (conventional group). The primary outcome was survival until hospital discharge.ResultsA total of 144 patients were included in the intervention group, and 87 were included in the conventional group. In the intervention group, 57 of 144 patients (40%) survived until hospital discharge, as compared with 17 of 87 patients (20%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 2.72; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.59 to 4.66; P = 0.002). At 6 months, a favorable neurologic outcome was reported in 51 of 141 patients (36%) in the intervention group and in 11 of 85 patients (13%) in the conventional group (odds ratio, 4.22; 95% CI, 2.82 to 6.32). There were 32 adverse events in the intervention group and 11 in the conventional group.ConclusionsAmong patients who were 50 years of age or younger with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, incorporating ECPR into HEMS was associated with improved survival until hospital discharge, as compared with conventional care. (Funded by the Dutch Ministry of Health; OnScene ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04620070.).

articles.title: [Articles] Cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI): a randomised, double-blind trial
articles.abstract: To our knowledge, this is the first randomised trial to compare P2Y12 inhibitor strategies specifically in patients with AMI-CS. Cangrelor achieved effective platelet inhibition more frequently than crushed ticagrelor at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Non-inferiority of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor was not demonstrated for the primary 30-day clinical endpoint. These trial findings can inform future trials of P2Y12 inhibition strategies in patients with AMI-CS.

articles.title: The Five Phases of cancer cells
articles.abstract: Beyond identifying individual malignant hallmarks, the central challenge in cancer biology is to uncover the fundamental organizing principles that underlie the interactive nature of cancer cell behavior. Here, we transform the ancient Wuxing theory into a mechanistically grounded, hypothesis-generating biological framework that conceptualizes cancer cell biology around five mutually interacting processes: Pliability, Hybridity, Aggressivity, Sociability, and Evolutivity (PHASE). By engaging in the circuit of mutual promotion and restriction, these phases form an integrated regulatory system that provides a rationale for organizing diverse malignant properties. Within this framework, cancer traits emerge as context-dependent manifestations of the proposed core interactions. Collectively, PHASE offers a complementary perspective for understanding disease progression that could advance interaction-guided therapeutic strategies to target human cancers.

articles.title: A Witness for Quantum Correlations Using Nonlinear Spectroscopy
articles.abstract: The ability to detect and quantify entanglement in molecular systems is essential for understanding their quantum correlations and to evaluating molecules as platforms for quantum technologies. Here we show how signals from existing spectroscopic techniques can provide sufficient information to witness entanglement. The main ingredient is a spectroscopic map from admissible quantum states to a finite-dimensional space of signal coefficients, which are expectation values of state-independent effective observables. The molecular response model and measurement protocol determine the effective observables for a fixed system bipartition, and the spectroscopic map defines sets of joint expectation values compatible with all admissible quantum states and their separable subset. We illustrate the construction of the effective observables and their expectation value sets using rotational invariants and the spectral structure of optical signals. Fluorescence dynamics and photon coincidences provide a complementary example. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for entanglement certification with established spectroscopic techniques.

articles.title: Can AI Agents Reliably Optimize Computational Chemistry Codes?
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches have opened new possibilities in computational and theoretical chemistry. AI agents can now execute computational workflows autonomously, and their use in scientific software development represents another promising direction. Herein, we present a general strategy for the controlled optimization of scientific software using a dual-agent harness. By using separate worker and controller agents for optimization and evaluation, respectively, we find that this approach can reduce computational costs while preserving numerical accuracy for the computational chemistry methods examined. We apply this strategy to TIP4P water simulations in LAMMPS, as well as to Coulomb and exchange matrix construction and linear-response time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations in PySCF. Among these applications, the largest speedups are obtained for TDDFT. We then extend this strategy from optimizing established packages to developing efficient parallel CPU- and GPU-accelerated implementations of an initially serial molecular dynamics code, resulting in speedups of two to three orders of magnitude. Finally, we apply the protocol to open-ended algorithm development by constructing an adaptive self-consistent field approach that coordinates the use of multiple solvers. We find that the resulting approach can converge some challenging systems and occasionally reach lower-energy solutions than those obtained with the standalone solvers tested. These applications demonstrate that a strategy developed for improving code efficiency may also support the systematic development of computational methods. Overall, our benchmark study provides an example of AI-assisted advances in computational chemistry.

articles.title: Coupled plasmonic Fabry-Perot resonances modulating electromagnetic enhancement at a silver nanowire-nanoparticle junction proved by surface-enhanced fluorescence spectroscopy
articles.abstract: We investigated the surface-enhanced fluorescence (SEF), which is the broad background spectrum underlying the surface-enhanced resonant Raman scattering of dye molecules, emitted from junctions between silver nanoparticles (NPs) and nanowires (NWs). We found that the electromagnetic enhancement factors (FR) derived from the SEF exhibited spectral modulation, such as complicated oscillatory structures. This property became clearer when the emission polarization was perpendicular to the long axis of the NWs. The FR spectra of the long and short NWs exhibit fine and broad oscillatory structures, respectively, when the NPs are positioned near the NW centers. When the NPs were near the NW ends, a combination of fine and broad structures was observed. Numerical calculations of the position-dependent FR spectra successfully reproduced these properties, indicating that the spectral properties originated from the interaction between two plasmonic Fabry-Perot (FP) resonators within the NW, separated by a NP. Based on this result, an analytical model of coupled FP resonators was developed to evaluate these spectral features using experimentally measured NW lengths and NP positions while varying the inter-resonator coupling efficiency. This analysis revealed that the interference and superposition of the two FP resonances resulted in these complex spectra, the energy of which was radiated by the localized plasmons of the NPs.

articles.title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
articles.abstract: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.

articles.title: Molecular Photoionization Spectra from Signed Dyson Orbitals and Anharmonic Nuclear Motion
articles.abstract: Molecular photoelectron bands couple changes in nuclear structure to the energy-dependent scattering of the departing electron. Band intensities require both nuclear transition moments and electronic continuum amplitudes. We present SPARKS (Scattering and Photoionization: Amplitudes, Response Kernels and Spectra), a molecular photoionization approach that connects signed Dyson orbitals to complex molecular dipole amplitudes and harmonic or anharmonic nuclear transition moments. Compact B-spline and finite-element discrete-variable representations support spectral and sparse outgoing-boundary solvers. Independent molecular checks reproduce a reference H$_2^+$ spectrum and CO continuum amplitudes, while analytic hydrogen photoionization tests establish the continuum normalization. For H$_2$O/H$_2$O$^+$, electronic derivatives activate a Franck--Condon-dark fundamental and enter the same nuclear operator used in harmonic, perturbative and internal-coordinate variational calculations. Furan extends the nuclear treatment to all 21 vibrational coordinates in a selected configuration-interaction window, including low-lying out-of-plane states. Four epichlorohydrin ionization channels show how orbital mixing reshapes cross sections and angular distributions at similar Dyson norms. Energy conservation is imposed separately for every vibronic transition at fixed photon energy. The resulting spectra retain vibrational assignments and electronic interference, connecting weak-band activation, anharmonic spacings and photoelectron angular distributions within one physical description.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal Energy Consistency Enables Reliable Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics from Diffusion Models
articles.abstract: Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD) extends molecular simulations to length and time scales inaccessible to atomistic models, but building thermodynamically faithful CG potentials remains a longstanding challenge. Energy-based diffusion models (EBDMs) provide a promising route for learning CG potentials through their zero-time energy. However, CGMD driven by diffusion-learned potentials can produce equilibrium ensembles that deviate substantially from the target distribution. We show that the zero-time distribution error is bounded by the sum of the spatial score error and temporal energy-derivative error, whereas conventional diffusion objectives directly supervise only the spatial component. Based on this finding, we introduce Spatiotemporal Energy Consistency (STEC) supervision, which complements spatial score matching by explicitly constraining temporal energy derivatives. We derive an exact and tractable objective for this temporal component, avoiding the substantial computational overhead associated with previous regularization schemes. Across peptide and fast-folding protein systems, STEC-trained EBDMs accurately reproduce equilibrium distributions with free-energy errors within chemical accuracy, while supporting stable long-time simulations that recover key metastable transition patterns. On held-out octapeptides, STEC reduces free-energy errors by more than 5-fold relative to the strongest competing baseline, while achieving a median production-cost reduction of approximately 1,700-fold relative to atomistic molecular dynamics under a defined structural-coverage benchmark. These results establish STEC as a scalable framework for learning thermodynamically reliable CG force fields for increasingly complex biomolecular systems.

articles.title: Symmetry and Redundancy in Cremer-Pople Phases for Ring Puckering
articles.abstract: Cremer-Pople (CP) coordinates provide an exact description of ring puckering, yet direct sampling of their phases generates many symmetry-equivalent representations of the same puckering pattern. We develop a general analytical framework that identifies these equivalences before Cartesian reconstruction and geometry optimization. For homogeneous rings of arbitrary size, explicit transformations of the CP phases and the signed special coordinate of even-membered rings generate the complete symmetry orbit of the ordered elevation pattern. We classify the redundancies into four types and derive a factorized orbit-size formula linking CP multiplicity to puckering symmetry. These results yield exact single-phase fundamental intervals and sequentially reduced multiphase covering domains, including the restriction to a positive special coordinate. The framework is extended to rings containing one heteroatom or two identical heteroatoms, with reductions determined by the operations that preserve their placement. We also introduce a semidiscrete conformational nomenclature that combines symbolic amplitude distributions with explicit active phases. In an application to cyclohexadecane, symmetry reduction alone decreases the number of sampled CP points by approximately a factor of thirty. Combined with selective phase-grid coarsening for three ordinary modes, the reduction approaches two orders of magnitude. These developments provide a systematic basis for generating, classifying, and efficiently sampling ring puckering patterns in CP space.

articles.title: Toward universal excited-state machine-learned potentials: a local excitation Hamiltonian for size consistency and transferability
articles.abstract: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials could make excited-state simulations across chemical space routine, but excitation energies, unlike ground-state energies, are not sums of atomic contributions. The excited states of noninteracting molecules are the union of their states, which pooled multistate readouts reproduce at best for the lowest state. We introduce LEH-MACE, whose excitation energies are the eigenvalues of a local excitation Hamiltonian assembled from atom-centred blocks, so this union holds exactly. We generated TD-DFT energies and forces for about 300,000 equilibrium, thermal, and excited-state geometries of over 100,000 molecules. LEH-MACE's advantage over direct readouts grew with the distance from the training data and was largest above $S_1$, with about half their $S_2$ and $S_3$ errors for long conjugated oligomers. For molecule pairs, only LEH-MACE kept its single-molecule accuracy, while a softmin readout remained superior for $S_1$ dynamics of larger chromophores. Exact size consistency is thus one step toward such potentials.

articles.title: Universal Approximation by Equivariant Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks with a Bilinear Readout
articles.abstract: We prove universal approximation for the bilinear-readout equivariant message-passing network (BREMP), a reference architecture for equivariant graph neural network interatomic potentials. Its layers combine equivariant convolutions with affine maps, and its readout forms invariants from products of the equivariant features. We construct a one-layer feature that determines the local environment up to permutations of atoms of the same type. The construction uses spherical harmonic filters of degree no larger than the largest number of neighbors at a common distance from the center. Iterating the construction recovers the environment reachable in as many hops as there are layers, using the same bound on filter degrees at the layer cutoff. The readout approximates every continuous invariant function of the features uniformly on compact sets. Together these give universal approximation of atomic energies at a prescribed physical range using a shorter layer cutoff. We assume that, throughout the admissible class, message passing reaches all neighbors in each physical environment within a common number of layers. Finally, DPA4, an interatomic potential architecture in production use, inherits this result by approximating the BREMP layers constructed in the proof and realizing the bilinear readout.

articles.title: Asymmetric Dual-Atom Ruthenium–Tungsten on CeO2 Enabled Highly Active and Selective NH3 Oxidation
articles.abstract: Ru single-atom catalysts are promising for NH3 oxidation but still suffer from poor activity and N2 selectivity, mainly owing to the poisoning of the isolated Ru active sites by the over-strong NH3 adsorption. Herein, we fabricated an asymmetric Ru-W atomic pair anchored on CeO2 (Ru1–W1/Ce) exhibiting considerable low-temperature activity (∼90% at 200 °C), high N2 selectivity (∼85% at 350 °C), and notable stability (∼500 h at 200 °C), surpassing most of the previously reported catalysts for NH3 oxidation. Systematic experimental and theoretical investigations demonstrated that a strong d-f orbital interaction between Ru and W atoms was revealed, inducing the smooth electron transfer from W to Ru atoms. The electron-rich Ru single atom not only weakened NH3 adsorption strength to alleviate NH3 poisoning but also reduced the energy barrier of the rate-determining step of NH3 activation. Besides, isolated W atoms coordinated with active Ru species, leading to a decrease in Ru–O–Ce coordination number. This could suppress the activation of O2 and thereby the deep oxidation of NH3. Accordingly, the reaction mechanism over this asymmetric Ru–W catalyst changed from the initial i-SCR to an imide-like pathway, accounting for its considerable catalytic performance. This work provided a paradigm for advanced Ru-based catalysts enabling both high activity and high N2 selectivity in NH3 oxidation.

articles.title: From Promiscuity to Specificity: Machine Learning-Driven Multidimensional Evolution of Tropinone Reductase for Challenging Substrates
articles.abstract: A fundamental challenge in harnessing substrate promiscuity for industrial biocatalysis lies in reconciling broad substrate acceptance with high catalytic specificity. Although promiscuous enzymes provide attractive starting points for accessing non-natural transformations, their native active-site architectures and conformational dynamics often lack the precision required for efficient and selective conversion of desired unnatural substrates. Thus, systematically decoding and reprogramming the interplay between promiscuity and specificity remains a key obstacle toward versatile biocatalysts. Here, we address this challenge by integrating virtual screening, machine learning, and molecular dynamics simulations into a unified engineering framework. A tropinone reductase from Cochlearia officinalis (CoTR) was identified as a broadly promiscuous scaffold. By converting complex enzyme–substrate interaction dynamics into quantifiable and actionable design principles, we predict and validate key residues that govern substrate promiscuity. Guided by these insights, distinct CoTR variants were engineered for three representative substrates. The optimized variants—CoTR‑8M, CoTR‑5M‑1, and CoTR‑5M‑2—exhibited 7.0‑ to 16.3‑fold higher catalytic efficiencies than wild-type CoTR toward their respective target substrates and supported substrate loadings of up to 50 or 100 g L–1 while maintaining >99% ee. This work not only delivers scalable routes to three industrially valuable chiral alcohols but also provides mechanistic insights into the synergistic modulation of promiscuity and specificity. This study demonstrates a general strategy for translating intricate molecular-recognition features into rational design principles, thereby facilitating the development of tailored biocatalysts for non-native substrates.

articles.title: Enabling Outdoor Operation of Tin–Lead Perovskite Solar Cells via Lamination-Based Encapsulation
articles.abstract: Tin–lead (Sn–Pb) perovskites are essential narrow-bandgap absorbers for two-terminal perovskite–perovskite tandem solar cells, yet their extreme air sensitivity has confined stability studies indoors, leaving real-world durability unexplored. Here, we substantially lower this barrier using industrially relevant, lamination-based encapsulation that enables, to our knowledge, the first outdoor demonstration of Sn–Pb devices. Combining polyisobutylene edge sealing with polyolefin elastomer encapsulation, we demonstrate that the lamination process is highly compatible with Sn–Pb devices, causing negligible performance loss while preserving optoelectronic quality during short-term air exposure. Under package-oriented accelerated aging, epoxy-based encapsulation fails rapidly, whereas the lamination-based package remains intact. Outdoors under tandem-relevant filtered illumination, lamination-encapsulated devices retain ∼80% of initial efficiency after 12 days, while epoxy-encapsulated devices lose all output within 6 days. By adapting manufacturable module packaging to Sn–Pb devices, this work enables their realistic field evaluation, marks a critical step toward deployable all-perovskite tandems, and strengthens confidence in their commercial viability.

articles.title: Dopant Dependent Grain Growth and Mechanical Property Heterogeneity in Al-, Cr- and Al/Cr-doped UO2 Nuclear Fuels

How to Build an Ecosystem: Early Animals of the Ediacaran and the Emergence of the Tangled Bank
articles.journal: Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics
articles.abstract: The early animal communities of the Ediacaran (∼580–539 Mya) provide novel insights into how the modern biosphere operates by recording the initial ecological framework from which ecological interactions first built up. These Ediacaran communities do not have direct counterparts because they are soft-bodied, largely heterotrophic, and predator free. However, the exceptional preservation of immobile, benthic Ediacaran animals enables the resolution of their community dynamics to similar levels to those of extant benthic systems. While many of the key processes shaping the modern benthos were present in early benthic communities, the diversity of ecological interactions within communities, and the variability of these interactions through time and space, was notably simpler than that found today. In the Ediacaran, ecosystem dynamics and complexity started with reproduction and dispersal, with adaptations and responses to the environment a secondary effect, followed by direct biotic interactions. As these biotic interactions became dominant, coevolution established a tangled bank of complexity.

articles.title: Revisiting the Role of Biological Nitrogen Fixation in Forest Recovery Under Global Environmental Change
articles.journal: Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics
articles.abstract: Classical ecosystem theory depicts biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) as a mechanism that replenishes disturbance-driven nitrogen (N) losses, thereby alleviating N limitation and facilitating ecosystem recovery. These assumptions persist in present-day theories, models, and applications. However, disturbance regimes and environmental conditions have changed dramatically since the formation of the original BNF theories, motivating a new evaluation of the role of BNF. Focusing on forests, we find evidence that disturbance effects on BNF range from net positive to net negative and that current BNF fluxes have a limited capacity to replenish N losses if disturbances become more severe and frequent, or if they create conditions that suppress or constrain BNF. The subsequent effects of BNF on ecosystem recovery also vary. N-fixing trees and shrubs can have positive to negative effects on the recovery of carbon stocks, and under novel disturbance regimes they may alter, and even impede, forest succession. We present an updated view of BNF–recovery relationships in forest ecosystems undergoing global environmental change.

articles.title: The Pollen-Reward Strategy: The Paradoxical Realities of Trading Gametes for Sex
articles.journal: Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics
articles.abstract: Pollen-rewarding plants face a fundamental tension: Pollen serves simultaneously as the male gametophyte and pollinator reward. Despite this apparent paradox, pollen is the second most common floral reward and the sole reward for an estimated 20,000 angiosperm species. We review the ecology and evolution of the pollen-reward strategy, synthesizing literature encompassing pollen chemistry, floral morphology, and sex allocation. We find that this reward strategy is unevenly distributed among plant families, that the resource costs of pollen rewards remain poorly characterized, and that this reward strategy may influence plant sexual-system evolution. We offer hypotheses regarding the evolution and maintenance of the pollen-reward strategy and examine the ecological and evolutionary consequences associated with its expression. We suggest that floral rewards are not isolated traits, but key elements of plant reproductive strategies, and that this perspective allows comparison among strategies and can advance our understanding of the evolutionary ecology of plant reproduction.

articles.abstract: Methane decomposition is a promising route for CO x -free hydrogen production, but the rapid deactivation of Ni-based catalysts remains a major challenge. This study investigates the effects of SiO 2 support crystallinity...

articles.title: Phase-separated SOX5 drives human cranial neural crest fate commitment
articles.abstract: How transcription factors drive human cranial neural crest fate is poorly understood. Huang et al. combine an hPSC model with a TFome CRISPR screen to identify SOX5 as a fate switch. SOX5 forms phase-separated condensates that organize active chromatin through KU80 to promote neural crest commitment.

articles.title: A genome-wide CRISPR screening identifies targets that drive tolerogenic dendritic cells
articles.abstract: Tolerogenic dendritic cells (TolDCs) contribute to immune tolerance and have demonstrated therapeutic potential in early clinical studies of autoimmune diseases. However, the key molecular pathways driving their differentiation and tolerogenic phenotype remain elusive. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the functional status of TolDCs in response to different tolerizing agents and identified CD86 as a consistent and robust marker downregulated in tolerogenic state. CD86 is functionally required for TolDC-mediated suppression of T cell proliferation and cytokine secretion, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of tolerogenic potential. Leveraging CD86 expression as a readout, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen and characterized genes associated with TolDC phenotypes. This approach positions UBE2L6 as a regulator of CD86 expression through modulation of an ISG15-USP18-associated pathway, implicating its involvement in tolerogenic functions. These findings describe therapeutically targetable pathways to promote immune tolerance.

articles.title: A pangene family atlas of cereals uncovers hidden intraspecific and interspecific diversity
articles.abstract: Pangenomes are reshaping gene-family analysis by shifting from single-genome views to pangene families, yet many studies still rely on orthogroups as proxies, overlooking crucial allele- and locus-level diversity. Here, we present a pangene-based and domain-defined framework to construct and analyze nearly 500 pangene families across four major cereals. Compared with single-genome analyses, pangenome-level family membership increases by 59-264%, and many families show pangene accumulation curves that remain far from saturation, indicating that substantial allelic diversity is still uncharacterized even when 320 rice genomes are included. We further quantify family behavior along three complementary dimensions and reveal extensive remodeling of membership and copy-number allocation that is largely invisible when only total family size is considered. Together, this framework and its associated resource provide a foundation for deeper use of plant pangenomes, offering new insight into how evolutionary constraints and diversification shape pangene families.

articles.title: Cell-type specific and nanoscale control of hippocampal presynaptic homeostatic plasticity
articles.abstract: The lifelong continuity of neuronal function rests upon the perdurance of neurons, synapses and neural circuits that are sustained, in part, by homeostatic signaling. Currently, the implementation of homeostatic signaling within complex brain circuitry remains poorly defined. Given the tremendous diversity of cell and synapse types, is homeostatic plasticity deployed in a cell-type specific manner and, if so, what are the rules? Here, we report that presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is achieved in a target neuron-specific manner. PHP is robust at synapses that contact parvalbumin-positive (PV+) and absent at somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons. Furthermore, PHP can be differentially induced at adjacent synapses that are present within single axonal boutons, separated by hundreds of nanometers. These highly localized effects are eliminated in the absence of Sema3A signaling, a homeostatic signaling molecule. Our data suggest a model where PHP is repressed throughout axons that contact SST+ interneurons and locally de-repressed with nanoscale precision.

articles.title: Chronotherapy leveraging dietary context overcomes circadian rhythm influence on cancer cell response to PPAR antagonists
articles.abstract: Circadian physiology coordinates systemic and cellular metabolism through a light-entrained central clock and metabolically synchronized peripheral clocks. Whether feeding-fasting cycles or tumor-intrinsic clocks primarily set tumor metabolic state is unclear. Here, we profiled colorectal cancer (CRC) responses to PPAR antagonists across 2D and 3D CRC models and tumor-bearing mice. In standard high-glucose, low-fat medium, Bmal1 oscillations and daily variation in PPAR antagonist sensitivity were apparent in CRC cells. By contrast, nutrient-defined media that recapitulate feeding and nighttime fasting abolished time-dependent variability and unified drug responses across models. Still, the fed state selectively sensitized spheroids and patient-derived organoids to PPAR-γ antagonism. In mice, dosing PPAR-γ antagonist in the fed state prolonged survival and reduced hepatotoxicity. The use of Bmal-1-silenced CRC cells validated that feeding-fasting rhythms, not tumor-intrinsic clocks, govern CRC sensitivity to PPAR antagonists. Our study also supports the predictive capacity of nutrient-alternating 3D tumor models, enabling metabolism-targeted anticancer treatment evaluation.

articles.title: Self-amplifying RNA vaccines encoding chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinins confer immunity against phylogenetically diverse influenza A viruses
articles.abstract: Seasonal influenza vaccines require annual reformulation due to antigenic drift and provide suboptimal protection. Here, we evaluate self-amplifying mRNA (samRNA) vaccines encoding chimeric (cHA) and mosaic (mHA) hemagglutinins representing influenza A virus HA phylogenetic groups 1 and 2. Following prime-boost immunization, group 1 cHA vaccines (cH8/1-cH5/1) elicit broad cross-reactive antibodies and confer complete protection against diverse H1N1 strains covering decades of antigenic drift. Group 2 vaccines (cH4/3-cH15/3 and mH10/3-mH14/3) provide comparable breadth against multiple H3N2 strains and heterosubtypic H7N9 challenge, with cHA samRNA showing superior cross-group protection. Protection is associated with Fc-mediated effector functions and CD4+ T cell responses, with minimal hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing titers. Passive serum transfer confirms antibody-mediated protection independent of cellular immunity. Protective immunity is maintained at doses as low as 0.4 μg, demonstrating the dose-sparing advantage of the samRNA platform. These results support samRNA-delivered cHA and mHA antigens as promising candidates for broadly protective influenza vaccines.

articles.title: Succinate promotes multiple myeloma cell proliferation through TCA cycle oxidation
articles.abstract: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy that develops within the bone marrow. The bone marrow metabolome is altered in myeloma, with implications for malignant cell growth. Here, the impact of elevated bone marrow levels of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle metabolite, succinate, was interrogated. Succinate was found to promote proliferation of several myeloma cell lines. This was linked to its uptake and oxidation in the TCA cycle, as indicated by increased ATP-coupled mitochondrial respiration and incorporation of succinate-derived carbons into downstream TCA cycle intermediates, which also occurs in primary myeloma cells. Succinate-driven proliferation was dependent upon mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and abrogated by ATP synthase inhibition. Furthermore, interrogation of large-scale transcriptomic data identified that elevated expression of a mitochondrial succinate transporter associates with accelerated disease progression in myeloma, indicating this mechanism may promote plasma cell growth in vivo and highlighting a target for therapeutic intervention.

articles.title: TNF- and IL-1-induced inflammation are enhanced through cooperative interactions between Nrf2 and NF-κB
articles.abstract: Reactive oxygen species are typically elevated at inflammatory sites due to influx of large numbers of neutrophils and other myeloid cells that produce oxygen free radicals as microbicidal agents. However, although oxidative stress is frequently implicated as an initiator or amplifier of inflammation, particularly in the context of cancer, the key mediators of reactive oxygen-driven inflammation require clarification. Here we show that the redox-responsive transcription factor, Nrf2, can act as an enhancer of TNF- and IL-1-initiated inflammation. Silencing or deletion of the Nrf2 antagonist, Keap1, led to robustly enhanced TNF- or IL-1-driven inflammatory cytokine production. Conversely, suppression of Nrf2 activation blunted inflammation in the same contexts. Mechanistically, Nrf2 enhanced inflammation through cooperative interactions with p65 RelA at NFκB-regulated promoters. These observations reveal a direct link between the Keap1/Nrf2 reactive oxygen-sensing pathway and TNF- or IL-1-initiated inflammation and suggest that Nrf2 can act as a rheostat for NFκB-dependent inflammatory outputs.

articles.title: Terminus est: Repurposing public RNA-seq data to map 3′ transcript termini in bacteria
articles.abstract: Bar and colleagues1 repurpose publicly available RNA sequencing data to identify 3' transcript termini across a diverse collection of bacteria. This presents a major resource for investigating transcript termination and processing, with initial investigations into the diversity and conservation of termini.

articles.title: Effects of dietary carbohydrate-to-fat ratio on the gut microbiome following weight loss
articles.abstract: Kohli et al. conduct an ancillary gut microbiome-focused study within a controlled feeding trial, where participants undergo calorie restriction and weight loss, followed by randomization to diets varying in carbohydrate-to-fat ratio. While weight loss results in major changes in the microbiome, the carbohydrate-to-fat ratio is not associated with microbiome differences.

articles.title: Propionate, a short-chain fatty acid, is associated with disease activity in pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis
articles.abstract: In young individuals shortly after multiple sclerosis onset, Schoeps et al. show that higher plasma and stool propionate levels are consistently associated with lower clinical and imaging disease activity. These findings suggest that a gut microbiome-derived short-chain fatty acid modulates early inflammatory activity and supports clinical testing of targeted supplementation.

articles.title: Senescent T cells within the tumor microenvironment are a potent driver for tumor growth, stemness, and chemotherapy resistance
articles.abstract: Zhang et al. identify that senescent T (Tsen) cells accumulate within tumors and drive tumor growth, metastasis, stemness, and chemotherapy resistance. Mechanistically, lipid-enriched Tsen SASPs reprogram tumor lipid metabolism and activate STAT1/STAT3 signaling. Targeting Tsen cells or their metabolic crosstalk with tumor cells suppresses tumor progression and enhances therapeutic efficacy.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal dynamic evolution of the tumor microenvironment during neoadjuvant immunotherapy for bladder cancer
articles.abstract: Hu et al. map phenotypic evolution of the bladder cancer microenvironment during neoadjuvant immunotherapy. Treatment drives divergent tumor cell fates, establishes an immunotherapy-induced tumor-myeloid barrier, promotes terminal T cell exhaustion, and induces a senescent iCAF phenotype. SERPINH1 emerges as a potential therapeutic target for acquired resistance.

articles.title: Unimodal imaging foundation models and vision-language models in MRI: A systematic review of emerging methods and clinical applications
articles.abstract: Tordjman et al. review 35 studies on MRI foundation and vision-language models, highlighting their diverse applications in diagnosis, segmentation, automated reporting, and outcome prediction. The authors identify methodological heterogeneity and a scarcity of paired image-text datasets as the primary barriers to widespread clinical translation.
