A frugal automated contact angle analyser for low-cost surface wettability characterization
articles.abstract: Contact angle measurement is a fundamental technique for evaluating surface wettability in materials science, biomedical engineering and coating technologies. However, the high cost of commercial contact angle analysers limits access to surface characterization, particularly in resource-limited laboratories. This study presents a low-cost automated contact angle analyser developed using frugal engineering principles and open-source hardware. The system integrates Arduino-based control, NEMA 17 stepper-motor actuation, automated microdroplet dispensing, smartphone-based optical imaging and a 3D-printed polylactic acid (PLA) framework. A calibrated 330-step dispensing cycle generated reproducible 5 μl water droplets, with fixed optical alignment minimized operator variability. Wettability measurements were performed on polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and aluminium substrates and analysed using ImageJ. Mean contact angles were 108.5° for PTFE, 73.9° for PVC and 85.8° for aluminium, closely matching published literature values. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) demonstrated significant differences between substrates (p < 0.001), with measurement variability of ±2.3° indicated good repeatability. The total fabrication cost was £114.26, representing approximately 99% cost reduction compared with commercial instruments. The proposed platform demonstrates that automated, reproducible surface wettability characterization can be achieved using low-cost, open-source instrumentation, providing an accessible solution for research, education and engineering laboratories while broadening access to advanced materials characterization.

articles.title: Beyond sperm competition: perspectives on sperm economy from external fertilizing fishes
articles.abstract: Research on sperm economy has traditionally focused on sperm competition as a major selective pressure shaping sperm production and allocation. In this review, we broaden this perspective by considering how other reproductive and ecological pressures influence the management of a costly and finite sperm supply. We synthesize evidence showing that in externally fertilizing fishes, high mating frequency, low female fecundity, prolonged spawning, rapid sperm dilution and costly male reproductive investment can favour sperm-economy strategies even when sperm competition is weak or absent. Across fish taxa, these constraints have led to convergent behavioural and physiological adaptations, including fractionated ejaculation, temporal matching of sperm release to egg deposition and manipulation of the fertilization microenvironment, which improve fertilization efficiency while minimizing sperm expenditure. We further highlight a recurring association between these strategies and semi-cystic spermatogenesis, consistent with the possibility that optimization of sperm use extends beyond ejaculate allocation to the regulation of sperm production during spermatogenesis. By integrating evidence from behaviour to reproductive physiology, this review reframes sperm economy as a general resource-allocation problem, with sperm competition representing one of several selective pressures. Externally fertilizing fishes emerge as an exceptional model for understanding the diverse evolutionary routes by which males optimize reproductive investment.

articles.title: Decoding the dead: new combined application of strontium and lead isotope analysis to Romano-British cremations from Colchester (UK)
articles.abstract: This paper presents an innovative application of two distinct isotope systems to paired otic capsule and outer petrous bone samples from cremated remains. This dual analysis approach, applied to 22 human cremation burials from Roman Colchester (UK), demonstrates evidence for origins outside Britain for several individuals, shedding fresh light on an emerging capital city within a new province of the Roman Empire. Results have implications for understanding the population dynamics of large Roman provincial urban centres following the conquest period in the north-western provinces, when cremation is the dominant burial practice. The method also allows a detailed reconstruction of individual mobility at different ages within an individual's life.

articles.title: Design principles for natural SGLT2 modulators from multi-scale computation
articles.abstract: Human sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (hSGLT2) is a membrane-embedded renal transporter and an established therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes. Hyperoside, myricetin, cyanidin-3-O-glucoside and isoliquiritigenin were investigated as a chemically diverse panel of natural scaffolds using a multi-scale computational workflow combining redocking-validated molecular docking, reconstruction of an unresolved transporter segment, molecular dynamics (MD) in an explicit POPC bilayer, molecular mechanics/Poisson–Boltzmann surface area (MM/PBSA) calculations, principal component and free-energy landscape analyses and density functional theory (DFT). The membrane simulations preserved the global hSGLT2 fold while revealing distinct ligand-dependent binding behaviours. Myricetin and cyanidin-3-O-glucoside exhibited limited positional deviations; hyperoside achieved persistent accommodation following an initial adjustment, whereas isoliquiritigenin underwent a marked late rearrangement. Ensemble-based energetic analysis prioritized cyanidin-3-O-glucoside, while hyperoside and myricetin formed an energetically comparable intermediate group and isoliquiritigenin displayed the least favourable profile. Electronic-structure analysis further characterized cyanidin-3-O-glucoside as the most responsive ligand within the DFT subset. Collectively, these findings indicate that glycone-assisted polar anchoring, aromatic complementarity and restricted conformational flexibility promote persistent hSGLT2 recognition. Direct hSGLT2 inhibition and hSGLT1 counter-screening assays remain necessary to establish potency and selectivity.

articles.title: Discovery of potential ALK inhibitors from Glycosmis phytochemicals via integrated machine learning and umbrella sampling approaches
articles.abstract: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is a key therapeutic target for various cancers because of its central role in tumor growth and survival signaling. This study employed an integrated computational workflow combining machine learning (ML), molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, umbrella sampling (US), and toxicity prediction to identify potential ALK inhibitors from 307 phytochemicals of the Glycosmis genus. A previously validated CatBoost regression model predicted binding free energies, leading to the selection of 26 compounds with ΔGML < −11 kcal mol−1. Molecular docking identified six top candidates with favorable binding affinities ranging from −5.856 to −9.667 kcal mol⁻¹, which subsequently underwent 200 ns MD simulations. Structural analyses confirmed the stability of all ALK–ligand complexes, while interaction studies revealed extensive hydrophobic contacts and conserved hydrogen bonds involving key ALK residues. US calculations estimated binding free energies from −8.354 to −13.272 kcal mol−1, with compound 54 exhibiting the strongest affinity (ΔGUS = −13.272 kcal mol−1). Several alkaloids, including acrifoline, heptazoline, and atalaphyllidine, also demonstrated promisingbinding properties and reported anticancer activities. Toxicity prediction indicated acceptable safety profiles, highlighting Glycosmis-derived phytochemicals as promising potential ALK inhibitor candidates and supporting the utility of ML-guided virtual screening combined with advanced molecular simulations for natural product-based anticancer drug discovery. Nevertheless, biochemical and cellular experiments are required to confirm their ALK inhibitory activity, selectivity, and therapeutic potential.

articles.title: Drivers of zoonotic spillover at human–domestic animal–wildlife interfaces: a multi-species model incorporating wildlife chronic stress
articles.abstract: Zoonotic disease emergence at the wildlife–domestic animal–human interface results from a complex interplay of ecological, physiological and anthropogenic factors. Here, we have developed a multi-environment, multi-host compartmental model to identify key drivers of spillover risk across urban, rural and natural environments. The framework incorporates heterogeneous host populations, inter-species contacts and host movement, and includes wildlife chronic stress as one factor influencing susceptibility, transmissibility and recovery. Sensitivity analyses show that domestic animal populations at agricultural interfaces strongly amplify spillover risk through their recovery dynamics and per-contact transmission probabilities, while within-wildlife transmission across environments also shapes system dynamics. Chronic stress effects can further increase spillover risk, and the model indicates that reducing wildlife stress alongside improving domestic animal health and management can markedly lower the likelihood of cross-species transmission. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining ecological conditions that reduce chronic physiological stress in wildlife populations and integrating physiological and ecological data into epidemiological modelling. Such models can inform both bottom-up interventions targeting domestic animals and top-down strategies that sustain resilient wildlife communities and, thereby, mitigate zoonotic spillover.

articles.title: First direct measurement of food transit time through the gastrointestinal tracts of plant-eating primates using isotopic tagging
articles.abstract: The time it takes for food to transit animal gastrointestinal tracts is essential information to fields from organismal evolution to ecosystem ecology. Nevertheless, current estimation methods do not measure food directly, are impractical for many species and often require unnatural conditions to administer. We overcome these limitations by adopting techniques from organic geochemistry. We trace isotopically tagged greens in lemurs, from ingestion to excretion, through isotopic analysis of higher plant biomarkers recovered in faeces. For frugivorous ruffed lemurs (Varecia rubra), omnivorous ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta) and frugo-folivorous sifakas (Propithecus coquereli), respectively, the biomarkers first appeared at 1.2, 4.3 and 23.4 h after ingestion and peaked at 2.9, 5.7 and 48.4 h after ingestion. These measurements generally match published estimates from pre-existing proxies. However, not all animals cleared the isotopic signal by the end of sample collection, yielding minimum gut retention times of 23.9–29.5 h for ruffed lemurs, 25.5–30.3 h for ring-tailed lemurs and 95.7 h for sifakas. We thus extend gut retention times approximately threefold from pre-existing proxies. Our interdisciplinary approach is applicable across diverse plant eaters, can help refine models of nutrient, seed and pathogen dispersal and be used to probe consequences of lifestyle and medical interventions on organismal nutrition and health.

articles.title: Generalized maximum entropy: when and why you need it
articles.abstract: The classical maximum entropy principle based on Shannon entropy is widely used to construct least-biased probability distributions from partial information. However, the Shore–Johnson axioms that single out the Shannon functional hinge on strong system independence—an assumption often violated in real-world, strongly correlated systems. When that assumption fails, enforcing the Shannon form imposes an independence the data do not support, and can systematically distort the inferred distribution. We provide a self-contained guide to when and why practitioners should abandon the Shannon form in favour of the one-parameter Uffink–Jizba–Korbel (UJK) family of generalized entropies. After reviewing the Shore–Johnson axioms from an applied perspective, we recall the most commonly used entropy functionals and locate them within the UJK family. The need for generalized entropies is illustrated with two applications, one in economics and the other in ecology. A simple mathematical model worked out in detail further shows the power of generalized maximum-entropy approaches in cases where strong system independence does not hold. We conclude with practical guidelines for choosing an entropy measure and reporting results so that analyses remain transparent and reproducible.

articles.title: Influence of soft coral density and depth on benthic communities on Fiji's Rainbow Reef
articles.abstract: Some soft corals have the potential to increase in prevalence on tropical coral reefs as the severity of anthropogenic climate change increases. While soft corals are therefore an increasingly important component of reef ecosystems, little is known about their ecological role on coral reefs and their influence on community dynamics and diversity. We used Bayesian network inference (BNI) to identify the associations among benthic taxa across sites with varying degrees of soft coral dominance on Fiji's Rainbow Reef, and then employed spatial point process analysis (SPPA) to reveal the ecological processes behind these associations. We found that depth was a dominant driver of community dynamics, and that white Nephtheidae soft corals were negatively associated with scleractinian corals and positively associated with algal proliferation—possibly owing to soft corals reducing grazing pressure. Our results show distinctions in reef benthos and ecological dynamics between scleractinian and soft coral-dominated components of the Rainbow Reef. We found that diversity levels were significantly lower on soft coral-dominated quadrats relative to scleractinian-dominated quadrats, potentially highlighting the reduction in benthic diversity when Nephtheidae soft corals dominate reef walls.

articles.title: Large language model developments
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are generative artificial intelligence (AI) models trained with vast amounts of data and context, and excel at processing, understanding and generating human language, using transformer models to learn statistical relationships between tokens. LLMs are a subset of transformer models, and hence are closely related but not interchangeable. Given the ‘explosion’ of LLM research, the challenge is tracking emerging developments and matching LLMs to applications. This paper reviews LLM developments with the aim of understanding the underlying models’ computational strengths and weaknesses, building on previous work focusing on LLM optimization (Sharkey & Treleaven 2025 Optimising large language models: taxonomy and techniques. SSRN Scholarly Paper no. 5278456. Rochester, NY: SSRN). We find that despite their power, LLMs (transformers) face several key challenges. These include: (i) computational complexity and resource requirements—training and deploying large models is extremely costly and slow, and energy consumption is a concern; (ii) understanding long sequences and dependencies—even with enhancements, models can struggle with very long-range dependencies or context lengths beyond their window (e.g. maintaining coherence in a long document), which reflects the more fundamental absence of continual learning; (iii) interpretability and bias—it remains difficult to interpret why a model produces a given output, and models can inadvertently amplify biases present in training data; and (iv) optimization challenges, including fine-tuning for specific tasks without overfitting or losing generality and ensuring efficient inference (latency, the delay before a response is completed) for real-time applications. In summary, this review focuses on architectural, optimization and interpretability developments in LLMs. It does not aim to provide a systematic benchmark comparison, exhaustive implementation details or empirical performance evaluation, which are covered extensively elsewhere. The authors are committed to updating this review aligned to constant changes in the technology; please reach out with any additions.

articles.title: Mast fruiting in a large tropical African legume tree species and the mineral nutrient limitation hypothesis
articles.abstract: The large grove-forming ectomycorrhizal tropical tree Microberlinia bisulcata displays strong mast fruiting on poor soils. Evidence is presented that masting is probably determined primarily by mineral nutrients and secondarily by radiation. To test the nutrient resource limitation hypothesis, phenological recordings were matched with climate variables and modelled using logistic time-series regression. A strong predictor was average daily rainfall in the dry season, low in the current year of masting and high in the year prior. Less strong was the increase in dry season radiation between prior and mast years. Masting events showed no relationship to annual stem increment. Masting intensity was reduced after two caterpillar attacks. Fallen-leaf phosphorus concentration increased in the inter-mast interval, and that for potassium peaked mid-interval. A drier dry season prior to masting may have increased tree carbon, while a wetter one increased nutrient uptake by roots and mycorrhizas. A rooting–fruiting trade-off in carbon is suggested. The long-term stochastic driver appears to be dry season rainfall. Synchrony across masting trees may be enhanced by equilibration of nutrients across the mycorrhizal–root network. A life-history strategy determined by mineral nutrient resource dynamics provides the best explanation and advanced model of the observed pattern of events.

articles.title: Patterns in conflict dynamics in Yemen and Syria
articles.abstract: Conflict fatalities tend to follow heavy-tailed statistical distributions. A 2005 fusion–fission theory predicts that, when armed groups operate through dynamically forming and fragmenting clusters, the number of fatalities per event should be approximated by a power-law distribution with exponent α near 2.5, with deviations reflecting the relative robustness of larger versus smaller fighter clusters. We use Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) event-level fatality data to estimate α in recent Yemen and Syria conflict periods during 2023–2025. These conflict event datasets are small, incomplete and imperfect and only produce very crude approximations to a power law; nonetheless, the best-fit α values occupy the range 2.5<α<3.5 across most periods, which is broadly consistent with predominantly fragmented or weakly consolidated armed-group organization. Temporary reductions in α are broadly consistent with episodes in which larger coordinated clusters become more consequential. More rigorous testing will require improved datasets to become available in the future.

articles.title: People and bats in Fiji: perceptions and interactions
articles.abstract: The management of wild bat populations often presents challenges in balancing the needs of biodiversity conservation and public health risks from zoonotic diseases. In Fiji, the most important recognized zoonotic infection is Leptospira, which was recently detected in wild bat populations. Five out of six species of Fijian bats are considered threatened to critically endangered on the IUCN Red List. This study investigates the perceptions of bats by people in Fiji and aims to identify and quantify the reported frequency and types of interactions between bats and people. In this mixed-methods study, 198 Fijian people were interviewed across the three main islands of Fiji: Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and Taveuni. Bats were generally perceived positively (63%, 125/198), mostly because they are perceived to be ‘clean, healthy and tasty’ meat sources (73%, 134/184). The majority of participants consume and come into contact with bats or with their urine, faeces, blood and saliva. Older adults, men and those who recognize that bats can cause harm are more likely to contact bats in Fiji. Quantifying these interactions and identifying other risk factors for bat exposure is an important step in targeting conservation efforts, community engagement and education, as well as determining at-risk groups for possible zoonotic pathogen exposure.

articles.title: Phenological shifts of low-latitude frogs over 15 years revealed by passive acoustic monitoring
articles.abstract: Phenological responses to climate warming are well-documented, yet limited data come from low latitudes. Because phenological sensitivity may vary with latitude, studies in low-latitude regions are essential to understand global patterns. To fill this gap, we analysed acoustic recordings collected daily over 15 years on Iriomote Island, in Japan's transitional zone between subtropical and tropical biomes. We applied the BirdNET deep learning model to quantify the breeding phenology of seven frog species. Seasonal calling patterns differed among species, with peaks occurring in various seasons while one species called nearly year-round. Among six species analysed for phenological trends, a winter-breeding tree-frog (Zhangixalus owstoni) showed a statistically significant shift in median calling date (3.8 days later per decade), whereas the other species showed no significant shifts of varying magnitude and direction. Sliding time window analysis indicated late-summer temperature—which increased during the study period—best predicted median calling dates in Z. owstoni, suggesting that climate warming delayed the phenology of a winter breeder even where year-round reproduction is possible. The absence of significant phenological advancement in our dataset contrasts with spring advancement commonly reported in temperate regions. These findings reinforce the importance of examining long-term phenological shifts across more sites in low-latitude regions.

articles.title: Quantifying ‘surprise’ in capuchin monkeys ( Sapajus apella )
articles.abstract: Violation-of-expectation (VoE) events offer a fascinating lens into the intersection of cognition and emotion. Research suggests that, like humans, many animals are susceptible to VoE events in many physical domains, susceptibility typically assessed through behaviours such as visual and physical exploration of a stimulus. In humans, such susceptibility has been further documented through emotional surprise, such as delight following positive surprise and frustration following negative surprise. However, evidence in animals remains relatively limited. To address this gap, this study examined behavioural, cognitive and emotional responses of capuchin monkeys (Sapajus apella) to bait-and-switch VoE events of food items. Capuchins were chosen for this study not only for their exploratory and information-seeking behaviours, but also for known emotional responses to VoE events (e.g. frustration following inequity aversion). Contrary to prior research, this study found no evidence for violation susceptibility via behavioural, cognitive or emotional responses. Overall, such findings contribute valuable information to the VoE literature in primates regarding methodology and information salience, as well as underscore the current challenges of investigating emotional surprise in animals. Future research may benefit from establishing stronger expectations (e.g. more salient stimuli), to better investigate and quantify surprise to VoE events in animal species such as capuchin monkeys.

articles.title: Spatial and chemical heterogeneity of insect cuticular hydrocarbon layers: insights from extraction methods and acclimation regimes
articles.abstract: Insect cuticles are covered by a complex mixture of cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) that are essential for desiccation resistance and chemical communication, yet the physical structure of CHC layers remains poorly understood. We extracted CHCs from five insect species (desert locusts, house crickets, American cockroaches and two ant species) using solvents of differing polarity and extraction durations, and from insects reared under different temperature regimes. Extractions with n-hexane were enriched in relatively solid CHCs (n-alkanes and terminally branched monomethylalkanes), while extractions with dichloromethane and dichloromethane–methanol yielded proportionally more fluid compounds (internally branched monomethyl and dimethylalkanes, unsaturated hydrocarbons). Solid-phase CHCs were proportionally more abundant in shorter extractions, whereas fluid-phase compounds were proportionally more abundant in prolonged or sequential extractions. These patterns are consistent with a model of cohesive solid domains surrounded by more accessible fluid regions, though this interpretation remains indirect and alternative explanations (e.g. differential solubility and diffusion kinetics) cannot be excluded. CHCs of similar phase behaviour covaried across treatments, indicating that they aggregate within shared domains. Warm acclimatization increased the proportion of solid compounds, whereas fluctuating temperatures enhanced CHCs with intermediate phase behaviour. Our results suggest spatial and chemical heterogeneity in the CHC layer, with patterns of differential extractability consistent with clustering into phase-distinct domains, though direct imaging is required to confirm spatial topology. This potential heterogeneity may facilitate CHC multi-functionality, with the phase behaviour and domain membership of each CHC depending on its biophysical properties relative to the individual's overall CHC profile.

articles.title: Spectral theory of spin relaxation
articles.abstract: A dynamical theory of spin relaxation previously formulated in terms of stochastic differential equations is extended beyond the extreme narrowed approximation to incorporate temporal correlation in the driving random magnetic fields. An analysis of spin–spin relaxation in this case is provided, which is non-perturbative in the random field and yields an exact solution to the spin dynamical equations for axial (longitudinal) field fluctuations. We provide a real-time dynamical derivation that leads to a generalized class of spin spectra that are essentially non-Lorentzian for all finite field parameters. A spectral-moment analysis and novel parameter-extraction scheme lead to distinct notions of observable relaxation timescales compared with the standard characteristic exponential. The Lorentzian case is recovered as the extreme narrowed limit.

articles.title: Sublethal insecticide exposure and inbreeding impose a developmental bottleneck but enhance crop-damaging traits in surviving Colorado potato beetles
articles.abstract: Intensive agricultural insecticide use often fails to eradicate pest populations completely, leaving small remnant populations exposed to persistent sublethal residues and potentially elevated inbreeding. How such remnant populations persist remains poorly understood. Here, we examined how inbreeding and sublethal imidacloprid exposure shape survival and post-emergence performance in the Colorado potato beetle (Leptinotarsa decemlineata), a major agricultural pest. We compared four groups differing in breeding status and insecticide exposure history, and quantified emergence rate, locomotor activity, feeding behaviour and reproductive output. We found that despite the insecticide dosage being sublethal, both chemical exposure and inbreeding imposed severe developmental costs, reducing the adult emergence rate with no significant interaction effects. However, among the adults, we observed trait-specific phenotypic plasticity. Male locomotor activity was reduced by both stressors, while female activity remained stable. Notably, herbivory significantly increased under both inbreeding and sublethal insecticide exposure. Furthermore, while inbreeding severely reduced both egg production and hatching success, sublethal exposure to the insecticide surprisingly increased hatching success in surviving pairs. These results demonstrate that sublethal insecticide exposure and inbreeding can create a strong developmental bottleneck. Yet, surviving individuals can exhibit compensatory plasticity that maintains or even enhances their capacity for crop damage.

articles.title: Triterpenoid saponins from the aerial parts of Phytolacca americana and their anti-influenza A virus activity
articles.abstract: Phytolacca americana L. (Phytolaccaceae), a perennial species native to North America, is rich in oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins. In this study, ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC–QTOF–MS) profiling of the aerial-part extract revealed characteristic fragment ions of phytolaccagenin- and phytolaccagenic acid-type saponins with diverse glycosylation. MS-guided annotation enabled targeted isolation and structural elucidation of two previously undescribed compounds, one oleanane-type triterpenoid saponin (1) and one neolignan (3). Additionally, compound 2, which had been reported only based on mass spectrometric data, was isolated, and its structure was fully elucidated for the first time, together with those of 10 known oleanane-type triterpenoid saponins (4–13). Their structures were elucidated by comprehensive one-dimensional and two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic analyses combined with UPLC–QTOF–MS data. Although P. americana extracts have been reported to inhibit influenza A virus infection in previous studies, the bioactive constituents responsible for this antiviral activity have not been identified. The crude extract and isolated saponins were evaluated using complementary in vitro assays. In H1N1-infected A549 cells, compound 11 (3-O-trisaccharide phytolaccagenic acid) reduced viral NS1 RNA levels at 6 and 24 hpi as determined by RT–qPCR. Antiviral activity was further confirmed by plaque reduction and immunoblot analyses, with a plaque-assay IC50 of 57.98 ± 0.26 µM.

articles.title: What drives the winter behaviour and ecology of the temperate coral Astrangia poculata? An examination of thermal and nutritional cues
articles.abstract: In temperate ecosystems, accessing subtidal environments in the winter is challenging, and therefore, winter ecology and seasonal variation are understudied. For the temperate coral Astrangia poculata, winter is thought to be a period of biological ‘reset’, in which many cellular processes slow or stop, and the microbiome and symbiont community shift dramatically. The period of quiescence, when corals enter a dormant state with limited feeding or metabolic activity, is primarily driven by cold temperatures. However, other ecological drivers of quiescence remain unclear. Here, we documented quiescence in symbiotic and aposymbiotic colonies of A. poculata over a four-month winter period at two depths. First, we confirmed that quiescence is strongly associated with water temperatures under 6°C. Although we quantified a thermocline associated with depth, there was no influence of depth on quiescence. Symbiotic corals were more likely than aposymbiotic corals to enter quiescence, and higher chlorophyll α concentration was associated with lower quiescence, indicating a nutritional link to quiescence in A. poculata. Finally, we compared our results with previous quiescence observations and determined that the dormancy period is shorter in warmer winters, which has implications for the future ecology and behaviour of A. poculata in an era of global change.

articles.title: A synthetic heparin oligosaccharide decouples anticoagulation from heparin-induced thrombocytopenia risk
articles.abstract: Low–molecular weight heparin (LMWH) remains clinically indispensable for the prevention and treatment of thrombosis in cardiovascular surgery, hemodialysis, and other critical care settings. However, LMWH is constrained by heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and supply chain vulnerabilities of animal-derived sources. This study used chemoenzymatic synthesis to engineer homogeneous dodecasaccharide 12G-2, decoupling anticoagulant efficacy from HIT risk via dual structural modulation. Substitution with 2- O -sulfated glucuronic acid conferred conformational rigidity, and engineered sulfation attenuated platelet factor 4 (PF4) binding, whereas the antithrombin-binding domain remained intact. 12G-2 exhibited nanomolar anti–Factor Xa (FXa) activity in vitro, enoxaparin-equivalent venous antithrombotic efficacy, and superior arterial antithrombotic activity in murine thrombosis models, and it showed diminished PF4 binding, attenuated pathological β sheet formation, and minimal recognition by HIT-related antibodies in vitro. Both in vitro and in a murine tail-bleeding model, 12G-2 demonstrated high protamine reversibility, exceeding standard LMWH enoxaparin neutralization efficiency. In washed human platelets, 12G-2–PF4 complexes with the HIT-mimicking antibody KKO failed to induce integrin αIIbβ3 activation or P-selectin release and elicited minimal platelet spreading comparable to resting controls. Safety assessments in mice showed no hepatotoxicity at tested doses and low immunogenicity in a murine PF4-heparin immunization model. In PF4-heparin antibody–positive mice, 12G-2 attenuated platelet activation while exerting stronger FXa inhibition than enoxaparin. These findings established 12G-2 as an alternative to LMWH.

articles.title: Cancer-specific T cell receptor discovery using 150,000 clinical genomics samples
articles.abstract: T cell receptors (TCRs) can enable detection and elimination of cancer cells via recognition of cancer-specific peptides presented on human leukocyte antigen (HLA). We speculated that shared cancer antigens could be recognized by recurrent (“public”) TCRs, which might be identifiable using statistical methods. Here, we identified public TCRs against therapeutically relevant targets via computational analysis of large-scale bulk RNA sequencing data obtained from routine clinical genomics testing. Using data from ∼150,000 patient tumor samples, we identified TCR chains that were associated with well-known cancer antigens, including human papillomavirus, mutated KRAS, and CT83. We devised methods for pairing enriched TCR-α and TCR-β chain sequences and validated 44 TCRs across nine peptide-HLA targets for antigen recognition, including potent cytotoxic TCRs. Our results suggest that public anticancer TCRs are common and may represent a new source for the development of cancer therapeutics.

articles.title: Distinct tau PET dynamics in early versus late age-of-onset Alzheimer’s disease
articles.abstract: Early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (EOAD) and late-onset AD (LOAD) differ in clinical presentations and rates of progression. We aimed to compare baseline and longitudinal tau positron emission tomography (PET) burden measured with 18 F-flortaucipir and its relationship with clinical variables in amyloid PET–positive, cognitively impaired participants from the Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer’s Disease Study (EOAD; n = 390) and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (LOAD; n = 211). Participants with EOAD showed higher baseline tau PET burden, broader neuroanatomical involvement, and stronger associations of tau PET with amyloid PET and global cognition. Higher baseline tau PET burden in EOAD was independently validated in participants with EOAD from ADNI. Longitudinally, tau PET increased more rapidly in EOAD than in LOAD, independent of amyloid PET and clinical stage. We conclude that earlier age of onset in AD is linked to a more aggressive tauopathy, which in turn is a primary driver of clinical decline.

articles.title: Erratum for the Research Article “CRISPR-engineered human brown-like adipocytes prevent diet-induced obesity and ameliorate metabolic syndrome in mice”
Extended in vivo activity of VRC01 HIV-1 prophylaxis entails initial protective efficacy and subsequent breakthrough infections
articles.abstract: The two parallel antibody-mediated prevention (AMP) efficacy trials evaluated whether intravenous infusion of the anti-CD4 binding site broadly neutralizing antibody VRC01 prevents HIV-1 acquisition. Here, we analyzed HIV-1 acquisition in AMP through the week 104 final study visit. Against viruses considered highly sensitive to VRC01 [80% inhibitory concentration (IC 80 ) < 1 microgram/milliliter], VRC01 prophylaxis maintained cumulative prevention efficacy of 66.3% (95% confidence interval: 32.4, 83.2%), suggesting that the antibody successfully blocked or cleared these infections. In the post–week 80 period (after the final dose at week 72), HIV diagnosis and resistance to VRC01 were more frequent and greater in the VRC01 groups versus placebo. For instance, more HIV diagnoses with viruses considered moderately sensitive or resistant to VRC01 (IC 80 ≥ 5 microgram/milliliter) were made in the VRC01 groups compared with placebo groups (11 versus 1). Plausibly, as in vivo VRC01 concentration waned, suppressed viruses—often evolving greater resistance because of selective pressure—emerged as detectable infections. Our findings suggest that, whereas single antibodies can block sensitive strains, multiple antibodies are likely required to prevent both viral escape and breakthrough infections.

articles.title: Longitudinal remodeling of the tumor-immune microenvironment during regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer
articles.abstract: Previous studies combining the multikinase inhibitor regorafenib with a PD-1 inhibitor showed promising activity in gastric cancer. We conducted a phase 1b/2 trial (NCT05394740) of first-line regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in 30 patients with mismatch repair–proficient gastric cancer and investigated its impact on the tumor microenvironment. The primary end point was met; 22 of 30 patients showed objective tumor response (73%; 80% confidence interval, 60.3 to 83.8). Single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing were performed on biopsy samples at baseline, during treatment, and at disease progression. The combination treatment increased tumor antigen–reactive CD8 + T cells and M1-like proinflammatory macrophages and decreased immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting populations, including activated CCR8 + regulatory T cells, LRRC15 + cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), RGS5 + pericytes, and APLN + tip cells. At progression, LRRC15 + CAFs and APLN + tip cells remained reduced, activated CCR8 + regulatory T cells reexpanded, and additional treatment-resistant subsets emerged, including APOC1 + lipid-associated macrophages. In murine models of acquired resistance, therapeutic targeting of these suppressive immune cell populations with antibodies against CCR8 or TREM2 in combination with PD-1 blockade restored antitumor immunity. These findings demonstrate dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

articles.title: TWEAK signaling drives the transition from psoriasis to atopic dermatitis–like inflammation in paradoxical eczema
articles.abstract: Targeted biologics have transformed the treatment of inflammatory skin diseases such as plaque psoriasis. However, some patients with psoriasis paradoxically develop eczematous skin reactions after therapy targeting tumor necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin-17 (IL-17), or IL-23. Although paradoxical eczema (PE) resembles atopic dermatitis (AD) clinically and histologically, the molecular mechanisms that drive its development remain poorly understood. Here, we generated high-resolution cellular and spatial maps of human skin using single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, immunohistochemistry, and in vitro assays, profiling lesional biopsies from patients with PE ( n = 8 donors), alongside healthy control, psoriasis, and AD skin ( n = 4 donors per group). In PE, we identified distinct transcriptional changes characterized by myeloid and T cell expansion and an altered keratinocyte phenotype shaped by TNF-like weak inducer of apoptosis (TWEAK; encoded by TNFSF12 ) signaling through its receptor TNFRSF12A , confirmed at the protein level by immunohistochemistry. To define the underlying mechanism, we stimulated immortalized (N-TERT) and primary human keratinocytes and found that TWEAK acted together with IL-13 to drive a T helper 2– and type I interferon–polarized epithelial program that partially recapitulated the keratinocyte signature of PE lesions. We validated key target genes by quantitative polymerase chain reaction in primary keratinocytes. In THP-1 cells and primary human CD14 + monocytes, anti-TNF treatment induced TWEAK expression, suggesting a compensatory inflammatory circuit. Together, these findings identify the TWEAK–IL-13 axis as a key driver of PE and suggest how cytokine blockade may reshape cutaneous immune responses.

articles.title: Do abortion drugs pollute the water supply?
articles.abstract: On 9 September the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced that it will begin testing water supplies for mifepristone and misoprostol,1 the drugs used for medical abortion, among more than 1400 pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and other chemicals.2The testing is to “improve the agency’s understanding of what pollutants may be present in drinking water,” the EPA stated, implying that the listed substances are pollutants or contaminants.The testing is separate from water testing for unregulated contaminants under the Safe Drinking Water Act. Screening will also include hormones and reproductive health drugs such as testosterone, progesterone, and levonorgestrel. Levonorgestrel is used in contraceptives, including in emergency contraception such as Plan B.Anti-abortion activists are calling the testing “a victory for common sense,” claiming that the drugs’ excretion in water can affect human health and the environment.3“Abusers and pill pushers, an emerging abortion cartel, love the quick sale of deadly pills, but the fallout may go...

articles.title: Don’t “scapegoat” GPs for rising hospital demand, leaders say
articles.abstract: Improved access to general practice is causing pressure on NHS hospitals, the chief executive of NHS England has warned.Speaking to MPs, Jim Mackey said that increased access to GP appointments was leading to a spike in demand and long waits for secondary care.But GP leaders have hit back, stating that primary care should not be made a “scapegoat” for increased activity in hospitals and that long waits should not put pressure on GPs to reduce necessary referrals.Mackey made his comments while giving evidence to the Commons Public Accounts Committee about pressures on NHS hospitals after a summer of high demand.1media-1vid1Video 1Public Accounts Committee, 2 November 2026bmj-2026-101349-vid1Mackey said that demand for urgent hospital care was up 6% this September from the same month in 2025, which he said was “pretty significant when you’re on fine margins. We also had a significant growth in elective demand this year as well, which we’re...

articles.title: Fireworks are an underestimated danger to public health
articles.abstract: In 2025, 13 000 people were injured by fireworks.1 Some countries have taken a firm stance: the Netherlands has banned consumer use of fireworks, joining Ireland, Chile, and Australia.2 But in many countries, where consumer bans are not in place (including India, the UK, and the US), there remains a critical need for education and regulation of fireworks.Burns and hand surgeons, ophthalmologists, and emergency doctors brace themselves during holiday festivities every year for an influx of devastating, yet entirely preventable injuries. Fireworks related injuries are a leading cause of vision and limb loss globally, largely affecting young boys from low socioeconomic backgrounds.3Burns and blast injuries caused by shockwaves during detonation are common, with enough pressure to rupture an eardrum.4 Proximity to the blast increases the risk of traumatic injuries to the brain and eyes and other sequelae that might be missed initially but can have delayed downstream consequences, especially for...

articles.title: Interventions for adhesive capsulitis: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo compare the benefits and harms of therapeutic interventions for adhesive capsulitis.DesignSystematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.Data sourcesMedline, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to 1 May 2025, with an update in November 2025.Eligibility criteria for selecting studiesRandomised controlled trials enrolling adults with adhesive capsulitis, comparing active treatment with another intervention, placebo, or usual care.Main outcome measuresPain, function, range of motion, and adverse events.ResultsA total of 189 randomised controlled trials involving 12 988 participants and 59 interventions were included. Most trials contributing to principal outcomes were at high risk of bias (71% for pain, 72% for function, and 71% for range of motion). At short term follow-up, moderate certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy probably reduced pain compared with usual care (mean difference -1.97 on a 0-10 scale, 95% confidence interval (CI) -2.97 to -0.97). Low certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy may improve function (mean difference -11.42 on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -16.68 to -6.15), although direct and indirect estimates were limited by important incoherence. For short term range of motion, moderate certainty evidence suggested that manipulation under anaesthesia combined with intra-articular steroid injections probably improved flexion (mean difference 33.29°, 95% CI 11.19° to 55.39°), as did manipulation under anaesthesia alone (26.16°, 8.19° to 44.13°). Low certainty evidence suggested that extracorporeal shockwave therapy may improve flexion (22.42°, 12.99° to 31.84°) and abduction (18.62°, 8.09° to 29.14°), but both comparisons were limited by important incoherence. At mid-term follow-up, evidence for possible improvements in function with extracorporeal shockwave therapy and flexion with passive mobilisation was of low certainty, while evidence for pain reduction with extracorporeal shockwave therapy was of very low certainty. Most other comparative estimates were supported by low or very low certainty evidence. Comparative safety remained highly uncertain because adverse events were incompletely and inconsistently reported; the absence of reported adverse events should not be interpreted as evidence of absence of harm.ConclusionModerate certainty evidence suggests short term pain reduction with extracorporeal shockwave therapy and improved short term flexion with manipulation under anaesthesia, with or without intra-articular steroid injections. Most other treatment effects remain uncertain because of low certainty and incoherence, and comparative safety and mid-term effects are poorly established. The available evidence is mainly short term and outcome specific. Longer term comparative effectiveness, overall benefits and harms, and applicability beyond predominantly primary adhesive capsulitis remain uncertain.Systematic review registrationPROSPERO CRD420251070468

articles.title: Lenacapavir: Why a newly approved generic version of the blockbuster HIV drug won’t be available in the areas that need it most
articles.abstract: A cheap, generic version of one of the world’s best HIV prevention drugs will be out of reach for patients in at least 26 countries, the US manufacturer of the original drug has confirmed.The first generic version of lenacapavir—the only twice-a-year injectable pre-exposure prophylaxis—was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration this week.Made by the Indian company Dr Reddy’s Laboratories, this generic version is expected to cost just $40 (£30; €36) a year, a fraction of the $28 218 list price of the branded version made by the US manufacturer Gilead Sciences.1 However, 26 middle income countries and territories, including some with growing HIV epidemics, will be unable to buy the new generic because of conditions set out by Gilead.Gilead struck an agreement in October 2024 with six drug companies intending to develop a generic version of lenacapavir. This agreement included stipulations about which countries would eventually be able...

articles.title: Measles: New York reports first death in over 30 years as US outbreak continues to surge

The US Centers for Disease Control...

articles.title: [Articles] Preparing for responsive management versus renal dialysis in older people living with kidney failure and frailty or multimorbidity in the UK (Prepare for Kidney Care): a two-arm, superiority, parallel-group, open-label, pragmatic, phase 3, individually randomised controlled trial
articles.abstract: Among older people living with kidney failure and frailty or multimorbidity, we found no evidence that either preparing for responsive management or preparing for renal dialysis was superior in terms of QALYs over a mean follow-up duration of 4·5 years. This trial provides novel comparative information for clinical decision making.

articles.title: [Comment] Climate–health actions: global scale-up yields economic and fiscal benefits
articles.abstract: The disease burden attributable to climate change and its costs are large and growing.1 Preventing these health and economic losses in line with climate–health goals2 requires scaling up climate–health actions globally.3 Climate–health actions are policies, programmes, or other interventions in health or health-determining sectors to anticipate, prevent, prepare for, manage, or reduce health risks from climate change.4 Many climate–health actions constitute global common goods for health, safeguard human rights (eg, to health and a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment), and advance climate justice and health equity.

articles.title: [Comment] Inclusion of pregnant and lactating women in the Tumaini vaccine efficacy trial: a landmark advance
articles.abstract: The Tumaini trial protocol (NCT07842107) developed by the National Institute of Biomedical Research of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and partners to evaluate the efficacy of vaccines against Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) includes pregnant and lactating women. This trial represents a groundbreaking ethical and public health advance for two reasons: (1) it addresses the substantial threat of severe disease and death for pregnant women in the BDBV outbreak; and (2) it reverses a historical pattern of exclusion of pregnant and lactating women from trials of epidemic vaccines, which has led to delayed access to efficacious vaccines because pregnancy and lactation-specific evidence was unavailable.

articles.title: [Comment] Left main coronary artery disease: PCI or CABG for revascularisation strategy
articles.abstract: Clinical guidelines generally favour coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) over percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as the revascularisation strategy of choice in patients with left main coronary artery disease.1–2 An individual patient-level meta-analysis of four randomised controlled trials comparing PCI with CABG has suggested that PCI was not associated with a significantly higher risk of all-cause mortality at 5 years.3 The PRECOMBAT trial4 and SYNTAX Extended Survival trial5 similarly demonstrated no significant differences in all-cause mortality at 10 years between patients who underwent PCI with first-generation drug-eluting stents and those who underwent CABG.

articles.title: [Seminar] Retinoblastoma
articles.abstract: Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, represents a substantial global health equity concern, exemplifying profound disparities in global burden and outcome despite being a largely curable cancer. Retinoblastoma is thought to arise from cone photoreceptor precursor cells of the developing retina, mainly driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB1 tumour suppressor gene. Fewer than 2% of cases have no detectable RB1 pathogenic variant; approximately half of these cases instead show high-level amplification of the MYCN oncogene.

articles.title: A council of the willing for cancer in the Commonwealth
Addressing gaps in cancer care in the Caribbean
Armamentarium of scientific tools enough to win cancer fight in the Commonwealth
Cancer in the Commonwealth: a Lancet Oncology Commission
articles.abstract: Cancer is now one of the defining health and development challenges of our time. The 56 nations of the Commonwealth, home to 2·7 billion people, mirror this global burden. Recorded cancer cases across member states rose by 35% in 2008-18 and the number of deaths reached almost 1·7 million in 2018. The Lancet Oncology Commission on cancer in the Commonwealth was convened to ask a deceptively simple question: how can 56 diverse nations act collectively to close the widening gap between the burden of cancer and the capacity of each country to respond? 80 researchers, clinicians, policy makers, and civil society members, organised into five working groups and ten research streams, spent 2 years assembling the evidence base for this report. Using a validated microsimulation model, we estimate that 5-year net survival across eleven common cancers in the Commonwealth stood at just 30·7% in 2020, ranging from 4·1% in low-income countries (LICs) to 59·0% in high-income countries (HICs), driven overwhelmingly by late-stage presentation, which affects 62% of patients in LICs compared with 43% in HICs. This difference in survival is compounded by chronic underinvestment. Infrastructure gaps are equally stark: only 12% of countries meet international benchmarks for CT imaging, 22% for hospital density, and 40% for radiotherapy. Governance is underdeveloped too: barely one-third of Commonwealth countries have a national cancer control plan meeting basic quality criteria. Research investment also mirrors these inequities: between 2016 and 2023, Commonwealth countries collectively invested only US$165 per cancer-related disability adjusted life year. Yet the case for investment is unambiguous. Our modelling shows that a comprehensive scaleup of treatment, imaging, and quality of care could raise 5-year net survival across the Commonwealth from 30·7% to 52·9%, averting an estimated 5·8 million deaths and adding 113 million life-years between 2025 and 2035, at an incremental cost of $36·7 billion, delivering a return of between four and twenty dollars on every dollar invested. Crucially, this investment need not depend chiefly on external aid, which is contracting sharply at present. Our modelling for 38 low-income and middle-income Commonwealth countries suggests that up to $701 billion in additional domestic fiscal space could be mobilised between 2025 and 2030, through budget reprioritisation, macroeconomic growth, targeted taxation, and prudent borrowing. On this evidence, the Commission proposes six priority actions. These commitments are ambitious, set against an unusually turbulent geopolitical backdrop of declining official development assistance, fiscal retrenchment, and contested multilateralism. Yet it is precisely this backdrop that gives the Commonwealth its distinctive advantage: a voluntary association spanning every income level and continent, bound by common legal and regulatory traditions, capable of collective action that neither purely bilateral aid nor multilateral institutions under strain can easily replicate.

articles.title: From Commonwealth ambition to African action on cancer
Small island developing states and the Commonwealth
Survival in patients with renal cell carcinoma and brain metastases: an update of the Renal Graded Prognostic Assessment
articles.abstract: BackgroundBrain metastases are a common and serious consequence for patients with renal cell carcinoma. This study aimed to determine if survival has changed since the introduction of current therapies, identify prognostic factors, update the prognostic index (the Renal Graded Prognostic Assessment [GPA]) in the context of contemporary multi-modal therapies, compare outcomes with legacy cohorts, and determine whether overall survival correlates with intracranial progression-free survival.MethodsAn international consortium of 21 academic institutions contributed uniformly-curated retrospective data from 1049 patients with newly-diagnosed renal cell carcinoma with brain metastases (RCC-BM) treated between Jan 1, 2016, and Dec 31, 2022. Patients treated between 1985-2007 (n=286) and 2006-15 (n=711) were considered legacy cohorts and compared to the current cohort. Significant prognostic factors for survival were identified through combined multivariable analyses and used to update the Renal GPA. Intracranial progression-free survival was defined as the interval from date of initial RCC-BM diagnosis to date of first salvage treatment.FindingsOf the 1049 patients, 773 (73·7%) patients were male and 276 (26·3%) were female; the majority (851 [81·1%]) were White, and the median age was 63·9 years (IQR 56·2-70·3). The median overall survival was 20·0 months (95% CI 18·0-23·4), with a median follow-up of 53·4 months (95% CI 50·2-56·8). Overall survival for the legacy cohorts were 9·6 months (95% CI 8-11) and 12·0 months (5-11), respectively. In combined multivariable analyses, significant prognostic factors for inferior survival were lower Karnofsky Performance Status, lower baseline serum albumin, higher number of brain metastases, and presence of extracranial metastases. These factors were incorporated into the updated Renal GPA. Median survival was 4·8 months (95% CI 3·0-8·1) for patients with GPA 0-1·0, 12·4 months (10·6-17·2) for GPA 1·5-2·0, 33·6 months (27·5-40·0) for GPA 2·5-3·0, and 51·2 months (34·1-undefined) for GPA 3·5-4·0. Median intracranial progression-free survival was 9·6 months (95% CI 8·4-10·6). The Spearman's rank correlation between intracranial progression-free survival and overall survival was moderately strong (0·74 [95% CI 0·70-0·78]; pInterpretationSurvival has improved compared to the legacy cohorts but varies widely by GPA. The updated Renal GPA can be used to estimate survival, intracranial progression-free survival, individualise treatment, design and stratify clinical trials, and refine clinical trial eligibility.FundingUS National Institutes of Health (NCI P30CA014236), the Duke Center for Brain and Spine Metastases.

articles.title: The Commonwealth's cancer moment
Turning shared inheritance into shared action
Beyond sequence: a half-life × localization framework for lncRNAs
articles.abstract: Why do long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) with similar sequences behave differently across cell types and stimuli? This opinion article argues that reading half-life together with subcellular localization provides a practical organizing dimension for lncRNA function, one that helps make sense of the context-dependent, stimulus-responsive, and tissue-specific behaviors that sequence and structure alone leave unexplained. Drawing on transcriptome-wide turnover data from RNA sequencing and related metabolic-labeling approaches, I propose a half-life × localization matrix that groups lncRNAs into four functional categories, ranging from short-lived nuclear timing encoders to long-lived cytoplasmic buffers. Representative lncRNAs illustrate these categories; several shift between categories under stimulus, with the turnover change itself serving as the regulatory output. The matrix is a lens, not a final taxonomy.

articles.title: A tug-of-war in the niche: balancing forces to preserve stemness
articles.abstract: Stem cell niches are mechanically self-regulating systems. Segú Cristina and colleagues show that reciprocal adhesion between glial niche cells and neural stem cells buffers tensile forces, preserving nuclear and mitotic integrity and sustaining stem cell proliferation. They identify immunoglobulin complexes as critical mechanoregulators, linking adhesion, tissue mechanics, and stemness.

articles.title: Two faces of molecular strain in olefin metathesis
articles.abstract: Using molecular bows to impose intramolecular tension on olefins, Liu and colleagues reveal an unexpected divergence in metathesis kinetics: increasing strain slows cis-olefins but accelerates trans-olefins. Calculations attribute this contrast to configuration-dependent changes in the relative energies of catalytic intermediates and transition states, highlighting the complexity of strain-controlled reactivity.

articles.title: Lost, then found: transient forgetting in humans and machines
articles.abstract: Forgetting can be permanent or transient. An intriguing, recently described form of transient forgetting (TF) in artificial neural networks is the stability gap: a network that has already learned a first task exhibits transient yet substantial forgetting when it begins additional training on a second task alongside the first. Could an analogous phenomenon be found in humans? Following a literature survey, six types of TF in humans were identified, categorised by their sources: learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching, and multitasking. Although all differ in important ways from the stability gap, it is hypothesised that some underlying mechanisms are shared. This opinion article concludes by proposing experiments to test whether a ‘stability gap-like’ form of TF also occurs in humans.

articles.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
articles.abstract: What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?

articles.title: Cancer cells differentially modulate mitochondrial respiration to alter redox state and enable biomass synthesis in nutrient-limited environments
articles.abstract: The cell NAD+/NADH ratio can constrain biomass synthesis and influence proliferation in nutrient-limited environments. However, which cell processes regulate the NAD+/NADH ratio is not known. Here, we find that some cancer cells elevate the NAD+/NADH ratio in response to serine deprivation by increasing mitochondrial respiration. Cancer cells that elevate mitochondrial respiration have higher serine production and proliferation in serine-limiting conditions than cells with no mitochondrial respiration response, independent of serine synthesis enzyme expression. Increases in mitochondrial respiration and the NAD+/NADH ratio promote serine synthesis regardless of whether serine is environmentally limiting. Lipid deprivation can increase the NAD+/NADH ratio via mitochondrial respiration in some cells, including cells that do not increase respiration following serine deprivation. Thus, in cancer cells where lipid depletion raises the NAD+/NADH ratio, proliferation in serine-depleted environments improves when lipids are also depleted. Taken together, these data suggest that changes in mitochondrial respiration in response to nutrient deprivation can influence the NAD+/NADH ratio in a cell-specific manner to impact oxidative biomass synthesis and proliferation. Given the complexity of tumor microenvironments, this work provides a metabolic framework for understanding how levels of more than one environmental nutrient affect cancer cell proliferation.

articles.title: Estimating bone marrow adiposity from head MRI and identifying its genetic architecture
articles.abstract: Bone marrow (BM) adiposity changes radically through the lifespan, but this phenomenon is poorly characterized and understood in humans. Large datasets of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head have been collected to study the human brain, but also contain unexploited information about other organs. We developed an artificial neural network that localizes calvarial BM in T1-weighted MRI head scans, enabling us to study its composition in several large MRI datasets, and to model sex-dimorphic age trajectories, including the effect of menopause. We revealed high heritability in single-nucleotide polymorphism and twin data, and identified 41 genetic loci significantly associated with the trait, including six sex-specific loci. Integrating mapped genes with existing BM single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed patterns of adipogenic lineage differentiation and lipid loading. Finally, we identified significant genetic correlations with several human traits, including cognitive ability and Parkinson’s disease, which is intriguing in light of the recently discovered channels that link calvarial BM to the meninges.

articles.title: Expression of concern: Insect metamorphosis is regulated differently between sexes by members of a microRNA cluster
Targeting tankyrase scaffolding in the β-catenin destruction complex by PROTAC overcomes the limitation of catalytic inhibitors in colorectal cancer
articles.abstract: Aberrant WNT/β-catenin signaling drives tumorigenesis and metastasis in cancer. Although enzymatic inhibitors of tankyrase (TNKS) effectively block AXIN degradation and stabilize the β-catenin destruction complex (DC), they have demonstrated limited efficacy in various colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Here, we demonstrate that, unexpectedly, the induction of AXIN puncta represents a major barrier to achieving therapeutic efficacy. Mechanistically, catalytic inhibition of TNKS prevents TNKS turnover and drives its accumulation in the DC, wherein the scaffolding function of TNKS induces AXIN puncta formation, rigidifies the DC, and impedes β-catenin turnover. Chemically induced degradation of TNKS overcomes this limitation by stabilizing AXIN without puncta formation, providing a deeper suppression of the WNT/β-catenin pathway activity and the proliferation of CRC cells harboring dysfunctional APC mutations. Collectively, these findings provide an explanation for the unsatisfactory outcomes of drugging the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway by TNKS inhibitors and highlight TNKS degradation as a promising approach to treat WNT/β-catenin-driven CRC.

articles.title: Microscopic Intricacies of Self-Healing in Halide Perovskite–Charge-Transport-Layer Heterostructures
articles.abstract: The operational stability of halide perovskite photovoltaics is critically limited by progressive defect generation and nonradiative losses. Self-healing of defects offers a promising route to sustained performance, yet the coupled microscopic processes underlying it remain poorly understood, particularly at device-relevant interfaces. Here, we elucidate self-healing and defect evolution in photodamaged triple-cation mixed-halide (TCMH) perovskite films and their device-relevant charge-transport-layer (CTL) heterostructures. Using correlation clustering imaging (CLIM), our recently developed microscopic functional imaging tool, we map spatiotemporal photoluminescence heterogeneity to track defect dynamics. Each CTL distinctly modulates local trap activity, healing kinetics, and spectral redistribution in the TCMH layer, and the heterostructures exhibit faster optical recovery than pristine films, beneficial for device resilience. Healing follows biphasic kinetics, with fast electronic relaxation over minutes to tens of minutes and slower ionic redistribution and lattice relaxation over hours. Although quantitative device stability improvements are not established here, these microscopic insights into dynamic evolution of defects and ion redistribution at interfaces provide a framework for rationally designing stable perovskite optoelectronics.

articles.title: Reconfiguring Quinone Cathodes via Transition Metal Coordination for Advanced Calcium Batteries
articles.abstract: Calcium-ion batteries (CIBs) are promising for next-generation energy storage. However, their development is hindered by the lack of high-performance cathode materials. Organic carbonyl compounds possess structural flexibility and redox activity, yet their overall energy density remains fundamentally constrained. Here, we report a molecular engineering strategy to prepare metal (Cu and Ni)-coordinated quinone cathodes. The incorporation of transition-metal centers reconfigures the conjugated molecular framework, simultaneously enhancing reversible capacity and operating voltage. The optimized cathodes deliver reversible capacities of up to 203 mAh g–1 at an average voltage of ∼3.1 V vs Ca2+/Ca, corresponding to an energy density exceeding 600 Wh kg–1. Mechanistic investigations based on in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations reveal a bipolar charge-storage mechanism involving Ca2+ coordination with the carbonyl and imine sites during discharge and TFSI– storage at high charging potentials. This metal-coordination strategy provides a promising strategy for developing high-energy multivalent battery systems.

Decompression With or Without Fusion Across Subgroups With Degenerative Lumbar Spondylolisthesis
articles.abstract: Randomized trials have shown limited benefits and increased risks of adding spinal fusion surgery to decompression for degenerative spondylolisthesis. Decompression with fusion has increasingly been used in the United States. To examine the comparative effectiveness of decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for patient subgroups. Cohort study using the target trial framework. Norwegian Registry for Spine Surgery and nested NORDSTEN-DS (Norwegian degenerative spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis) randomized trial. Adults aged 18 to 80 years with lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis and symptomatic back or leg pain lasting at least 3 months. Lumbar spinal decompression surgery with fusion versus lumbar spinal decompression surgery alone. The primary outcomes were Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) score and reoperation at 12 months. Linear regression models with inverse probability weighting to control for baseline confounding were used to obtain effect estimates with 95% CIs for decompression with fusion versus decompression alone for prespecified subgroups, including sex, age, smoking, body mass index (BMI), back pain intensity, and American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade. Of 2252 patients, 236 were in the NORDSTEN-DS randomized trial. The mean age was 66 years, and 1576 (70%) women were included. A total of 1446 patients had decompression alone, and 806 had decompression with fusion; respective unadjusted baseline ODI scores were 38.9 (SD, 14.9) and 41.4 (SD, 14.7). At 12 months, the ODI score was 22.3 (95% CI, 15.5 to 29.1) for decompression alone and 20.0 (CI, 13.9 to 26.2) for decompression with fusion; the mean difference was 2.2 (CI, -1.6 to 6.1). In exploratory analyses, the ODI score was worse for decompression with fusion for men with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher. Reoperation risk at 12 months did not differ. Possible residual confounding. Patient subgroups did not have differential effects from the addition of fusion to decompression at 12 months. Research Council of Norway.

articles.title: Measles
articles.abstract: Measles is reemerging, with cases and outbreaks increasing across the United States and other countries where measles had previously been eliminated. Most U.S. physicians have no experience with treating measles. However, the increasing likelihood of encountering not only children but also adults with measles requires a clinical review of the epidemiology, prevention, diagnosis, and management of this previously uncommon infection for general internal medicine physicians and hospitalists who care for adults in settings with measles reemergence. Prompt clinical suspicion, infection control measures, and notification of public health departments support timely diagnosis and disease control.

articles.title: Q&A: Hospital medicine looks ahead
Timing of Long COVID Improvement in Prospectively Followed RECOVER-Adult Participants
articles.abstract: Long COVID (LC) is widespread; however, limited information has been reported on the likelihood that symptoms remit over time. To evaluate the likelihood of improvement among persons with likely LC. Prospective, multisite cohort study (RECOVER-Adult [Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery]). 83 U.S.-based sites across 33 states; Washington, DC; and Puerto Rico. 1019 persons in RECOVER-Adult with likely LC (LC Research Index [LCRI] ≥11) 12 months after first SARS-CoV-2 infection. The primary outcome was time until 2 consecutive study visits with LCRI less than 11. Secondary outcomes were time until LCRI measure reduced 50% or more and quality of life was good or better, and LCRI decreased to 0. Unadjusted estimates of cumulative incidence and adjusted marginal cumulative incidence by age, sex, SARS-CoV-2 wave, and LC subtype were reported across all follow-up time points. An estimated 36.2% (95% CI, 33.0% to 39.5%) met the primary outcome by 24 months after infection, and 50.1% (CI, 46.1% to 54.0%) met the primary outcome by 36 months. An estimated 56.4% (CI, 52.2% to 60.4%) and 26.9% (CI, 23.3% to 30.5%), respectively, met the 2 secondary outcomes by 36 months. Among persons who still reported likely LC at 18 months and 24 months after first infection, relative timing of subsequent symptom improvement was similar. Findings in this observational cohort are interpretable in a population with prevalent likely LC and do not address causal relationships between individual characteristics and symptom improvement. Among persons with likely LC 12 months after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, one half experience meaningful reductions in symptoms by 36 months, whereas a quarter experience complete remission of symptoms. These findings underscore both the potential for natural recovery and the urgent need for placebo-controlled therapeutic intervention trials. National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: Use of GLP-1 RAs before or during pregnancy was not linked to maternal pregnancy complications
Clonality in Preleukemic Conditions
articles.abstract: Preleukemia, historically a morphological and cytogenetic diagnosis, is now understood as a continuous clonal process in which somatic mutations, environmental influences, and stem cell pool dynamics interact over decades. Clonal hematopoiesis, the expansion of blood cells carrying somatic mutations, is near-universal in adults over age 70 and confers elevated risk of hematological malignancy, while also acting as a risk factor for cardiovascular and other age-related diseases. Here, we review the genetic and environmental factors that predispose to clonal expansion, organize the mechanisms of clonal expansion into three overlapping and interacting mechanisms (cell-autonomous fitness gain, context-conditional fitness, and nongenetic heritable states), and trace the trajectories that lead from clonal expansion to specific myeloid and lymphoid malignancies. We also discuss methods that have enabled mapping of clonal architecture in human tissue and close on the key questions that we anticipate will define the next decade of research in this field.

articles.title: Labor Unions and Better Health
articles.abstract: Social-class inequities in health arise from power imbalances in our political-economic system. However, through labor-union organizing, workers can build power to improve their life chances and health. In our review, we describe the rich historical, theoretical, and mechanistic evidence linking unions and health and critically evaluate the state of quantitative research on the topic. Most individual-level and ecological studies have estimated small beneficial or null union-health associations. However, as we describe, the studies are limited in number, particularly outside the Global North, and face many technical and conceptual challenges, including feedback loops between unions and societies’ political-economic contexts. We conclude with recommendations for enhancing the rigor and utility of union-health research, including by richly contextualizing studies’ findings and by answering questions raised by workers themselves. As social and economic inequities intensify and workers face heightening attacks on their well-being, unions remain crucial organizations for advancing health justice.

articles.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
articles.journal: Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application
articles.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This review provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley–Terry–Luce model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from artificial intelligence feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.

articles.abstract: Wang et al. establish a systematically benchmarked framework integrating long reads and genome assemblies for accurate detection and source tracing of somatic mobile element insertions. articles.title: Toward comprehensive maps of somatic mosaic mutations
articles.abstract: The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network has established complementary benchmarks for somatic mutation detection, extended mutation analysis into underexplored genomic regions, and highlighted chromatin states as potential records of cellular history. These studies show that detection performance depends on reference representation, benchmark quality, and experimental design, requiring careful calibration when integrating technologies.
