An insight into molecular identification and DNA barcoding of bamboo: current status, challenges, and future prospects
articles.abstract: IntroductionBamboo exhibits a complex taxonomy due to polyploidy, hybridisation, and long flowering periods, which complicate species identification. Traditional morphological taxonomy often struggles with limited diagnostic traits and considerable phenotypic variability, leading to taxonomic ambiguities and misinterpretations. The convergence of similar traits among unrelated species further complicates phylogenetic classification. To address these challenges, integrative taxonomic approaches are needed to combine morphological, molecular, and ecological data for accurate bamboo classification. This review synthesises the current status, recent advances, and emerging trends in molecular identification and DNA barcoding of bamboo, highlighting their potential to improve taxonomy, conservation, and the sustainable utilisation of bamboo genetic resources.MethodTo provide a framework for the review, a scientometric analysis was performed using bibliographic records.ResultsThe review suggests that no single marker or combination of markers can currently serve as a universal barcode across bamboo. The performance of commonly used markers such as ITS, matK, rbcL, psbA-trnH, rps16-trnQ, and alternative plastid regions provides valuable insights into species identification. Comparative evidence indicates that barcode performance is strongly marker- and lineage-dependent. These markers have improved plant taxonomy by providing more reliable species identification than traditional morphological methods.DiscussionDNA barcoding has been effectively used to understand complex species relationships and identify cryptic species that are difficult to distinguish morphologically. Furthermore, next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have transformed genomic data acquisition, enabling species discrimination. Integrating machine learning with DNA barcoding further improves species identification accuracy and shows promise for improving conventional methodologies in bamboo systematics. However, the application of ML and NGS in bamboo is still in its early stages and will require substantial work on bamboo databases to achieve greater accuracy.

articles.title: The intermediate social resilience hypothesis: a testable framework linking animal sociality to population resilience under environmental change
articles.abstract: Sociality can improve access to information, cooperation, collective defense, parental care, collective decision-making, and social buffering, but it can also intensify competition and pathogen transmission, spread outdated information, and create dependence on particular partners, roles, or traditions. In this article, we propose the Intermediate Social Resilience Hypothesis (ISRH), which predicts that, under specified conditions, population resilience may be greatest at an intermediate value of a defined social dimension. We do not rank all animal societies on a single universal scale. Instead, low, intermediate, and high values must be defined within a measurable dimension, such as group size, cohesion, network connectivity, cooperative effort, or reliance on social information, and within a biologically comparable system. Resilience must likewise be specified as resistance, recovery, temporal stability, or persistence under a defined form and scale of environmental change. The distinctive contribution of the ISRH is not simply the recognition that sociality can generate both benefits and costs, but the explicit prediction that their balance can, under identifiable conditions, produce a testable intermediate maximum in population resilience. An intermediate optimum is expected only when social benefits initially increase but eventually saturate, whereas one or more relevant social costs continue to rise. Environmental harshness, variability, unpredictability, and the flexibility, modularity, redundancy, or multilevel organization of social systems may shift, flatten, or eliminate this relationship. The hypothesis generates two falsifiable predictions that can be tested through comparative, longitudinal, experimental, phylogenetic, network, and population-monitoring approaches. By integrating behavioral ecology, social evolution, resilience theory, and conservation, the framework explicitly recognizes the multidimensional nature of animal social systems while providing explicit criteria for distinguishing support for the ISRH from monotonic, threshold, flat, or context-dependent alternative relationships.

articles.title: When wildlife damage threatens livelihoods: why national park residents consider a transition to tourism
articles.abstract: Wildlife damage is often expected to push national park residents toward new sources of income, but the appraisals that turn damage into a willingness to move into tourism remain unclear. Drawing on protection motivation theory and questionnaire data from 513 residents in and around the Wuyishan City section of Wuyishan National Park, China, this study distinguishes perceived tourism adaptive efficacy from tourism self-efficacy and examines how these two beliefs relate to intentions to shift household livelihoods toward tourism. Greater perceived wildlife damage was related to stronger threat appraisal of traditional livelihoods. Residents who perceived greater livelihood threat also reported stronger transition intentions and were more likely to view tourism as a workable livelihood alternative. However, no clear relationship emerged between livelihood threat and tourism self-efficacy, although both adaptive efficacy and self-efficacy were positively related to transition intention. As a moderator, perceived tourism development opportunity was more relevant to adaptive efficacy than to self-efficacy. When residents perceived greater tourism opportunities, the positive relationship between livelihood threat and adaptive efficacy was stronger, as was the corresponding indirect relationship with transition intention. In contrast, perceived opportunity made little difference to the relationship involving self-efficacy. These findings suggest that livelihood threat was associated with greater perceived usefulness and feasibility of tourism without a corresponding association with residents’ confidence in their own ability to engage in tourism activities. Policies aimed at encouraging livelihood diversification in national park communities may therefore need to combine the creation of tourism opportunities with training, skills development, and other forms of support that strengthen residents’ capacity to participate.

articles.title: Mitochondrial DNA abundance is a determinant of immunogenic cell death in cancer
articles.abstract: Mitochondrial stress can trigger either immunogenic or apoptotic cell death. Tanaka et al. find that mitochondrial DNA abundance, shaped by oncogenic KRAS signaling and mitophagy, determines the immunological outcome of mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, providing a mechanistic basis for targeting mitochondrial stress to augment antitumor immunity.

articles.title: Host seasonal trophic strategies linked to dietary‐microbiota coupling: A potential mechanism mediating the coexistence of sympatric small rodents
articles.abstract: This study reveals that host trophic strategy, not shared seasonality, drives gut microbiota plasticity in sympatric rodents. Herbivorous voles show tight diet–microbiome coupling; granivorous gerbils exhibit functional stability. This highlights gut microbiota as a potential key mechanism for niche differentiation and coexistence. Abstract The coexistence mechanisms of sympatric species have long attracted widespread research attention. However, it remains unclear whether sympatric species experiencing the same seasonal conditions exhibit convergent or host‐specific gut microbiota responses. We compared the herbivorous Brandt's vole (Lasiopodomys brandtii) and the granivorous Mongolian gerbil (Meriones unguiculatus), two sympatric rodent species with divergent trophic strategies inhabiting the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, China. By integrating plant DNA metabarcoding, gut microbiota profiling and microbial functional output analyses across seasons, we investigated seasonal dietary–microbiome associations. Our results revealed that although seasonal dietary variation affects the composition of the host gut microbiota, the taxonomic and functional plasticity of gut microbiota is strongly influenced by host trophic strategies. Brandt's voles maintained a fermentation‐oriented microbiota tightly coupled with seasonal shifts in Poaceae and Cyperaceae intake, exhibiting coordinated changes in microbial taxa, short‐chain fatty acid production and cellulase activity. In contrast, Mongolian gerbils exhibited substantial seasonal dietary turnover between Chenopodiaceae and Caragana plants, while maintaining comparatively stable microbial functional outputs, suggesting metabolic buffering. Host trophic strategy, rather than shared environmental seasonality, is related to the strength and functional consequences of the coupling between diet and microbiome. Our results emphasize the gut microbiome as a potential key mechanism underlying trophic niche differentiation and ecological coexistence in wild mammalian communities.

articles.title: Mechanistic insights and structure–reactivity relationships of Ru(II)–Imidazole complex catalysts for formic acid dehydrogenation: A combined DFT and machine learning study
Small-molecule structural regulators enable strain-adaptive molecular ordering in intrinsically stretchable organic photodetectors
Comparison between interfacial pyroelectric and transient interfacial photovoltaic effects
articles.abstract: Interfacial pyroelectricity and transient interfacial photovoltaic effects provide two distinct routes for converting thermal and optical fluctuations into transient electrical signals through interfacial charge redistribution. This review compares their mechanisms, output characteristics, evaluation metrics with particular emphasis on polarization-mediated lyroelectric responses, and potential in sensing, energy conversion, and event-driven optoelectronics.

articles.title: Structural basis for the non-canonical nucleosome remodeling by ATRX
articles.abstract: Wang et al. show that ATRX remodels chromatin through an unusual mechanism that favors nucleosome disassembly over repositioning. ATRX also captures histones and cooperates with ASF1 for tetrasome assembly, linking chromatin remodeling to histone chaperoning for reassembly and helping explain how ATRX functions at accessible chromatin regions.

articles.title: Asymmetric Migration Shapes Genetic Structure of the Invasive Avian Vampire Fly (Philornis downsi) Across the Galápagos Islands
articles.abstract: Biological invasions on islands provide a natural framework to study how dispersal and connectivity influence evolutionary and ecological processes. The avian nest parasitic fly, Philornis downsi—first recorded in Darwin's finch nests in 1997—causes high mortality in endemic land birds, yet its inter‐island and sex‐specific patterns of dispersal and genetic structure remain poorly understood. We use low‐coverage whole genome sequencing to investigate genome‐wide patterns of genetic diversity, directional migration and effective population size in P. downsi across five major Galápagos Islands and its native range in mainland Ecuador. We find evidence for a genetic bottleneck in the Galápagos, isolation by distance, and evidence that the island closest to the Ecuadorian mainland, San Cristóbal, is genetically divergent from the other four islands sampled, despite retaining the highest genetic diversity. No evidence was found for sex‐biased dispersal; however, sex‐biased genetic structure was detected using only markers from inferred autosomal scaffolds. We found asymmetric gene flow with higher migration rates from San Cristóbal westward to the other islands, matching the direction of both southeast trade winds and major cargo shipping routes. Our results suggest both natural and human‐mediated colonisation of P. downsi from the mainland through San Cristóbal to the other islands, followed by high inter‐island dispersal among closely situated sink islands. Our findings are critical for prioritising islands for control strategies that will reduce P. downsi impacts on vulnerable endemic birds and underscore the value of understanding directional migration patterns for managing invasive species in metapopulations.

articles.title: A user’s guide to building the Universe
Rapid growth in a dual active galactic nucleus during a gas-rich merger at z ≈ 4.5
articles.abstract: Observations reveal two rapidly growing supermassive black holes in a gas-rich galaxy merger just 1.3 billion years after the Big Bang. Both already lie on the black hole–host mass relation, indicating a period of early co-evolution.

articles.title: ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression
articles.abstract: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the fibroblastic stroma constitutes most of the tumor mass and is remarkably devoid of functional blood vessels, leaving unresolved how PDAC cells obtain essential metabolites and water-insoluble lipids. We find that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) acquire and transfer lipids from blood-borne particles to PDAC cells through trogocytosis of CAF plasma membranes, a process requiring the CAF-expressed phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6) to promote PDAC cell survival. Cancer cells and CAFs form synapse-like contacts that induce cytosolic calcium influx in CAFs through Orai channels, activating ANO6 and driving phosphatidylserine exposure on CAF membranes, which initiates trogocytosis and transfer of membrane lipids, including cholesterol, to PDAC cells. This ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine externalization also supports CAF-mediated immunosuppression of cytotoxic T cells through trogocytosis. Blockade of ANO6 antagonizes tumor growth, partly by disrupting cholesterol delivery to cancer cells, and attenuates immune suppression, identifying ANO6 as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC. Ogier et al. uncover that cancer-associated fibroblasts fuel pancreatic tumor growth and immune suppression by transferring membrane lipids to cancer cells through anoctamin 6-dependent trogocytosis.

articles.title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion
articles.abstract: Wang et al. reveal that epigenetic remodeling driven by BAZ2A in renal cancer cells induces the production of palmitate that is taken up by tumor-infiltrating cells, resulting in impaired metabolic fitness of CAR-T cells via PGC-1α palmitoylation.

articles.title: GALE is a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing
articles.abstract: Shan et al. identified UDP-galactose 4-epimerase as an immune checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated cancer cell killing by enhancing interaction of CD155 and CEACAM1 with their receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, and simultaneously inhibiting CD155 binding to CD22.

articles.title: Targeting GALE harnesses γδ T cells for cancer immunotherapy
articles.abstract: Cancer cells can evade the immune system through mechanisms such as downregulation of MHC I molecules and expression of inhibitory ligands. Research now shows that targeting the metabolic enzyme GALE in tumor cells boosts the killing of these cells by γδ T cells through altering the glycosylation of key immune-checkpoint ligands.

articles.title: Photoenzymatic stereodivergent hydrophosphinylation enabled by nicotinamide-dependent imine reductases
articles.abstract: Stereocontrol of phosphorus-centred radicals remains a major challenge, limiting access to P-chiral organophosphorus compounds. Now a photoexcited imine reductase is reprogrammed to enable stereodivergent hydrophosphinylation, delivering C-, P- and C/P-chiral phosphine oxides with high selectivity.

articles.title: From poppies to pain relief
articles.abstract: Madison Sowden discusses the origin of morphine, how the structure and medical effects were first studied, and how the compound is produced today.

articles.title: How expansive and flexible is the matrix of life?
articles.abstract: All known life needs water, but its operative mechanisms are extraordinarily diverse. Bruce Gibb discusses the chemistry of some of Earth’s most extreme ecosystems and what they reveal about life beyond our planet.

articles.title: An extra beat every minute
articles.abstract: Small deviations in the power system frequency are routinely attributed to stochastic fluctuations in load and generation. New research reveals a disturbance recurring precisely every minute in grids worldwide, caused by clock-synchronized self-tests in battery-based uninterruptible power supplies that inadvertently act in unison.

articles.title: Caloric cooling devices and systems
articles.abstract: Caloric cooling offers a promising solid-state alternative to conventional refrigeration, but system-level challenges continue to limit practical deployment. This Review evaluates the state of the art, identifies the key barriers to scalable devices and outlines a roadmap for sustainable cooling.

articles.title: Durable reactive CO2 capture exceeding 1,000 h via self-reinforcing molecular catalysts
articles.abstract: Reactive CO2 capture integrates carbon capture and electrochemical conversion in a single process, but poor catalyst durability remains a major challenge. Here the authors show that pH-swing-driven acidification accelerates catalyst demetallation and develop a cobalt phthalocyanine catalyst that suppresses metal loss, sustaining efficient CO production for 1,000 h.

articles.title: Ironing out oxygen instability
articles.abstract: Oxygen redox in layered-oxide cathodes could facilitate the development of high-energy sodium-ion batteries, but poor reversibility has limited its practical application. Now, an iron-mediated redox strategy offers a pathway to substantially improving oxygen-redox reversibility.

articles.title: One-minute frequency disturbances from unintended synchronization in cyber–physical power systems
articles.abstract: Power grids on five continents show frequency oscillations with a period of exactly 1 min. The authors trace this to clock-synchronized software in devices such as uninterruptible power supplies that creates coherent, repeating demand peaks.

articles.title: Autophagy limits steady-state IL-1α expression to restrain innate immunity
articles.abstract: Autophagy controls pulmonary innate immunity at the steady-state by restraining IL-1α expression by alveolar macrophages. Disrupting this regulatory pathway primes lung innate immunity and enhances resistance to distinct respiratory infections, identifying an unexpected role for autophagy in determining host immune readiness.

articles.title: Linda J. Miller (1958–2026)
Climate change threatens malaria elimination in the Asia Pacific
articles.abstract: A multidisciplinary group of policymakers and researchers discusses the impacts of climate change on malaria in the Asia Pacific, identifies gaps in national adaptation strategies and outlines five priority actions for the region.

articles.title: Continuous mass measurement of single proteins
articles.abstract: We developed an approach to monitor the mass of individual proteins and the complexes they form for up to an hour by mass photometry. The ability to follow the mass of individual species enables the detection and characterization of interactions as a function of time — the essence of biomolecular mechanisms.

articles.title: Foundation models unlock robust phenotypic representations from Cell Painting images
articles.abstract: We pretrained and systematically benchmarked a suite of self-supervised foundation models on the largest public Cell Painting dataset, enabling robust morphological feature extraction directly from multichannel high-content images without cell segmentation or feature engineering. These models outperformed classical methods and demonstrated generalizability across cell types.

articles.title: Multivalent ADAR1 recruitment for precise RNA editing
articles.abstract: Current ADAR-recruiting RNA editing systems suffer from limited efficacy and bystander editing. We developed a system in which the multivalent recruitment of endogenous ADAR1 p150 through its Zα domain enables up to 100% A-to-I editing in vitro and 84% in vivo, enabling precise correction of disease-associated mutations at the transcript level.

articles.title: Spatial single-cell mapping of transcriptional differences across genetic backgrounds in mouse brains
articles.abstract: Genetic variation can alter organ structure and function. Comparative statistical analysis of organs across genetic backgrounds requires spatial, single-cell, atlas-scale data in replicates. Here we introduce atlas-scale transcriptome localization using aggregate signatures (ATLAS), a scalable tissue mapping method that learns transcriptional signatures from single-cell RNA sequencing data, encodes them in situ with tens of thousands of oligonucleotide probes and decodes them to infer cell types and imputed transcriptomes. We validated ATLAS against direct MERFISH measurements of marker genes and through quantitative comparisons to four other technologies. We profiled 40 million cells across more than 400 coronal sections from central brains of five male and five female C57BL/6J mice and five male BTBR T+tf/J mice, an idiopathic autism model. Our analysis revealed more than 40 significant differences in cell-type distributions and identified 16 regional composition changes across male–female and B6–BTBR comparisons. ATLAS thus enables systematic comparative studies, facilitating organ-level structure–function analysis of disease models. ATLAS is a highly scalable tissue profiling method that leverages existing atlas data and in silico decoding to generate imputed cell maps.

articles.title: Automated inverse design of metainterfaces with tailored friction laws
articles.abstract: Providing dry solid contacts with on-demand macroscale frictional behaviour remains a formidable challenge in tribology, haptics and robotics. It has been shown that metainterfaces created from surfaces with engineered asperity-based topographies can achieve such friction control. However, only a few types of friction behaviour were demonstrated because suitable topographies were identified on the basis of human intuition. Here we introduce a numerical-optimization-based inverse design framework to automatically discover new metainterfaces that satisfy specified friction laws—relationships between friction and the normal force. To illustrate the framework’s versatility, we first expand the range of achievable friction coefficients for a given pair of materials. We next unlock friction laws showing power-law variation of frictional force with normal force, with exponents ranging between 2/3 and 1.35. We then achieve bilinear variation when the range of normal force is divided into segments, including cases for a smaller slope in the second segment than in the first. We validate relevant cases experimentally. Our automated framework enables systematic exploration of large parameter spaces, not limited to topography but potentially incorporating the individual asperities’ bulk material or surface physicochemistry. It offers design solutions for different friction laws and provides insights into the relationship between local interfacial properties and macroscopic friction. Understanding friction between contacting surfaces is important to improve device performance. Now a method is shown to discover materials that offer on-demand frictional behaviour using inverse design based on genetic algorithms.

articles.title: Motors use biased diffusion to shepherd diffusible proteins on microtubules
articles.abstract: Far-from-equilibrium mixtures of active and passive molecules self-organize, but the principles remain unclear. Microtubules are cytoskeletal polymers composed of 13 protofilaments bound by mixtures of actively moving motors and passively diffusing microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs). They can serve as a model system for self-organization on a multi-lane lattice. Here we show that motors can shepherd diffusive MAPs along the lattice by rectifying Brownian motion into net directional drift without motor–MAP binding. Our model reveals that biased movement increases when fewer protofilaments are accessible or when lateral diffusion between protofilaments is limited, and identifies local dimensionality and diffusion as key parameters governing spatial patterning. In particular, shepherding depends on the total number of motors bound to the microtubules, and not on the individual motor processivity. We experimentally recapitulate micrometre-scale shepherding with a kinesin-1 motor (K401) and a diffusive MAP (PRC1), which show no detectable binding. These findings suggest shepherding is an emergent mechanism by which ensembles of motors generate micrometre-scale spatial patterning and transport of MAPs without direct binding interactions. Microtubules are bound by active motors and passively diffusing proteins. Now it is shown that this mixture of active and passive molecules is a realization of rectified Brownian motion in active matter.

articles.title: Multiparticle quantum walks in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model
articles.abstract: A strong potential gradient can localize individual particles in a crystal or optical lattice by making ordinary hopping energetically costly. Interactions can nevertheless enable correlated hopping processes that preserve the system’s centre of mass or, equivalently, its dipole moment. This constraint gives rise to fractonic behaviour, in which isolated excitations are immobile but their bound states can move. Here we realize individual mobile bound states of fractons in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model and observe their coherent quantum dynamics. Starting from a one-dimensional chain of ultracold bosonic atoms in an optical lattice, we use site-resolved optical potentials to deterministically generate localized dipole and antidipole excitations, which represent mobile bound states of a hole and a doublon. We track their individual quantum walks and characterize their strongly interacting scattering dynamics. Our study provides a bottom-up investigation of a Hamiltonian with kinetic constraints and offers an approach to exploring low-energy phases of fractonic matter. Strong potential gradients can localize individual particles, but interactions can still generate collective motion. An experiment with ultracold atoms in a tilted lattice now shows this collective motion by tracking mobile bound states of fractons.

articles.title: The challenge of recognition in large scientific collaborations
articles.abstract: The authorship practices of large collaborations can hide individual contributions. A recognition programme developed by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration publicly documents verified contributions to research, infrastructure and community service.

articles.title: Thermodynamic demonstration of tetracriticality and multicomponent superconductivity in UTe2
articles.abstract: The candidate topological superconductor UTe2 exhibits a complex phase diagram with multiple superconducting states, and the nature of their coexistence is not yet resolved. In particular, the apparent observation of two intersecting second-order phase boundaries at a triple point in the pressure–temperature phase diagram is thermodynamically forbidden. This suggests either a hidden phase transition or a fundamental misunderstanding of the superconductivity in this material. Here we observe an additional phase boundary that is characterized by an upward jump in the sound velocity. This is direct thermodynamic evidence for a phase transition in which superconducting order is lost on cooling. Our results establish a tetracritical point beyond which the ambient and pressure-induced superconducting order parameters form a multicomponent state. We use the measured phase diagram to demonstrate that strong competition between the two superconducting order parameters drives the loss of order when cooling, and leads to phase locking that suppresses superconducting fluctuations. These findings provide the definitive magnetic field–pressure–temperature phase diagram of UTe2 and establish a thermodynamic foundation for multicomponent superconductivity. Prior measurements of the phase diagram of UTe2 contain a triple point that is forbidden by thermodynamics. Now, an additional phase boundary is discovered that resolves this problem and confirms multicomponent superconductivity in this material.

articles.title: Enhanced neutral seawater photoelectrolysis by fast hydrogen pumping at subnanometre triple interfaces
articles.abstract: Atomically dispersed Cr(OH)x on Pt/GaN creates subnanometre triple interfaces that couple water activation, hydrogen transfer and Pt–H formation across adjacent interfaces for fast hydrogen pumping in photoelectrochemical seawater splitting. This overcomes hydrogen-utilization limitations in single-interface catalysis and enables high-current outputs under neutral seawater photoelectrolysis in low-bias and bias-free devices.

articles.title: Expanding atropisomerism to C–P bonds
Emergent Gauge Flux in Mixed ${\mathrm{QED}}_{3}$ with Flavor Chemical Potential: Implications for Magnetized U(1) Dirac Spin Liquids
articles.abstract: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations reveal that a Zeeman field drives Dirac spin liquids into a chiral flux phase, forming relativistic spinon Landau levels and gapless photon excitations of the emergent gauge field theory.

articles.title: The paths we take
Antibodies to distinct epitopes on MPXV enveloped virion provide additive and complete protection
articles.abstract: The continuing evolution of monkeypox virus (MPXV) clades capable of sustained human-to-human transmission poses an escalating global health risk, yet no effective therapy exists for poxvirus infection. Here, we investigate a panel of human monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), derived from an antibody library, which targets A35 and B6 antigens located on the extracellular enveloped virion (EV). Four high-affinity mAbs target the central groove of the A35 dimer, whereas one targets a previously unidentified epitope on the A35 protruding loop. Three other mAbs recognize distinct, previously unmapped epitopes on the multidomain B6 antigen. Those epitopes are conserved across most orthopoxviruses. A combination of an anti-A35 and an anti-B6 antibody provides additive and complete protection from both morbidity and mortality in a lethal VACV mouse model, challenging the previous assumption that targeting both the EV and mature virion (MV) forms is required for full protection. These studies uncover critical information for next-generation therapeutics and vaccines against emerging MPXV as well as other Orthopoxvirus threats.

articles.title: Metabolic licensing of innate immune memory
articles.abstract: NAD + is revealed to be a metabolic signal that preserves an epigenetic mark central to trained immunity by inhibiting the histone demethylase KDM5a (see related Research Article by Jin et al. ).

articles.title: Nuclear NAD+ promotes innate immune memory by inhibiting KDM5A-dependent histone demethylation
articles.abstract: Trained immunity is tightly regulated by metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, yet how these changes are orchestrated at the chromatin level to establish long-term innate immune memory is not fully understood. Here, we show that induction of trained immunity elevates nuclear levels of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ), which directly binds to KDM5A demethylase and inhibits its activity, thereby sustaining H3K4me3 (histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation) levels and chromatin accessibility at inflammatory gene promoters to enhance “memory” responsiveness upon restimulation. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), the rate-limiting enzyme for NAD + synthesis, impaired trained immunity and associated antitumor activity. Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) supplementation rescued defective trained immunity–mediated antitumor activity in NAMPT-deficient and aged mice. In human cancer, NAMPT expression in myeloid cells correlated with an inflammatory tumor microenvironment. Our findings identify KDM5A as a nuclear NAD + sensor that orchestrates histone methylation and chromatin accessibility required for trained immunity.

articles.title: ERIS2: A deep-learning platform for predicting mutation-induced protein stability changes
articles.abstract: Ekambaram et al. present ERIS2, a deep learning framework that combines protein language model embeddings with structural features to predict how single mutations alter protein stability. Trained on large-scale experimental data, ERIS2 generalizes to blind benchmarks and is freely available as a web server for protein engineering and design.

articles.title: George Proud
articles.abstract: bmj;395/oct30_12/e101175/F1F1f1Initially having qualified in dentistry but changing to medicine, George decided to pursue a career as a maxillofacial surgeon. As no training posts were available, he changed to vascular surgery. He undertook basic surgical training at the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. He was awarded a Hunterian professorship by the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) and the prestigious Jacksonian prize for his research on blood transfusion and transplantation, the subject of his MD thesis. He was a skilled vascular surgeon, joined the transplant team, and was involved in a support group for transplant patients.George had a kindly manner towards patients and staff and was well respected. He was heavily involved in teaching and training and was the regional adviser on surgery for the RCS in London. He opened the first RCS provincial office in Newcastle in 1995. He was much involved in examining trainee surgeons, both in the UK and...

articles.title: Healthwatch: Plans to abolish patient watchdog are scrapped in government U turn
articles.abstract: Ministers have scrapped plans to abolish Healthwatch England and local Healthwatch groups, after pushback from health leaders and organisations.Launched in 2012, Healthwatch functions as a statutory independent voice for patients, helping the public hold the NHS accountable and push for patient centred improvements.Plans to abolish the Healthwatch network, consisting of 153 local groups and the national body Healthwatch England, were introduced as part of the Health Bill in May,1 amid wider governmental efforts to “simplify the patient safety landscape” of the NHS.It was proposed that the functions of the local Healthwatch organisations would be transferred to NHS integrated care boards, while the role of Healthwatch England would be transferred to the Department of Health and Social Care.2 This would mean an increased reliance on the NHS App for patient feedback. But critics warned that a loss of independence would have led to “health and care services marking their own homework.”Now,...

articles.title: Rama Shanker Singh
articles.abstract: bmj;395/oct30_11/e101174/F1F1f1Rama (known to many of his UK colleagues as “Ron”) was born in Bihar, India, in 1949. His father was an acclaimed general surgeon and, after Rama’s mother died suddenly, he was raised by his beloved second mother, a nurse. The eldest of four siblings, he was raised in Patna, a historic city on the banks of the Ganges. There he attended St Xavier School before transferring to Darbhanga for further college. In his teens he developed a lifelong passion for cinema and at one stage was keen to be an actor himself, before deciding to devote his life to medicine.He graduated from Darbhanga Medical College, Bihar, in 1972. He obtained his masters in general surgery in 1976 and moved to the UK in 1979. He worked in various hospitals and was subsequently appointed as a consultant in emergency medicine at Withybush General Hospital in Wales. From there he moved...

articles.title: Thousands of patients automatically deleted from electronic referral service, watchdog warns
articles.abstract: Patients waiting for specialist care were dropped off the electronic referral service (e-RS) without warning, a national safety watchdog has warned.A Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) report earlier this month found that from February to July 2026 over 120 000 referrals, including advice and guidance requests and referrals for review, disappeared from the e-RS.1The watchdog warned that these disappearances came to light only after GPs raised the alarm that patients had not heard from a provider about their referrals and otherwise might have been missed.The HSSIB’s report found no evidence of patients being harmed because of these referral disappearances. However, it acknowledged concerns that some patients could have avoided invasive treatment had they been seen earlier.The e-RS is a web based digital platform supplied by NHS England for referring patients to specialist providers.Responding to the HSSIB’s report, NHS England said that the e-RS was not designed for current referral...

articles.title: [Comment] Governing artificial intelligence for reliable research
articles.abstract: The report, Open Science and the Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Exchange: Policy Options for Reliable Research,1 published in October, 2026, was commissioned by the European Parliament's Panel for the Future of Science and Technology at a crucial moment for research. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how knowledge is created2 as AI systems are increasingly integrated across many stages of the research lifecycle.3 These methodological and epistemological challenges are leading to AI capabilities that now outpace human verification, transforming scientific disciplines faster than researchers or current governance can respond.

articles.title: 2026 ESMO Congress
Brazil improves access to cancer screening and care
India caps price of 137 cancer drugs
WHO releases framework for expanding access to early breast cancer care
A roadmap for quantifying metabolism in patients with cancer
articles.abstract: Advancements in in vivo stable isotope tracing have revolutionized our understanding of cancer metabolism, transitioning the field from static metabolomic snapshots to dynamic metabolic pathway activities. However, interpreting raw fractional enrichment data presents significant biological and analytical challenges. This review systematically examines the methodological landscape of in vivo tracing, addressing the interpretive gap created by clinical constraints, such as single-timepoint surgical sampling. We dissect how secondary circulating tracers and the inherent heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment can confound metabolic signals. We highlight the critical transition to metabolic flux analysis as the requisite computational step to overcome these challenges and to identify targetable metabolic vulnerabilities in precision oncology.

articles.title: Navigating clinical decisions through cancer cartography
articles.abstract: Multiplexed spatial profiling has shown that tumor architecture influences therapy response, yet few spatial phenotypes are in clinical use. We opine that the immediate priority is simplification and validation of complex spatial features. We draw a parallel to cartography: maps are useful because they carry a limited set of named features whose meaning is agreed. Tumor maps could be built the same way: from the presence of a defined cell type, its proximity to another, its location within a tissue compartment, its state of activation, or combinations of these. Such features may have more clinical applicability than variable, unsupervised two-dimensional ‘neighborhoods’. We propose cancer cartography as the process of assembling such validated features into tumor maps that guide treatment selection.

articles.title: Trends at 50: a mission that matters
articles.abstract: What makes a great review article in your field? As more research is published every day, it has become increasingly difficult to keep up with the latest developments and to ensure that you are hearing from the leading scientists driving these innovations and advances. How do you know what is new and what is valuable?

articles.title: Ultrastructure of multiciliated cell basal bodies revealed by expansion microscopy
articles.abstract: van Grinsven et al. combine tenfold expansion microscopy with a volumetric fluorescence averaging tool to map the human airway basal body at nanoscale resolution. They resolve the 3D organization of more than 20 proteins and assess the function of a subset of proteins in the organization of the apical microtubule network.

articles.title: Hydrogen bonds in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
articles.abstract: The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) can convert CO2 into value-added chemicals, but its efficiency and selectivity are limited by the thermodynamic stability of CO2 and competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). hydrogen bonding offers a design strategy beyond direct metal-site modification by stabilizing CO2-derived intermediates and mediating proton transfer. In homogeneous catalysts, hydrogen bonding units in the molecular outer sphere stabilize metal-bound intermediates and guide protonation pathways. In heterogeneous systems, analogous functions are implemented at solid–liquid interfaces, where catalyst-surface modification alters the stability of surface-bound intermediates and regulates proton transport pathways. This review highlights hydrogen bonding as a shared design element that bridges molecular precision and interfacial regulation in CO2RR catalysis, identifying common design requirements for balancing intermediate stabilization, proton delivery, and HER suppression.

articles.title: How do we know when invasive species control strategies work?
articles.abstract: Controlling invasive species is costly and difficult but can have major ecological, economic, and health benefits. Researchers commonly compare the efficacy of specific control methods. However, invasive species control programs vary greatly in overarching goals and often occur over large areas, long timeframes, and varied environmental and social contexts. The success of these programs likely hinges on factors including organizational structures, concurrent restoration activities, geographic and temporal scope of control, and the invasive species’ biology. To enable assessment of the relative influence of these common features, we propose clearer definitions of success in invasive species control and explicit comparisons among control programs. Post hoc assessment of existing programs’ success will complement system-specific studies to guide strategies that work in real-world situations.

articles.title: Compensation of hyperexcitability with simulation-based inference
articles.abstract: The activity of healthy neuronal networks is tightly regulated, and a shift toward hyperexcitability can cause various problems, such as epilepsies, memory deficits, and motor disorders. Numerous cellular, synaptic, and intrinsic mechanisms of hyperexcitability and compensatory mechanisms to restore healthy activity have been proposed. However, quantifying multiple compensatory mechanisms and their dependence on specific pathophysiological mechanisms has proven challenging, even in computational models. We use simulation-based inference to quantify the interactions of putative compensatory mechanisms in a spiking neuronal network model. Various parameters of the model can compensate for the changes in other parameters to maintain baseline activity, and we estimated their compensatory potential. Furthermore, specific causes of hyperexcitability – interneuron loss, excitatory recurrent synapses, and principal cell depolarization – have distinct compensatory mechanisms that can restore normal excitability. Our results show that spiking neuronal network simulators could generate hypotheses about the mechanisms of pathophysiological network mechanisms.

articles.title: Distinct gradients of cortical architecture capture visual representations and behavior across the lifespan
articles.abstract: The microstructure of cells within the human cerebral cortex varies across the cortical ribbon, where changes in cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture are thought to endow each region of the cortex with its unique function. While fine-scale relative to a cell, these changes at the population level impact architectural properties of the cortex measurable in vivo by noninvasive MRI, such as the thickness and myelin content of the cortex. This raises the question of whether or not we can use these in vivo architectural measures to understand cortical organization, function, and development more broadly. Using the human visual cortex as a test bed, we demonstrated two architectural gradients, one in which cytoarchitecture and myeloarchitecture converge and another in which they diverge. These two gradients underlie the structural and functional topography of the visual cortex, even predicting the presence of new visual representations. Moreover, the two gradients show distinct visual behavior relevance and lifespan trajectory. These findings provide a more general framework for understanding the human cortex, showing that architectural gradients are a measurable fingerprint of functional organization and ontogenetic routines in the human brain.

articles.title: Fitness level, but not sex, affects exercise-induced pain modulation
articles.abstract: In a previous study by our group (Nold et al., 2025), we investigated exercise-induced pain modulation after high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise in a heterogeneous sample of diverse fitness levels. Exploratory analyses suggested an interaction of sex, fitness level, and drug treatment, indicating that males showed increasing hypoalgesia after high- compared to low-intensity exercise with increasing fitness levels, which was diminished when naloxone was administered. In contrast, these effects were not evident in females. These exploratory findings warranted further investigation to determine if and to what extent exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level and/or sex. In this current study, we investigated an all-female sample (N=21) of high fitness levels using a similar paradigm as in the previous study, comparing heat and pressure pain ratings after high-intensity and low-intensity exercise. Our data show an interaction of exercise intensity and stimulus intensity in heat pain, with greater pain relief following high-intensity exercise, especially at the highest stimulus intensity. Despite results for pressure pain not reaching significance, a similar trend was evident. These results suggest that females at a high fitness level also show exercise-induced pain modulation for high-intensity compared to low-intensity exercise. Furthermore, we pooled the data of the current and previous study, providing evidence for fitness level but not sex to moderate exercise-induced pain modulation in heat pain. These findings suggest that exercise-induced pain modulation depends on fitness level but not on sex.

articles.title: Glutamate receptor composition at Drosophila neuromuscular junctions depends on developmental stage and muscle identity
articles.abstract: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) of larval Drosophila is widely used for studying synaptic transmission. Larval body wall muscles express five ionotropic glutamate receptor (iGluR) subunits that assemble into two tetrameric complexes, with subunit composition determining the strength and plasticity of synaptic transmission. Because NMJ function has been extensively characterized in larvae, it has commonly been assumed that adult fly NMJs share this molecular composition, despite substantial differences between life stages. Here, we systematically compare glutamate receptor expression across larval and adult Drosophila muscles. We find that adult leg and flight muscles exhibit different iGluR expression than larvae, lacking expression of several receptors previously considered essential. Adjacent muscles within the adult femur express distinct iGluRs, suggesting specialization of flexor and extensor muscles. Finally, the glutamate-gated chloride channel (GluClα) is expressed extrasynaptically in adult but not larval muscle fibers. Our results reveal unexpected heterogeneity in glutamate receptor expression across muscles and developmental stages, demonstrating the need for muscle-specific analyses in flies and other animals.

articles.title: Oxytocin neurons signal state-dependent transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal
articles.abstract: Core body temperature (Tb) is defended within narrow limits through thermoregulatory behaviors like huddling, nesting, and physical activity, as well as autonomic responses like brown fat thermogenesis. While Tb displays regulated fluctuations across different behavioral states and rest/arousal cycles, the neural control of these transitions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relationship between oxytocin neurons of the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVNOT) and behavioral and autonomic thermoeffector pathways across physiological states in mice. First, we show that PVNOT neurons are activated during social thermoregulation. We then demonstrate that in vivo PVNOT calcium dynamics align with transitions from rest to thermogenesis and behavioral arousal. Counter to our initial hypothesis, these dynamics were observed in both social and non-social contexts. Using a computer vision model to track thermoeffector pathways, we demonstrate that precisely timed stimulation of PVNOT neurons during low-Tb resting states increases thermogenesis followed by behavioral arousal. We therefore suggest a model in which PVNOT neurons facilitate homeostatic state-dependent transitions in thermo-behavioral states.

articles.title: SVEP1 enables efficient binding of angiopoietin-2 to the TIE1 receptor, allowing receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling
articles.abstract: The molecular mechanisms that drive (lymph-)angiogenesis are crucial to understanding diseases, such as lymphedema, that are caused due to malformations of the lymphatic vasculature. Recently, an interaction between the secreted protein Svep1, a key regulator in lymphangiogenesis, and the transmembrane receptor Tie1 was shown in zebrafish, humans, and mice. Here, guided by in silico AlphaFold-multimer structure predictions of SVEP1 complexes, we assert with protein binding studies that the human CCP20 domain is the primary binding site for TIE1. We further demonstrate that SVEP1 mediates strong binding of ANG2 and TIE1, and that combined stimulation of hdLECs with SVEP1 and ANG2 leads to phosphorylation of TIE1. TIE1 activation by SVEP1 and ANG2 enables downstream signaling and, in turn, potentiates nuclear exclusion of FOXO1 and phosphorylation of AKT compared to SVEP1 or ANG2 alone. We present a model in which ANG1/2 dimers bind to both SVEP1 and TIE1, resulting in the recruitment of multiple TIE1 receptor molecules to a multimeric complex at the cell membrane, potentially amplifying its signaling capacity.

articles.title: Predictive Design Principles for Plasma-Catalysis
articles.abstract: Centralized production of fuels and commodity chemicals emits 1.4–2 Gt CO2 yr–1 and depends on fossil-fuel supply chains that prevent distributed deployment. Nonthermal plasmas offer a path to decentralized, electrified production by generating vibrationally excited molecules, radicals, and ions without bulk heating of gas. Despite this potential, plasma-catalysis remains difficult to design because plasma excitation, surface reaction energetics, and intermediate removal are treated separately, and activity trends do not transfer across chemistries. This perspective develops a quantitative framework connecting nonequilibrium excitation, surface binding energetics, coreactant chemistry, and surface temperature to reaction rates, selectivity, and catalyst stability. Reactions are classified into three kinetic regimes by the balance between intermediate supply and removal rates, each with distinct rate-controlling steps and deactivation modes. Design tools and principles derived from this classification are applied to four example case studies that transfer across chemistries without reparameterization and provide a basis for reactor design at scale.

articles.abstract: Spatial profiles along the Rh monolith and in situ DRIFTS show NH 3 first oxidizes to NO, which is then reduced by residual NH 3 via the internal SCR pathway. Product selectivity is governed by both temperature and O 2 availability.

articles.abstract: Despite its potential as an attractive alternative for renewable energy transport, catalytic ammonia decomposition faces several challenges before it can be established as a viable hydrogen (H 2 ) carrier technology.

articles.title: Genetic coupling of floral rewards and signals underlies pollinator attraction
articles.abstract: Floral rewards and signals must be coordinated to attract pollinators, but the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Using melon as a model system, this study reveals how the developmental regulator YAB5 coordinates nectar production, flower opening, and floral signals to promote bee visitation.

articles.title: Innate sensor responses set a supra-unitary threshold for viral replication
articles.abstract: Single-cell analysis reveals that viral replication requires a supra-unitary input of viral genomes, which varies with different viruses and cell types. We show that supra-unitary viral genome quantities, independently of viral protein synthesis, activate negative feedback regulators of RIG-I, MDA-5, and PKR, suppressing the innate immune response and allowing replication.

articles.title: Microbial products trigger chemosensory dialogues through intestinal G protein-coupled receptors
articles.abstract: Kadoki et al. developed GPCR-seq, a high-throughput platform to identify how the gut senses environmental chemicals. They discovered gut microbial products that activate intestinal receptors, triggering serotonin release or linking to inflammatory bowel disease. This work provides a scalable template for decoding how host-microbe communication influences human health.

articles.title: Interpretable deep learning maps spatial morphological phenotypes to HCC and LUAD survival
articles.abstract: Liu et al. present MorphX, an interpretable deep learning framework that decodes cancer prognosis from whole-slide histological images and reveals morphological biomarkers. Across independent cohorts, MorphX identifies eight morphology-based biomarkers, supporting trustworthy, transparent, AI-driven precision oncology.

Selective depletion of these cells by uPAR CAR T cells remodels the dystrophic muscle niche, restores muscle regeneration, and improves limb and respiratory muscle function in preclinical murine models of DMD.

articles.title: Frontier Orbital Engineering of the Oxide Photocatalyst K2Zn2Nb4O13 by Coupling Crystal Structure, Electronic Structure, and Chemical Bonding
articles.abstract: Rational design of oxide photocatalysts with intrinsically efficient bulk carrier transport remains a major challenge because carrier migration is strongly governed by the complex interplay among crystal structure, electronic structure, and chemical bonding. Here, we propose a Frontier orbital engineering strategy to regulate intrinsic carrier transport by reconstructing the Frontier orbital composition within a structurally robust oxide framework. Based on the tunnel-type Na2Ti6O13 structure, the oxide semiconductor K2Zn2Nb4O13 was designed and synthesized through the cooperative substitution of Ti4+ by Zn2+/Nb5+. Combined high-resolution PXRD and NPD refinements confirm the successful realization of the designed tunnel framework with complete Zn/Nb ordering. Orbital-resolved electronic structure and chemical bonding analyses demonstrate that the valence band maximum (VBM) and conduction band minimum (CBM) are mainly derived from Zn 3d−O 2p and Nb1 4d−O 2p antibonding orbitals, respectively. Such orbital decoupling of Frontier orbital contributing units and the continuous covalent networks along the b-axis provide favorable pathways for bulk carrier migration and establish the structural and electronic basis for the proposed Frontier orbital engineering strategy. Experimentally, Pd-loaded K2Zn2Nb4O13 exhibits enhanced photocatalytic H2 generation activity, achieving a rate of 119(3) μmol/h. This work provides Frontier orbital engineering as a design paradigm for functional materials, enabling the rational manipulation of intrinsic charge transport properties through the synergistic regulation of crystal structure, electronic structure, and chemical bonding.

articles.title: High Temperature Stable Pt Nanoclusters Formation in Alumina-Encapsulated Pt Catalysts
articles.abstract: Metal nanoparticle sintering in high-temperature oxidizing atmospheres remains a primary deactivation pathway for platinum-group metal catalysts on alumina supports. Here, atomic layer deposition (ALD) was used to deposit alumina on supported Pt catalysts and develop alumina-encapsulated Pt/Al2O3 catalysts that were aged at 800 °C under different atmospheres and characterized by time-resolved high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM), CO-probe diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (CO-DRIFTS), and propene combustion kinetics. Within the alumina-encapsulated system, a sub-2 nm Pt cluster population formed under all oxidizing atmospheres tested but not under inert atmosphere, and this population persisted for at least 12 h at 800 °C under propene complete combustion (PCC) conditions. Unencapsulated Pt/Al2O3 controls, by contrast, developed only a transient sub-2 nm population, detected within 1 min of aging in air at 800 °C and no longer present afterward, consistent with the rapid disappearance of small particles predicted by Ostwald ripening theory. CO-DRIFTS confirmed the presence of undercoordinated Pt surface sites in all oxidatively aged samples, with no detectable signal when the sample was aged under inert atmosphere. Propene combustion rates measured after aging for an alumina-encapsulated catalyst were approximately two and five times higher than the fresh encapsulated catalyst for catalysts aged under inert atmosphere and under oxygen and steam, respectively. DFT calculations of Pt diffusion through defective Al2O3 identified kinetically accessible diffusion pathways at 800 °C, with activation barriers as low as 0.76 eV. Furthermore, Pt surface binding was calculated to be favored in the presence of O2. These results identify oxygen-driven surface segregation, mediated by defect-assisted diffusion through the ALD overcoat, as a possible mechanism responsible for nanocluster formation in this system. The persistence of the sub-2 nm cluster population for at least 12 h at 800 °C under PCC conditions demonstrates the thermal stability of these sites within the encapsulated architecture.

articles.title: Switching the Ordering Pattern of Bi2Rh4 Breathing Distortion by Isovalent Chalcogen Substitution in Bi2Rh3 X 2 ( X = Se, S)
articles.abstract: Layered inorganic materials can exhibit symmetry-breaking transitions in which electronic instabilities and local structural modes are strongly intertwined. Here we compare the isovalent chalcogenides Bi2Rh3Se2 and Bi2Rh3S2 by synchrotron single-crystal X-ray diffraction and density-functional-theory calculations, and identify a static Bi2Rh4 breathing distortion as the common local motif underlying their distinct low-temperature phases. In Bi2Rh3Se2, the transition near 240 K is characterized by the loss of C-centering without a change in the conventional unit-cell volume. The resulting primitive lattice contains inequivalent Rh4 quadrilaterals formed by alternating expansion and contraction, establishing a C-centering-breaking breathing order. Although previous spectroscopic studies have reported CDW-like signatures in Bi2Rh3Se2, the calculated Fermi surfaces of the high-temperature phase do not reveal an obvious nesting vector expected for a simple nesting-driven Peierls-type CDW scenario. Instead, the Rh 4d-derived electronic states at the Fermi level are naturally sensitive to the observed Rh4 breathing distortion, indicating that the transition is best described as a breathing-order transition accompanied by electronic reconstruction. In Bi2Rh3S2, a comparable Bi2Rh4 breathing distortion appears, but its ordering pattern is switched: when described in the high-temperature-cell setting, the Bi2Rh4 units form a large−small−small sequence along the aHT-direction, accompanied by an antiphase relation between neighboring chains, producing a commensurate 3× superstructure consistent with the first-order character of the transition. Calculations based on the experimentally refined structures further reveal a reduction of the density of states near EF and an anisotropic redistribution of occupied low-energy states in the breathing-distorted phases, supporting the coupling between the Bi2Rh4 motif and electronic reconstruction. These results show that isovalent chalcogen substitution selects the in-plane ordering pattern of an intrinsic Bi2Rh4 breathing distortion, thereby switching the collective symmetry-breaking pathway and associated electronic response.

articles.title: Synthesis of fcc/2H and f cc /4H Copper Nanodisks Towards Carbon Dioxide Reduction
articles.abstract: Two-dimensional Cu nanostructures containing noncanonical face-centered cubic/hexagonal close-packed (fcc/hcp) heterophase boundaries are attractive for CO2 electroreduction but remain difficult to prepare by wet-chemical methods. Here, we report a high-temperature solution reduction route to Cu nanodisks with a thickness of 26.5 ± 2.3 nm and a diameter of 85.6 ± 3.7 nm. Transmission electron microscopy reveals abundant fcc/2H and fcc/4H interfaces on the nanodisk side surfaces, where the 2H and 4H polytypes exhibit AB and ABCB stacking, respectively. In CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3, the nanodisks achieve a methane Faradaic efficiency of 60.4% at −1.25 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode and outperform fcc Cu nanoparticle and microsheet controls tested at the same catalyst loading. Density functional theory calculations indicate that the free-energy penalty for forming the *CHO intermediate is smaller on the fcc/2H and fcc/4H models than on fcc Cu. These results support a thermodynamic contribution of heterophase interfaces to the observed methane selectivity; the calculations do not establish a reduction in kinetic activation barriers. This solution-phase route therefore provides access to phase-engineered Cu nanodisks and enables structure−property relationships relevant to CO2-to-CH4 electrocatalysis.

articles.title: Reducing whale–vessel strikes through multiobjective vessel traffic routing
articles.abstract: Vessel strikes threaten many large whale species. Managers employ several mitigation measures to reduce vessel strike risk, including establishing or modifying vessel routing measures, such as shipping lanes. However, most studies utilized to inform the configuration of shipping lanes only consider a limited number of potential lanes, and in many cases, the criteria used to generate the lanes are unclear. We developed an approach to design, modify, or evaluate shipping lanes that involves clearly defining the objectives of the lanes and using the k least‐cost path (KLCP) algorithm, which identifies the KLCPs between two points on a cost surface, to identify all lanes that meet the objectives. We applied our approach to evaluate recommended shipping lanes in Cape Cod Bay, Massachusetts (United States), and off the Atlantic Coast of the southeastern United States with respect to the risk of vessel strikes to North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) and the time it takes vessels to travel the lanes. We identified all lanes with a risk of right whale strikes and a travel time less than or equal to that of the recommended lanes using the KLCP algorithm. In most cases, the lanes identified had similar spatial configurations to the recommended lanes and reduced the risk of strikes by <15%, which indicates that the existing recommended lanes are adequately, but not optimally, designed to reduce strike risk and travel time relative to potential alternative lanes. Our approach applying the KLCP algorithm provides a thorough, objective, and transparent way to identify vessel routing configurations that minimize whale–vessel strikes and meet other objectives. Reducción de las colisiones entre ballenas y embarcaciones mediante la planificación de rutas de tráfico marítimo con múltiples objetivos Resumen Las colisiones con embarcaciones suponen una amenaza para muchas especies de ballenas de gran tamaño. Los responsables aplican diversas medidas de mitigación para reducir el riesgo de la colisión, entre ellas el establecimiento o la modificación de medidas de trazado de rutas marítimas, como las rutas de navegación. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los estudios utilizados para definir la configuración de las rutas de navegación solo tienen en cuenta un número limitado de rutas potenciales y, en muchos casos, los criterios empleados para generarlas no están claros. Desarrollamos un enfoque para diseñar, modificar o evaluar rutas marítimas que consiste en definir claramente los objetivos de las mismas y utilizar el algoritmo k de las rutas de menor coste (KLCP), que identifica las KLCP entre dos puntos en una superficie de costos, con el fin de determinar todas las rutas que cumplen dichos objetivos. Aplicamos nuestro enfoque para evaluar las rutas marítimas recomendadas en la bahía de Cape Cod, en Massachusetts (Estados Unidos), y frente a la costa atlántica del sureste de Estados Unidos, con la consideración del riesgo de colisiones de buques con las ballenas francas del Atlántico Norte (Eubaleana glacialis) y el tiempo que tardan los buques en recorrer dichas rutas. Identificamos todas las rutas con riesgo de colisiones con ballenas francas y un tiempo de travesía inferior o igual al de las rutas recomendadas utilizando el algoritmo KLCP. En la mayoría de los casos, las rutas identificadas presentaban configuraciones espaciales similares a las de las rutas recomendadas y reducían el riesgo de colisiones en menos del 15%, lo que indica que las rutas recomendadas existentes están diseñadas de forma adecuada, aunque no óptima, para reducir el riesgo de colisiones y el tiempo de travesía en comparación con posibles rutas alternativas. Nuestro enfoque, basado en la aplicación del algoritmo KLCP, ofrece una forma exhaustiva, objetiva y transparente de identificar configuraciones de rutas para buques que minimicen las colisiones entre ballenas y buques y cumplan otros objetivos.

articles.abstract: Atomically dispersed W activates terrace Mn sites in β-MnO 2 via W–O–Mn charge delocalization, increasing accessible-site density and boosting OER sixfold. Strong W–O bonds suppress Mn dissolution, enabling stable operation for 1250 h at 300 mA cm −2 .

Prevalence, severity and factors exposing urban rock pigeons (Columba livia) to foot deformities in katima Mulilo, Namibia
articles.abstract: Urban environments expose wildlife to anthropogenic hazards, including materials capable of causing physical injuries. Among urban birds, the rock pigeon (Columba livia) is highly adapted to urban environments. However, frequent reports of digit entanglement and foot deformities in these environments suggest that urban conditions expose birds to foot injuries. Despite widespread observations of “string foot”, quantitative assessments of deformity prevalence and severity across urban land-use types remain limited, particularly within African cities. This study assessed the prevalence and severity of foot deformities in rock pigeons across three land-use zones in Katima Mulilo, Namibia: the Central Business District (CBD), market areas, and residential areas. A total of 300 pigeons were visually inspected during systematic field surveys. Foot deformities were recorded as present or absent and classified into three severity levels (mild, moderate, severe). Forty-six (15.3%) pigeons exhibited foot deformities. The prevalence of foot deformities varied significantly among land-use categories, with the highest recorded in the residential areas (22.5%), followed by the CBD (12.4%) and least in the market areas (10.4%). Moderate deformities were the most prevalent injury category (60.9%), followed by severe (23.9%) and mild deformities (15.2%). Pigeons observed in residential areas had significantly higher odds of deformities compared with those in the CBD (OR = 2.05, p = 0.044). Fibrous wastes, which constitute the important potential sources of entanglement hazard, were prevalent in the environment of pigeons. Results of this study suggest that foot injury in urban rock pigeons varied across land-use types and highlight the potential role of human-derived materials on pigeon health in urban areas. Targeted management of fibrous wastes in the CBD and residential areas is recommended to reduce entanglement-related foot deformities, with emphasis on improved local waste handling and disposal behavior.

articles.title: Global Change Is Reshaping Coral Communities and Threatening Reef Physical Functionality
articles.abstract: Coral reefs are undergoing profound compositional changes driven by climate change, disease, and chronic human disturbance. Coral cover is the primary metric used to track reef condition, but it often fails to capture the contributions of different coral species to reef carbonate production, structural complexity, and associated biodiversity. Here, I review evidence showing that global change disproportionately removes competitively dominant and architecturally complex corals, driving non‐random changes and coral community homogenisation. These changes erode reef functionality, even when overall cover is maintained. Species‐specific contributions to calcification and structural complexity span orders of magnitude, such that targeted losses of framework‐building taxa collapse carbonate budgets and habitat architecture in ways not predictable from cover trends. These structural changes cascade through associated communities, undermining functional diversity and the ecosystem processes on which reef resilience depends. Critically, rebounds in coral cover frequently reflect the colonisation by fast‐growing opportunistic species, which yield slow or absent recovery of physical functionality, while reassembly and the re‐establishment of large, structurally complex colonies (and the physical functionality they provide) might lag by decades. Furthermore, as mass disturbance events occur at ever‐shorter intervals, recovery windows close before reef‐building potential and complexity can be fully restored. Monitoring, management, and restoration should therefore focus on trait‐ and species‐explicit assessments that prioritise protection and restoration of keystone reef‐builders, target sites with high functional potential, and reduce stressors at appropriate scales. Integrating functional metrics into policy and restoration planning is essential to safeguard reef geomorphic and ecological services under continued global change.

articles.title: Growth factor VEGF-B sustains intestinal Tfh cell stemness to restrict Taurinivorans outgrowth and microbiota-driven obesity
articles.abstract: Zhou et al. show VEGFR-1 signaling in intestinal Tfh cells is essential for immune surveillance. Its loss impairs IgA immunity, allowing a gut bacterium to deplete taurine, impair fat burning, and drive obesity. Restoring this axis offers an immune-based strategy for metabolic disorders.

articles.title: Reporting guidelines of stretchable solar cells toward standardized evaluation
articles.abstract: Stretchable solar cells could energize portable and wearable electronics, yet their efficiency and mechanical durability are measured under conditions so divergent that devices of comparable initial performance defy cross-laboratory comparison. Ye and colleagues trace this divergence to routinely overlooked factors, among them substrate properties, strain rate, and strain-induced changes in illuminated area. They introduce metrics for tolerable strain and cycle lifetime, together with a reporting checklist, establishing a shared benchmark for the field and a path to formal standardization.
